bad-lieutenant-tokyo.title: Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo
bad-lieutenant-tokyo.synopsis:
A dizzyingly prolific auteur who never fails to imprint his signature on every project he undertakes, Japanese maestro Takashi Miike (TIFF ’01’s Ichi the Killer) returns to the Festival with this thrilling contribution to a one-of-a-kind cinema legacy. Like Abel Ferrara’s cult masterpiece Bad Lieutenant (TIFF ’92) and Werner Herzog’s gonzo Southern neo-noir Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call — New Orleans (TIFF ’09), Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is very much its own entity, not so much a sequel to its predecessors as a mood, a variation on shared themes, and a rollercoaster ride through the darkest crevasses of the Tokyo underworld.

The bad lieutenant this time around is a hardened, gambling-addicted Tokyo Metropolitan police officer (Godzilla vs. Kong’s Shun Oguri), who finds himself being investigated by the FBI after a politician's daughter (Liv Morgan) goes missing. The bad lieutenant and the FBI agent (Lily James, Swiped, TIFF ’25) must collaborate to find the missing woman — while, unbeknownst to them, a crazed killer monitors their every move.

Written by veteran screenwriter Daisuke Tengan, whose credits include Miike's international smash 13 Assassins (TIFF ’10), Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is an intricately plotted crime odyssey teeming with bizarre twists and unforgettable characters. Miike commandeers this wild ride with a characteristic blend of dynamic storytelling and shameless sensationalism. Whether coming as a fan of the Bad Lieutenant brand or of Miike's singular body of work, you will not be disappointed.
bad-lieutenant-tokyo.teaser: The latest from prolific maestro Takashi Miike, like Abel Ferrara’s Bad Lieutenant (TIFF ’92) and Werner Herzog’s Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call — New Orleans (TIFF ’09), is a sensational ride through the darkest crevasses of the criminal underworld.

black-sunflowers.title: Black Sunflowers
black-sunflowers.synopsis:
Black Sunflowers immerses us in the lives of twentysomething Ukrainians as they come of age during wartime. The film embodies a youthful spirit as it shifts between eclectic settings, from an underground dance club to a frontline barracks to a countryside swimming hole. We get to experience this generation in all its complexity as people grapple with tragedy, duty, disillusionment, and yearning for a better future.

“These soldiers never wanted to be soldiers,” says Nikoletta, a 21-year-old who had to switch her photography studies from nature to combat. She’s one of several distinctive figures in this mosaic. Another is Vania, a soldier, whose hobby is the illicit car sport of “drifting”: that is, screeching down city streets like a Grand Prix racer. His fellow drifter Zhenia has so far avoided the military, but feels the pressures of the compulsory draft age set at 25.

The American filmmaker James Marcus Haney teams with an esteemed crew of Ukrainian producers including Volodymyr Yatsenko (behind last year’s TIFF Platform winner To the Victory!). Haney is a gifted visualist known for working with musicians such as Mumford & Sons, Elton John, and Coldplay. He first visited Ukraine to film for an NGO. “I was surprised to see how much normal life carried on, despite the war,” he wrote in a director’s statement. “I couldn’t help but think that mainstream media is missing half of the story.”

Wartime films can often feel didactic or of the moment. Black Sunflowers strives to be more tiered and timeless.
black-sunflowers.teaser: Black Sunflowers is a mosaic of Ukrainian youth, shuttling between the frontlines and civilian life, captured by the gifted American filmmaker James Marcus Haney (No Cameras Allowed) collaborating with an esteemed Ukrainian crew.

bucking-fastard.title: Bucking Fastard
bucking-fastard.synopsis:
Filmmaker Werner Herzog is renowned for stories about highly unique characters. With Bucking Fastard, he tells the tale of sisters Jean and Joan Holbrooke, played by real-life siblings Rooney Mara (Women Talking, TIFF ’22) and Kate Mara (Friendship, TIFF ’24).

The Holbrookes speak in unison, dress alike, have shared dreams, and, consequentially, fall in love with the same man (Orlando Bloom, The Cut, TIFF ’24). The sisters’ obsession with their lover reaches a boiling point which ultimately must be resolved in court. Jean and Joan passionately defend themselves side by side as they have their whole lives, showing their unusual bond. A media frenzy, driven by the sisters’ strange and inextricably bound lives, inevitably ensues.

Hoping to escape the scrutiny of the trial and their heartache, the sisters seek various forms of refuge and encounter trials and tribulations along the way. Herzog conjures a fascinating and original story, bringing together the Mara sisters in one of their most captivating performances.
bucking-fastard.teaser: Director Werner Herzog and real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara enliven the story of siblings who speak as one, fall in love with the same person, and eventually spiral.

coward.title: Coward
coward.synopsis:
The opening scenes of Lukas Dhont’s extraordinary third feature introduce an array of newly minted Belgian soldiers in 1916. Like so many young men of the era, they initially approach the front lines not with a feeling of trepidation but a spirit of excitement and freshly forged camaraderie. Of course, the characters of Coward soon wake up to the First World War’s many horrors. Yet, traces of that brighter energy still persist in the uncommonly poignant love story at the film’s centre.

Among those new arrivals in the trenches is Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia), a taciturn farmboy who’s mostly content to blend into the background of his troop. That makes him very different from Francis (Valentin Campagne), the son of a tailor and the enthusiastic lead performer in the ad hoc revues that the most theatrically inclined soldiers stage for their comrades as a welcome distraction. The spark of attraction between the two men leads to another means of escaping the misery and tragedy that surrounds them.

Macchia and Campagne were the very deserving recipients of Best Actor honours from the jury when the film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May. Coward also marks a triumph for Dhont, who makes the shift to the much larger scale of a period drama without losing the sense of intimacy, specificity, and humanity that distinguished his Camera d’Or winner Girl (TIFF 2018) and Close (2022), which followed its own Cannes success with an Academy Award nomination. The grace, beauty, and tenderness that the director captures here all make Coward a film to be treasured.

Content: mature themes (war trauma), nudity, violence, sexual content (innuendo, sexually suggestive scenes)
coward.teaser: Belgian director Lukas Dhont’s poignant third feature celebrates a love that blooms amid the hardships and horrors of the First World War.

musk.title: Musk
musk.synopsis:
Elon Musk has amassed so much power, he’s like a character in a Marvel comic book. A short recap of his handiwork: Tesla popularized electric vehicles; Starlink expanded the reach of the internet; Twitter bowed to his takeover; and DOGE radically transformed the US government. Musk has been at the centre of AI development and this past summer, the IPO for SpaceX made him the richest man in the world. His influence arguably touches everyone on the planet. Surely this is worth fresh scrutiny.

After nearly four years of work, Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney delivers his most ambitious and epic documentary, seeking to understand the history and motivations of the ultimate tech bro. When this film was first announced, Musk immediately denounced it on Twitter and refused to participate. But that didn’t impede Gibney, who draws upon countless hours of interviews that Musk has given over the years. Even more revealingly, Gibney conducts new interviews with figures who have known Musk up close and personal, including the mogul’s father, Errol Musk.

The news cycle moves so fast, it’s hard to remember that Musk was once at home among liberals, with his companies promoting clean energy and invoicing the Obama administration for hundreds of millions in tech contracts. What drove him into the world of Donald Trump?

Musk frequently invokes science fiction stories and has coyly wondered aloud if we’re living in a video game–like simulation. Playing off this idea, Gibney leans visually into an innovative graphic treatment throughout the film. But make no mistake: this is really happening.
musk.teaser: The Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney delivers his most ambitious and epic work in exploring the history of the world’s richest man, Elon Musk.

rapinoe.title: Rapinoe
rapinoe.synopsis:
Megan Rapinoe gets a documentary treatment that’s as bold and original as her career. Her play making was crucial to the US women’s team that won two World Cups and an Olympic gold medal. Off the pitch, she’s been a trailblazer in calling out injustice when she sees it.

Rapinoe could have easily picked a safe director for a predictable portrait. Instead she handed editorial control to filmmaker Rebeca Huntt, known for her dazzling debut Beba (TIFF ’21). Huntt has a talent for decoding the family dynamics that forge character. Always playful, Rapinoe lays down on a couch as if she’s doing therapy. It’s a joke, but Huntt is catching Rapinoe at a deeply introspective moment as she ends her professional career and starts looking back.

Her journey has enough drama for multiple lives. Raised in a small, conservative town, she experienced both love and turmoil in her large working-class family. She came out as queer despite societal pressures to stay closeted. She was a standout in a generation of women players who elevated the sport. Then she used her voice to campaign for equal pay between men and women, setting a precedent that reverberated around the world.

We watch her grapple with what it means to win and lose under intense scrutiny. She counts success not only on the stat sheet, but also the hard-won victories in making peace with loved ones and herself. She redefines what it means to be a champion.
rapinoe.teaser: Soccer star Megan Rapinoe explores what it means to win and lose in this intimate portrait by Rebeca Huntt (Beba).

the-face-of-horror.title: The Face of Horror
the-face-of-horror.synopsis:
Perennially adapted since 1825, Tsuruya Nanboku IV’s Yotsuya Kaidan is Japan’s most famous ghost story. It describes a husband’s duplicitous betrayal of his wife, whose vengeful spirit returns to haunt him, and has long been appreciated for its feminist catharsis.

Now behold Anna Biller (The Love Witch) who deploys her consummate emulation of vintage aesthetics to concoct a wickedly camp yet insightful retelling of this morality tale. As The Face of Horror, this macabre trajectory is transposed to 14th-century feudal England where Biller cannily reflects the misogyny of a medieval milieu right back at our own, while stunningly fashioning a gory tribute to Technicolor shockers.

Jonah Hauer-King (William Tell, TIFF ’24) stars as Edward, a solipsistic knight errant who murderously schemes with his squire to seize a farmer’s estate by marrying the farmer’s daughter — quite literally over her father’s dead body. Blinded by grief and courtly love, the guileless Eleanor (Kristine Froseth, TIFF ’22’s How to Blow Up a Pipeline) accepts Edward’s hand, but it’s not long before the rogue’s insatiable libido pulls him towards more royal aspirations in the form of a wealthy countess (Bella Heathcote, TIFF ’17’s Professor Marston & the Wonder Women), and so yet another murder of convenience foments.

Shooting on sumptuous 35mm, Biller (who also designed the film’s vibrant costuming) achieves an extraordinary pastiche of bygone style and form that recalls Powell and Pressberger as much as Corman and Hammer. But it is her tonal tightrope walk that is most remarkable, as every aspect of the production is so precisely calibrated — from the pitch-perfect stylized performances to the brightly accented violence — that the sincerity of its underlying melodrama is never diluted by its pervasively wry wit.

Content advisory: suicide, self-harm, explicit violence, mature themes, sexual content
the-face-of-horror.teaser: The Love Witch’s Anna Biller stunningly adapts the famous Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan for 14th-century England in this gory tribute to classic Technicolor shockers.

edward-said-between-worlds.title: Edward Said: Between Worlds
edward-said-between-worlds.synopsis:
Edward Said had an unusual prominence as a public intellectual from his base at Columbia University. He wrote foundational texts such as Orientalism and The Question of Palestine, and frequently appeared on television to explain the Palestinian cause and battle willful distortions. When he died of leukemia in 2003 at age 67, the world lost a vital and complex thinker.

Edward Said: Between Worlds provides the opportunity to reengage that voice and share it with new generations, which feels as timely as I Am Not Your Negro was for James Baldwin. Filmmaker Maiken Baird teams with Palestinian-American producers Sarah Mowaswes and Razan Ghalayini along with the scholar’s daughter Najla Said as a consulting producer. They have combed the world’s archives to uncover hundreds of hours of interviews, public talks, and documentaries that capture Said in his prime. The film team skilfully braids these eclectic sources together to deliver a moving portrait in Said’s own words.

His life is a roadmap for the dilemmas that remain central to global politics today. Born in Palestine in 1935, he had firsthand experience of his family being uprooted by conflict. Said brings insights to historical flashpoints including the 1948 establishment of Israel and the subsequent dispossession of Palestinians known as the Nakba, and the 1993 Oslo Accords when he broke with the leadership of Yasser Arafat. He possessed a rare ability to move between the worlds of academia, mass media, and diplomacy, challenging preconceived notions every step of the way.
edward-said-between-worlds.teaser: Palestinian scholar Edward Said is profiled in his own words, drawing upon decades of archives, to explore the legacy of his groundbreaking works including Orientalism and The Question of Palestine.

the-ultra-runner.title: The Ultra Runner
the-ultra-runner.synopsis:
For Tiberiu Uşeriu, every step that he takes when competing in some of the world’s most gruelling sports events is part of a longer journey. Indeed, however astonishing it is to witness an exhausted, frost-bitten Uşeriu pushing forward for days without sleep and testing the limits of human endurance as an ultramarathon competitor, The Ultra Runner presents a life story that may be even more incredible.

Thankfully, viewers of director Mila Aung-Thwin’s superb documentary do not have to go out in the cold themselves to witness Uşeriu compete in the 6633 Arctic Ultra, an infamously brutal footrace across over 600 kilometres in the Canadian north. Along with riveting footage of the athlete weathering the subzero temperatures and trying to survive the race’s most punishing effects, Aung-Thwin’s film makes highly skilful and stylish use of re-enactments to convey key moments from Uşeriu’s difficult childhood in Romania and the downward spiral that led to a years-long stint for armed robbery in a high-security German prison. It’s there in the tight confines of a prison yard where Ușeriu began to find a way out of his darkness.

Vividly and compellingly captured in The Ultra Runner — which is itself a triumph for Aung-Thwin and Montreal’s EyeSteelFilm team — this extraordinary man’s process of rehabilitation provides a route not just to triumphs at events like the race across the Arctic. It also points a way toward the most profound joys of love, family, and human connection.
the-ultra-runner.teaser: Punishing tests of human endurance become a means of escaping past demons for the unforgettable subject of Mila Aung-Thwin’s superb new film.

union-town.title: Union Town
union-town.synopsis:
Union Town is an invigorating look at three crucial labour battles as they unfold in New York City during the past three years. They involve the workers of UPS, Amazon, and the deliveristas for the food apps DoorDash and GrubHub. Each group has slightly different battles, but by winding their stories together, we see a shared struggle. “This is going to be the most important battle for the next 25 years,” says Vinnie Perrone, President of the Teamsters Local 804 as he rallies UPS workers to brace themselves for a possible strike.

The film rounds out an extraordinary trilogy by director Barbara Kopple that started with her debut documentary about striking Appalachian mine workers, Harlan County, U.S.A (that played at the Festival in its first year). She returned to labor struggles for her second film American Dream, about meat packers in Minnesota. Both works demonstrated Kopple’s deep empathy for working people and her doggedness to follow the story wherever it goes.

In Union Town, she captures indelible portraits among the delivery workers who transport 2.4 million packages and 300,000 meals every day in New York City — no matter if the weather is blizzarding or blazing. Over the course of several years, Kopple follows three campaigns for better pay and conditions. Lined up in opposition are corporations that spend millions to bully and undermine the union efforts. The intimidation is fierce, but as one organizer reminds her comrades, “We shouldn’t be fearful of demanding what we deserve.” This film is a testament to their courage.
union-town.teaser: Barbara Kopple (TIFF ’76’s Harlan County, U.S.A.) looks at three crucial labour battles as they unfold in New York City involving workers from UPS, Amazon, and deliveristas for DoorDash and GrubHub.

fjord.title: Fjord
fjord.synopsis:
In the latest from masterful Cristian Mungiu (Graduation, TIFF ’16; R.M.N, TIFF ’22), Lisbet (Renate Reinsve, TIFF ’25’s Sentimental Value) and Mihai Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan, TIFF ’23’s Dumb Money) are a conservative Christian couple who’ve relocated from Romania to an isolated Norwegian town with their five children.

Unlike their new neighbours, the Gheorghius enforce daily bible study and don’t allow trappings like smartphones and YouTube. The family’s rigid beliefs cause a stir when one of the children is accused of introducing religious bias into their school by criticizing another student’s sexual orientation. This, however, is just the beginning of the family’s problems. When a teacher notices a bruise on another of their kids, a cascade of events — mimicking the avalanches we see behind the schoolyard in the icy locale — is set in motion.

Unlike her strong-willed husband, Lisbet, Norwegian by birth, is fluent in the local language and adept at navigating cultural nuances. Meanwhile, Mihai, steadfast in what he sees as his right to educate his offspring as he sees fit, admits to the occasional spanking. This triggers a storm of controversy — and is certain to evoke strong, varying opinions from viewers.

Winner of the prestigious Palme d'Or at Cannes, Fjord is an intricate, gripping courtroom drama driven by a profound moral dilemma, where private lives are laid bare for public scrutiny. Shot by frequent Mungiu collaborator Tudor Vladimir Panduru, the film marks a powerful return for the auteur whose 2007 masterpiece 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days helped launch the celebrated Romanian New Wave.
fjord.teaser: Winner of the prestigious Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, the latest from writer-director Cristian Mungiu is a gripping high-stakes courtroom drama driven by a profound moral dilemma.

look-back.title: Look Back
look-back.synopsis:
Look Back, adapted from manga creator Tatsuki Fujimoto’s acclaimed one-shot, is perhaps the author’s most personal — and arguably his finest — work. Beneath the spectacle and intensity that have come to define his shōnen manga, Look Back reveals the deep humanity that has always been at its heart.

First adapted as an animated feature by Kiyotaka Oshiyama (animator on TIFF ’23’s The Boy and the Heron), Look Back has found its way to the hands of visionary auteur Hirokazu Kore-eda (Monster, TIFF ’23), whose humanist sensibilities make him a natural fit for telling Fujimoto’s story in a live-action format.

Fourth-grader Fujino (Furi Nanase) is admired for the comics she makes for her school newspaper. Her world is upended when asked to share the space with her reclusive classmate Kyomoto (Rokka Okada), whose stunning artwork is better than anything she can make. When the girls finally meet, Fujino discovers Kyomoto has been idolizing her from afar all along. Her one-sided rivalry abates, and the two are pulled into an all-consuming love of drawing that carries them into adulthood as aspiring manga artists. The adult Fujino (Natsuki Deguchi) and Kyomoto (Aju Makita) embark on a shared journey where the joys of artistic expression collide with the unpredictability of life.

Shot entirely on 35mm and unfolding across the four seasons, Kore-eda imbues the story with an emotional intensity, following its characters with the same tenderness that has defined his own cinema. What emerges is a meditation on the purpose of creation itself: perhaps the only answer to life’s brevity is to create — a drawing, a story, a memory, a piece of ourselves.
look-back.teaser: Visionary auteur Hirokazu Kore-eda helms this tender and slow-burning adaptation of manga creator Tatsuki Fujimoto’s acclaimed story, following two young artists whose friendship and bond become the engine of their art.

arrested-memory.title: Arrested Memory
arrested-memory.synopsis:
A deliberate return to the poignant genre farces that defined writer-director SABU’s early career, Arrested Memory is a delightful confluence of his signature scenarios. Multi-pronged chases, mistaken/disordered identities, ruminations of guilt, dance numbers, the irreverent interventions of both incompetent police and hapless Yakuza — they’re all here. As is Shin’ichi Tsutsumi, who led SABU’s first five films from Dagan Runner to Drive, and is now among the many intimidating foils barking “baka” (idiot) at the filmmaker’s patented put-upon protagonist.

In the wake of a disastrous sting operation, veritable supercop Detective Lee (Ethan Juan) is hit with a medical diagnosis of onset memory loss that salts his already wounded spirit. But before anyone can be briefed on his condition, Lee is assigned to a new case and finds himself without a clue — both literally and figuratively.

Suddenly entrusted with a multimillion-dollar ransom for the son of a Japanese magnate (Tsutsumi) but with no recollection of either its source or intended recipient, Lee’s deteriorating mind soon propels him on a nocturnal odyssey. Pursued by both cops and crooks, the absent-minded officer must rely on his investigative instincts and martial prowess, as he is guided by an innate impulse to serve and protect, and that special comedic kismet that SABU so skilfully divines.

That Arrested Memory comes to us now on the 30th anniversary of SABU’s first feature marks a welcome opportunity to celebrate one of Japan’s most remarkable pulp-fiction practitioners, and to relish his latest rocambolesque romp of action, romance, and those fates that doth conspire.

Content advisory: suicide, self-harm, accident trauma, coarse language, drug use, violence
arrested-memory.teaser: A seasoned detective (Ethan Juan) recently diagnosed with dementia is doggedly pursued by both cops and crooks after he unwittingly wanders off with a multimillion-dollar ransom in a new absurdist crime caper from cult auteur SABU.

ladies-and-gentlemen-brian-mulroney.title: Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney
ladies-and-gentlemen-brian-mulroney.synopsis:
It may be hard to imagine a more perverse programming choice than a National Film Board documentary chronicling the rise of Brian Mulroney, Canada’s 18th prime minister, appearing in TIFF’s storied and sordid Midnight Madness section. Yet Matthew Rankin’s kaleidoscopic culture jam warrants such curatorial chaos, as the visionary filmmaker behind Universal Language (TIFF ’24) conjures an electric, retro-pop fever dream that mythologizes and scrutinizes the mutation of Canadian progressive conservatism as it was understood under John “Dief the Chief’ Diefenbaker to its contemporary, rightward, populist pathology — err, I mean ideology.

Through an episodic remix that transforms thousands of hours of archival footage, Rankin astutely tracks the political maneuvering that took place during the 1976 Progressive Conservative leadership convention and into the 1980s Canadian landscape right before Mulroney’s clinching the title of prime minister. Only he infuses this political soup with nostalgic intrusions of Canadian television and outlandish dramatizations, from Mulroney conferencing with a former PM’s pickled brain to Pierre Trudeau despotically ruling the country as a floating head like TRON’s Master Control Program. The result is reminiscent of Rankin’s debut feature, The Twentieth Century (TIFF ’19), which reimagined the ascension of William Lyon MacKenzie King as a German Expressionist farce, and especially his early collage work.

Culminating as if documentarian Adam Curtis overdosed on a psychic stream of Heritage Minutes, Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney is a dank, elucidative experiment that distills historical record through savvy psychedelic abstraction and satirical irreverence. If that ain’t Midnight Madness, then Téléfrançais!’s Ananas ain’t a talking pineapple.
ladies-and-gentlemen-brian-mulroney.teaser: This kaleidoscopic culture jam from visionary filmmaker Matthew Rankin (The Twentieth Century, Universal Language) details the rise of Canada’s 18th prime minister through a satirical collage of archival footage, television nostalgia, and national mythmaking.

drifter.title: Drifter
drifter.synopsis:
As an alumnus of the mighty Fast & Furious franchise, Sung Kang is no stranger to beautiful cars careening through seemingly impassable spaces — and igniting our dreams. With Drifter, Kang nods towards his hot-rod history while setting out on an entirely different sort of road, lighting upon a perfect balance of automotive awe and soulfulness.

A solitary custodian at Rosamond, California’s Willow Springs Raceway, Tree (Kang) is used to keeping a low profile. Haunted by a tragic past and saddled with generational debt, he avoids getting close to others, preferring to use his off hours behind the wheel of his battered but beloved vintage Toyota AE86 Corolla — which he’s nicknamed Lola — and drifting in the desert twilight. Tree’s immense talent is eventually noticed and he’s granted a chance to compete in a pro drifting event. But is talent alone enough to win? In order to realize his secret dream, Tree must learn to overcome his aversion to others and seek out a mentor — which also means coming to terms with the ghosts he’s spent his life trying to keep at bay.

By turns melancholy and exhilarating, Drifter is an existential action film, establishing Kang as a sensitive observer and confirming his singular charisma as a leading man. But Kang is also committed to making the sport as real to life as possible, evidenced in the film’s casting of genuine car-world icons such as Adam LZ, Dai Yoshihara, Rutledge Wood, James Pumphrey, and Brian Scotto, co-founder of the motorsport lifestyle brand Hoonigan. Get ready to hold your breath, oversteer, and glide.
drifter.teaser: Fast & Furious alum Sung Kang directs and stars in this alternately melancholy and exhilarating character study of a lonesome racetrack custodian with a secret talent for drifting.

ink.title: Ink
ink.synopsis:
Director Danny Boyle (TIFF ’08’s People Choice Award winner Slumdog Millionaire) stylishly adapts playwright James Graham’s wild recounting of how The Sun became one of the most successful newspapers in British history while launching tabloid culture.

Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce, The Brutalist, TIFF ’24) persuades newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) to oversee his newly acquired but flagging daily, The Sun. But how to grab readers in the highly competitive British media market? Be extreme, throwing anything onto the page that will make a splash, the more titillating, the better. The tactic works, and soon the notorious Sun sees a massive spike in circulation.

The goal of casting a wide net for new readers creates just enough space for one woman (Claire Foy) to break through and pitch articles with a modern woman’s perspective. It’s not long before she starts to brush against the limits of the prevailing boys’ club culture within the industry. And as readership numbers rise, so do the paper’s detractors.

O’Connell is riveting as the ambitious and morally compromised Lamb, pushing the team to go ever further while Pearce gives a carefully calibrated portrayal of Murdoch as both reticent and ruthless, driven by an outsider’s resentment. Fast-paced and gripping, Boyle’s Ink traces this dark journalistic legacy that continues to reverberate today.

Content advisory: violence, sexual content, nudity, drug use, coarse language, crude content, strobing effects
ink.teaser: Director Danny Boyle’s latest thrillingly charts the meteoric rise of Rupert Murdoch’s fledgling but instantly notorious The Sun newspaper as he and editor Larry Lamb create the blueprint for UK tabloid culture. Guy Pearce (The Brutalist, TIFF ’24) and Jack O’Connell star.

neil-peart-no-ones-disciple.title: Neil Peart: No One's Disciple
neil-peart-no-ones-disciple.synopsis:
If the surest means of determining the talent of the musician behind the kit is the number of air drummers in a packed arena, then no one matched Neil Peart. During his four-decade tenure with Canadian power trio Rush, Peart continually astonished and thrilled both fans and fellow drummers who became friends before his untimely death from brain cancer in 2020.

That’s why it’s especially meaningful to listen in on the conversations — musical and otherwise — that fill co-directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn’s note-perfect documentary about Peart and his surviving bandmates’ celebration of their friend’s life, legacy, and artistry. In exhilarating performance sequences, Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson revisit some of Rush’s greatest songs with Peart’s chair filled by four of his musical “brothers”: The Police’s Stewart Copeland, Tool’s Danny Carey, Chad Smith of the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Gavin Harrison of Porcupine Tree and King Crimson.

That Peart’s parts are so challenging even for such revered players says a lot about the ingenuity and dexterity he brought to Rush’s music. The performances also become one of several means of commemorating a man who — as the film reveals — was equally complex. The remembrances and anecdotes of the musicians and other intimates help fill out the portrait that McFadyen and Dunn create via archival interviews and other footage.

Particularly poignant is the story of Peart’s own grief journey after the devastating loss of his daughter and wife in the late 1990s. Yet the vibe of Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple is more joyful than mournful, eliciting laughs and tears along with plenty more air drumming.
neil-peart-no-ones-disciple.teaser: Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson team up with four revered drummers — Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith, and Gavin Harrison — for an exhilarating and poignant tribute to late Rush legend Neil Peart.

the-assassins.title: The Assassin(s)
the-assassins.synopsis:
Based on the attempted assassination of South Korean President Park Chung-hee, the latest from Hur Jin-ho (TIFF ’23’s A Normal Family) is a large-canvas procedural in which a handful of police officers and journalists risk everything to root out a seemingly impenetrable conspiracy. With an all-star cast including Lee Min-ho (Gangnam 1970), Park Hae-il (TIFF ’22’s Decision to Leave), and Yoo Hai-jin (A Taxi Driver), The Assassin(s) is a suspenseful tale of perseverance in the face of overwhelming corruption.

August 15, 1974. Gunshots are fired during the president’s speech at the 29th Liberation Day ceremony. President Park survives, but First Lady Yuk Young-soo and a young girl are killed. Security officers seize the assassin, Mun Se-gwang, a Korean Japanese man deemed a Maoist radical. But did he act alone? There were six shots fired, but Mun’s pistol only carried five bullets.

Inconsistencies in the official report accumulate, but every time the press or police make inquiries, they’re accused of being communists or ordered to leave the incident alone. A senior inspector (Yoo), a veteran journalist (Park), and a rookie reporter (Lee) resolve to do whatever it takes to uncover the truth, despite threats against their careers — and lives.

Returning to TIFF for his third Gala Presentation, Hur is a skilled conductor of set pieces, multi-threaded storytelling, and character development. His heroes are confronted with danger at every turn, but forge ahead with the conviction that a free press is essential to a functioning democracy, and the truth, however ugly, will always set you free.
the-assassins.teaser: Based on the attempted assassination of South Korean President Park Chung-hee, the latest from Hur Jin-ho (TIFF ’23’s A Normal Family) is a large-canvas procedural about police and journalists determined to uncover a seemingly impenetrable conspiracy.

wild-horse-nine.title: Wild Horse Nine
wild-horse-nine.synopsis:
In his newest, highly anticipated black comedy, Oscar-winning writer-director Martin McDonagh (Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, TIFF ’17; The Banshees of Inisherin, TIFF ’22) trades the remote Irish island and small-town Missouri of his last two films for the tropical shores of Easter Island. Set in the early 1970s, just before the coup in Chile that overthrew Salvador Allende, Wild Horse Nine follows a pair of eccentric CIA agents with a history of meddling in global events.

Like any excellent buddy film, contrasting personalities are key. Chris (John Malkovich, TIFF ’25’s Sacrifice) is an aging, eccentric officer in charge of mentoring Lee (Oscar winner Sam Rockwell, TIFF ‘17’s Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri), the brash, foul-mouthed protégé who just wants to enjoy the exquisite scenery. Conspiracies abound, paranoia ensues, and their trust in one another is pushed to the limits by their handler MJ (Steve Buscemi, also at this year’s Festival in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York).

Along the way, the duo cross paths with two rebellious young women and the encounter spurs the ailing Chris to look back on his actions as a spy, unsettling Lee and threatening to derail the assignment. What was supposed to be a typical case of foreign intervention begins to spiral out of control.

With the cast rounded out by Tom Waits (TIFF ’12’s Seven Psychopaths) as Chris' brother and Parker Posey (TIFF ’14’s Ned Rifle) as Marge, Lee's wife, Wild Horse Nine is a darkly funny story with McDonagh’s signature incisive dialogue slyly commenting on the contemporary political climate.
wild-horse-nine.teaser: Two CIA agents (John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) are sent on a mission to Easter Island, where one faces an existential crisis over his past actions, in Martin McDonagh’s latest dark comedy.

glaxo.title: Glaxo
glaxo.synopsis:
“All is lost when a friend betrays you,” declares a narrator, ominously, during the opening sequence of Glaxo, a film that unfolds as the fulfilment of that unsettling promise.

For his adaptation of the 2009 novel by fellow Argentinian Hernán Ronsino, talented auteur Benjamín Naishtat (Rojo, TIFF ’18) crafts an absorbing narrative that takes place in three different timelines and centres on Flaco and Miguelito, two of four close friends with ties dating back to their teenage years.

Flaco is sent to prison, framed for a crime he did not commit by Ramón Folcada, an ex-policeman with a violent past. The injustice stems from a lie told by Miguelito, who falsely identified Flaco as the lover of Folcada’s wife. In return, Folcada helps him avoid military service and secures him a coveted position at Glaxo, the town’s only factory.

Featuring multiple stars of contemporary Argentinian cinema — Marcelo Subiotto as the shady Folcada, Lali Espósito as La Negra Miranda, Folcada’s seductive wife, and Esteban Bigliardi as Flaco — the film delivers a deeply atmospheric sense of time and place.

The suspenseful story unfolds gradually, exposing the complex motivations, betrayals, and lasting impact of its characters' choices. It also offers an intense, uncompromising look at some of the most painful chapters of Argentinian society during the second half of the 20th century.
glaxo.teaser: Glaxo, Benjamín Naishtat’s riveting adaptation of Hernán Ronsino’s novel, transforms a single betrayal into an absorbing tale of guilt, loyalty, and memory, weaving personal tragedy with Argentina’s turbulent twentieth-century history through an atmosphere of mounting mystery and suspense.

julian.title: Julián
julian.synopsis:
From Cartoon Saloon, the acclaimed Irish animation studio behind The Breadwinner (TIFF ’17), Wolfwalkers (TIFF ’20) and many others, comes another enchanting gem, this one adapted from Jessica Love’s beloved bestselling children’s book, Julián Is a Mermaid. Oscar-nominated director Louise Bagnall (Late Afternoon) makes a remarkable feature debut, expanding Love’s cherished story into a sumptuously rendered celebration of unforgettable summers, belonging, and the extraordinary power of being truly seen.

While his father is away for work, seven-year-old Julián goes to stay with his Dominican grandmother in Brooklyn. Their time together begins sweetly, if a little awkwardly, but the neighbourhood soon opens itself to him as a place of imagination, new friendships, and discovery. Immersed in the sights, sounds, and traditions of the borough’s Caribbean community, Julián develops a deeper connection to his family’s roots. When he learns of the city’s upcoming Mermaid Parade, he dreams of marching as a mermaid alongside his three new pals. But Julián's joyful certainty about who he is unsettles his abuela’s expectations, setting them both on a path towards greater understanding.

Bagnall’s charmingly expressive animation is filled with moments of humour, tenderness, and heartfelt emotional honesty. The result is a family film that embraces kindness while celebrating the joy of being accepted just as you are by the people whose love matters most.
julian.teaser: From the acclaimed studio behind Wolfwalkers and Song of the Sea comes a joyful adaptation of Jessica Love’s beloved children’s book about a young boy whose dream of becoming a mermaid transforms both his summer and his relationship with his grandmother.

minotaur.title: Minotaur
minotaur.synopsis:
Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) is a successful company director, whose high-pressure corporate life is balanced by a picture-perfect family — including his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) — and a luxurious dacha on the outskirts of a medium-sized town.

But when the Russian invasion of Ukraine begins, pressure mounts on employers to fill draft quotas for the notorious miasorubka (meat grinder) of relentless front-line warfare. With desperate workers fleeing to avoid conscription, Gleb finds an inventive — yet deeply sociopathic — way to secure the 14 "tributes" demanded from his company, echoing the Greek myth of the Minotaur's labyrinth.

Meanwhile at home, Gleb and Galina — mirrored in their shallowness — barely look at each other, with her gaze focussed on someone else. Upon realizing what’s happening right under his nose, Gleb snaps into action — and this time, the blood on his hands will be much harder to cover-up.

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev (The Return, TIFF ’03; Leviathan, TIFF ’14; Loveless, TIFF ’17), is back in full form, reuniting with cinematographer Mikhail Krichman for his sixth feature, based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 classic La femme infidèle (The Unfaithful Wife). When the film won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival, Zvyagintsev used his acceptance speech to issue a direct, personal plea to President Vladimir Putin to bring the war on Ukraine to an end.

Ultimately, Minotaur is a devastating work that cuts through the heart, bones, and fragile ethos of a nation collectively hell-bent on destruction.
minotaur.teaser: After a nine-year hiatus, during which he fled his native Russia into exile, Andrey Zvyagintsev (The Return, TIFF ’03, Leviathan, TIFF ’14) returns with a reworking of Claude Chabrol's La femme infidèle, adapted to his homeland's current rhetoric of patriarchy and warmongering.

mr-nelson-did-you-kill-people.title: Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?
mr-nelson-did-you-kill-people.synopsis:
In his first film shot primarily in English, Shinya Tsukamoto returns to the subject that has haunted his recent work: the physical, psychological, and moral devastation war leaves behind. Yet this is no repetition. Tsukamoto once again reinvents his cinematic approach, confronting violence from a deeply unsettling perspective.

Years in the making, the film recounts the experiences of Vietnam War veteran Allen Nelson (Rodney Hicks, with newcomer Mark Merphy portraying the younger Allen). Born into poverty in Brooklyn, Nelson joins the Marines at eighteen and is sent to Vietnam. Combat destroys his belief in military heroism and leaves him profoundly traumatized. Decades later, after losing his family and becoming homeless, he is forced to confront the memories he has tried to suppress, aided by a Veterans Affairs psychologist and challenged by a child’s devastating question: “Mr. Nelson, did you kill people?”

Tsukamoto offers no comforting moral distance. War does not simply drive ordinary people to violence. It authorizes, organizes, and transforms violence into duty, unleashing the darkest impulses buried within the human soul. “Why did you kill?”, a question repeatedly asked by Nelson’s psychologist (Geoffrey Rush), becomes the film’s moral centre, echoing and deepening the haunting query posed in its title.

Propelled by relentless narrative momentum that keeps the viewer emotionally engaged throughout, Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? unfolds as a fierce, harrowing, and profoundly humane experience. Combining a visceral visual language with uncompromising moral intelligence, it is both a portrait of one veteran and an indictment of the systems that manufacture killers and abandon survivors: urgent, devastating, and impossible to dismiss.

Content advisory: explicit violence, strobing effects, coarse language, crude content, mature themes
mr-nelson-did-you-kill-people.teaser: Cult Japanese filmmaker Shinya Tsukamoto directs acclaimed Broadway actor Rodney Hicks and Oscar winner Geoffrey Rush in a harrowing, visceral, and morally urgent portrait of Vietnam veteran Allen Nelson.

paradise-lost.title: Paradise Lost
paradise-lost.synopsis:
Director Yeon Sang-ho (Hellbound, TIFF ’21; The Ugly, TIFF ’25) evokes the suspenseful story of Ryu (Kim Hyun-joo), a mother devastated by the loss of her son who mysteriously vanished along with a busload of fellow campers, leaving parents with profound grief but no answers about what happened to their children.

A new technology company offers unusual comfort with augmented reality glasses able to create a near-lifelike version of the missing children, giving grieving parents simulated interactions with those they lost. But living with angelic memories of Ryu’s son conjured by the glasses are disrupted by strange new events linked to the bus tragedy. The artificial reality she created is shattered with the arrival of disturbing truths about her real son.

Paradise Lost is a complex and at times frightening exploration of human darkness and trauma, provoking questions about motherhood, love, and responsibility in a gripping psychological thriller. From his zombie classic Train to Busan to The Colony, Yeon Sang-ho is a vanguard voice in Korean genre storytelling today.
paradise-lost.teaser: A bus full of children mysteriously vanishes. When an altered version of a grieving mother’s son returns years later, she must grapple with the technologically revised reality she has created in this sharp thriller from Yeon Sang-ho.

phoolan.title: Phoolan
phoolan.synopsis:
A small village in the heartland of India forms the backdrop of a high-intensity 48-hour siege where a young Phoolan Devi and her group of outlaws must outsmart the Indian police. Richie Mehta’s interpretation of the life and legend of Devi centres on a pivotal moment in her life, contextualized by but never exploitative of her traumatic past. Though young, Devi is already mythologized widely and garners support across caste, class, and gender barriers, showcasing precisely why she was a force to be reckoned with.

Mehta (Amal, TIFF ’07) brings his restrained and realistic true-crime sensibilities from Delhi Crime to this biopic, heavily inspired by her 1996 autobiography, I, Phoolan Devi: The Autobiography of India’s Bandit Queen. In the book, Devi recounts the trauma of her child marriage, the caste discrimination she experienced, and her journey to becoming the Bandit Queen. Devi eventually surrendered, served a prison sentence, and ultimately grew to political power as a Member of Parliament before she was assassinated in 2001. Those familiar with her life story will appreciate this immersive, taut thriller that highlights her moment of becoming.

Brought to life by Sneha Kumari, this Devi is riveting — unflinchingly challenging the suffocating patriarchy and commanding respect from the men around her in ways that belie her age. Supported by compelling performances by Anurag Thakur, Vikram Pratap Singh, Aakash Dahiya, Prateek Pachori, and Dev Dutt Budholiya, Kumari shines on screen.

Content advisory: discussions of sexual violence; coarse language, explicit violence, misogynistic language and behaviour
phoolan.teaser: In the heartland of India, a young Phoolan Devi becomes one of the most famous outlaws in Indian history and the target of 2,000 heavily armed men sent to kill her over a gruelling 48-hour siege.

the-beloved.title: The Beloved
the-beloved.synopsis:
Featuring arrestingly complex performances from Oscar winner Javier Bardem (TIFF ’07’s No Country For Old Men) and Victoria Luengo (Pedro Almodóvar’s The Room Next Door, TIFF ’24), the latest from Oscar-nominated director Rodrigo Sorogoyen (The Beasts, TIFF ’18’s The Realm) is at once an intriguing depiction of the filmmaking process and an unflinching examination of what happens when dysfunctional family dynamics fuse with artistic hubris.

In a Madrid restaurant, Esteban (Bardem, also at this year’s Festival in Bunker), a charismatic, world-renowned director, has lunch with Emilia (Luengo), a young actor — and his long-estranged daughter. Esteban offers Emilia a role in his next film, a Sahara-set historical drama about the Sahrawi uprising against their Spanish colonizers. Esteban and Emilia have not seen each other in 13 years and their reunion is tense: when Emilia tries to remind her father of their difficult past, he tells her she remembers it all wrong. Nevertheless, Emilia takes the role, and soon father and daughter are on location, where, surrounded by cast and crew, a kind of emotional showdown unfolds, one rife with cruelty, manipulation, and the reopening of old wounds.

The film, written by Sorogoyen and frequent collaborator Isabel Peña, will inevitably draw comparisons to TIFF ’25’s Sentimental Value. Though it also shares piercing psychological insights and artful filmmaking, The Beloved is a darker portrait of creative control — and it is more brutal.

As in No Country For Old Men, Bardem delivers an unforgettable performance. Luengo matches her co-star with a turn of immense intelligence, mystery, and depth.
the-beloved.teaser: Starring Oscar winner Javier Bardem and Victoria Luengo (TIFF ’24’s The Room Next Door), the latest from Rodrigo Sorogoyen (TIFF ’18’s The Realm) chronicles an unnerving collaboration between a charismatic, manipulative director and the actor daughter he hasn’t seen in 13 years.

a-talent-for-murder.title: A Talent for Murder
a-talent-for-murder.synopsis:
This smouldering chamber thriller from Anton Corbijn (Control) stars Oscar winner Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich (Fair Play) as opponents in a strange confrontation between a youthful literary agent and The Talented Mr. Ripley author Patricia Highsmith.

This smouldering chamber thriller from director Anton Corbijn (TIFF ’07’s Control) imagines a strange confrontation between a literary agent and legendary author Patricia Highsmith, whose acclaimed, icily intelligent crime novels were the source material for such classic films as Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train and The Talented Mr. Ripley. Adapted by Joanna Murray-Smith from her play Switzerland and starring Alden Ehrenreich (TIFF ’23’s Fair Play), Olivia Cooke (TIFF ’19’s Sound of Metal; also at this year’s Festival in Slow Horses) and Oscar winner Helen Mirren, A Talent For Murder pits ruthless careerism against dark genius in a slippery battle of wills.

It is 1995, and American author Highsmith (Mirren), now in her seventies and in poor health, has retired to the Swiss Alps, where she largely confines herself to her study, surrounded by her books, her cats, and her collection of antique weapons. Enter Edward Ridgeway (Ehrenreich), emissary for a New York publisher sent to persuade Highsmith to craft one last instalment in her bestselling series of mysteries featuring the murderous antihero, Tom Ripley. Irritated by this youthful, overly eager visitor, Highsmith refuses the offer — unless, that is, Ridgeway can dream up the perfect murder along with her.

Highsmith was famously charismatic and problematic — and as wickedly manipulative as her most celebrated character. Mirren embodies the formidable scribe with seductive wit, while Ehrenreich infuses Ridgeway with enough duplicity to keep us unsure of his motives. With its brilliant twists and trenchant dialogue, A Talent for Murder is a deeply intriguing foray into the realm where history and myth become deliciously entangled.
a-talent-for-murder.teaser: This smouldering chamber thriller from Anton Corbijn (Control) stars Oscar winner Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich (Fair Play) as opponents in a strange confrontation between a youthful literary agent and The Talented Mr. Ripley author Patricia Highsmith.

being-heumann.title: Being Heumann
being-heumann.synopsis:
All screenings will be presented with open captions. ASL interpreters and live captioning will be present for the live onstage components during the screenings on September 10.

Every bit as moving as her Best Picture Oscar winner, CODA, Siân Heder’s Being Heumann tells the remarkable true story of the woman who led a world-changing campaign for accessibility. Judy Heumann rallied a handful, then dozens, then hundreds of ordinary Americans with disabilities to push the US government to live up to its commitments.

The year is 1977. Raised in Brooklyn by German Jewish immigrants, and using a wheelchair since a childhood case of polio, Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) knows it takes grit and tenacity to get things done. So when Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo) refuses to sign meaningful regulations for Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the first national civil rights legislation designed to provide protections for people with disabilities, Judy devises a plan to force his hand, beginning with the occupation of a federal building in San Francisco, before going all the way to DC — and Califano’s front door — with a diverse team of self-described “radical crips,” creating solidarity through coalitions of marginalized groups.

The signing of 504 seems an impossible dream — Califano keeps reminding everyone that the Rehabilitation Act’s price tag is in the billions, and that pushing it through will cost him his job — but Judy and her crew have courage and a flair for media attention on their side. Though set in the past, Being Heumann couldn’t be more pertinent to our present. When change can seem overwhelming, we need heroes like Judy to galvanize us.
being-heumann.teaser: Featuring a breakout performance by Ruth Madeley and Oscar nominee Mark Ruffalo (TIFF ’15’s Spotlight), this inspiring historical drama from Oscar-winning filmmaker Siân Heder (CODA) celebrates the paradigm-shifting activist Judy Heumann, “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement.”

hope.title: Hope
hope.synopsis:
Here lies Hope, a seaside Korean village nestled between the mountains on the southern side of the DMZ. In a community ever watchful for a ground invasion from the North, the discovery of mutilated livestock sparks a two-pronged investigation led by a beleaguered police chief, Beom-seok (Hwang Jung-min), and his wilful cousin, Sung-ki (Zo In-sung). As nearby wildfires soon sever communication across the countryside, Beom-seok rushes back to defend his largely elderly constituency with his eager deputy (Hoyeon), and Sung-ki musters a hunting party to venture into the surrounding wilderness and root out the threat. Both are in for a rude and wicked awakening of monstrous proportions (portrayed in part by Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander).

As he bounds between suspense and spectacle, in a marathon of breathless set pieces, writer-director Na Hong-jin conducts the subsequent escalating chaos with a feverish zeal that seems to epitomize the whole history of action cinema, from Buster Keaton to Bong Joon Ho. At first recalling the small-town terror of Steven Spielberg’s Jaws, as well as its inspired derivatives like Jordan Peele’s Nope, Na further accrues a rollicking momentum with the elasticity of a Tex Avery cartoon or Hideki Kamiya video game as he propels his hayseed protagonists through a crucible of harrowing and hilarious daring do and dumb. And when all his enigmatic cards are finally turned over in a series of revelations, both sobering (and scatological), an epic tragedy finally emerges, but one whose semi-parodic connotations rocket to cosmic heights.All ye who enter: hold on to your butts.

Content advisory: explicit violence, animal abuse, accident trauma, coarse language, crude content, mature themes, scenes of surgery
hope.teaser: In this madcap marvel from Na Hong-jin (The Chaser, The Wailing), a police chief (Hwang Jung-min) and deputy (Hoyeon) investigate a monstrous incursion upon their remote village, as a headstrong local (Zo In-sung) musters a hunting party to root out the threat.

tenzing.title: Tenzing
tenzing.synopsis:
The latest from director Jennifer Peedom (TIFF ’15’s Sherpa) recounts the story of Himalayan Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay who, alongside Edmund Hillary, became the first to reach the summit of Mount Everest in 1953. Written by Oscar-nominated screenwriter Luke Davis (TIFF ’16’s Lion), and starring Tom Hiddleston (TIFF ’24’s The Life of Chuck), Caitríona Balfe (TIFF ’21’s Belfast), Oscar nominee Willem Dafoe (TIFF ’17’s The Florida Project), and Genden Phuntsok (TIFF ’18’s Jinpa), Tenzing is the inspiring exploration of an extraordinary life fuelled by ambition, tenacity, and a true sense of wonder.

Hard work and sheer charisma found Tenzing (Phuntsok) working on British expeditions to Everest in the 1930s. Nearly two decades would pass before he joined the team that would finally complete the ascent to the world’s tallest peak, led by John Hunt (Dafoe) and Edmund Hillary (Hiddleston), whose survival would ultimately depend on Tenzing’s skills, dedication, and profound courage.

Gorgeously photographed by Stefan Duscio (The Invisible Man), Tenzing is a transporting experience, ushering us along a seemingly impossible trek to the top of the world. The film’s stellar cast make expert guides on this journey, but its single greatest asset is Phuntsok, who embodies its larger-than-life hero with grace and vulnerability — and somehow captures Tenzing’s legendarily irresistible smile.
tenzing.teaser: Starring Tom Hiddleston (TIFF ’24’s The Life of Chuck), Oscar nominee Willem Dafoe, and Genden Phuntsok (TIFF ’18’s Jinpa), this wondrous biopic recounts the story of Himalayan Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay who, alongside Edmund Hillary, became first to top Everest in 1953.

alpha-gang.title: Alpha Gang
alpha-gang.synopsis:
When you think of alien invasions of Earth, you typically think big — epic battles, mass destruction, and ambitions of global conquest. But according to filmmakers David and Nathan Zellner, that takeover would actually be contested by something much smaller and more human: emotions.

The Zellners’ titular Alpha Gang includes Léa Seydoux, Riley Keough, and Dave Bautista. Decked out in ’50s-era leather jackets, they look like a badass group of old-school bikers. Here to conquer, their plans begin to falter when they start to feel just how the human world can shift perspectives. Moments of intimacy, art, joy, and sadness start to seep into the gang and the intended directives become muddled. As they experience the pleasures of music and dance, and observe the beauties of the natural world — down to even the smallest ant colony — each becomes far more impacted by Earth than they could have ever expected.

With creative humour, a fantastic soundtrack, and stellar performances from an eclectic cast, Alpha Gang makes a timely statement about the human condition.
alpha-gang.teaser: Léa Seydoux, Dave Bautista, Lily-Rose Depp, and Cate Blanchett star in the Zellner brothers’ look at an alien gang coming to Earth to conquer, but finding the human world has a plague they weren’t ready for.

everest-the-other-side.title: Everest: The Other Side
everest-the-other-side.synopsis:
Thousands of people have ascended Mount Everest from the southeast ridge in Nepal. But only five had ever summited from the more daunting direct North Face route from China. This became a quest for Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson, who sought not only to summit, but then to ski down through the near vertical Hornbein Couloir. It’s a test of athleticism that only a few have attempted with a zero success rate. The last person to try disappeared on the descent.

Filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin are renowned for capturing adventurers who push to extremes in films such as the Oscar-winning Free Solo (TIFF ’18). In this new work, made for the IMAX screen, they enable us to witness a history-making endeavour, while revealing the interior lives of risk takers. Opinions may vary on whether these acts are courageous or crazy. Even the two directors have differing viewpoints that arise in a raw moment in the film.

What’s undeniable is the determination shared by Morrison and Nelson. They gained recognition separately for their outdoor adventuring, then came together each having been in a prior marriage. As they both approach age 50, they’ve already set records and are well acquainted with tragedy. Their goal for the North Face will require many exhausting days of climbing, followed by a descent on skis that will take several hours. One false move is the difference between mortality and immortality. The film is its own achievement of spectacle and emotion in capturing what took place.
everest-the-other-side.teaser: Professional ski mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson seek to ski down the North Face of Mount Everest, a feat never achieved, as the Oscar-winning filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin (Free Solo, TIFF ’18) follow their journey, shooting for the IMAX screen.

josephine.title: Josephine
josephine.synopsis:
When eight-year-old Josephine (Mason Reeves) and her father Damien (Channing Tatum, TIFF ’25’s Roofman) walk through Golden Gate Park one morning, they witness a disturbing incident. Though her father manages to stop the attack, the event leaves Josephine emotionally scarred. In the aftermath, Damien enrolls Josephine in martial arts to help her reclaim her sense of power, while her mother Claire (Gemma Chan) advocates for therapy and insists she testify in court. Caught between her parents’ conflicting approaches and still struggling to process her trauma, Josephine begins acting out violently at school and becomes hypervigilant, constantly scanning her surroundings for threats.

Inspired by director Beth de Araújo’s own childhood memory, the film is a devastating portrait of a young girl who is forced to confront impossible cruelty and surrender the safety she once knew. Newcomer Reeves delivers an impressive and sensitive performance. Through cinematographer Greta Zozula’s skilful lens, we are drawn into Josephine’s paranoia, where the sight of a man walking down a school hallway can trigger survival instincts. Following her 2022 psychological thriller Soft & Quiet, which unfolds over a single continuous take, de Araújo once again uses formal rigour and grounded direction to capture the raw, specific weight of a brutal experience.
josephine.teaser: After witnessing an event, a young girl is haunted by the trauma of the disturbing incident, opening her eyes to the violence that surrounds her.

stuffed.title: Stuffed
stuffed.synopsis:
Love and desire can make us do the strangest things. Stuffed gleefully asks just how far we’re willing to go.

In an inventive feature debut, director and co-writer Theo Rhys simultaneously serves up a dark comedy, an offbeat romance, and a twisted musical that dances between the macabre and the heartfelt. At its centre are Araminta, an isolated mortician-cum-taxidermist with a dream, and Bernie, a lonely factory worker whose extraordinary request draws these two outsiders together.

Rhys — here adapting his acclaimed 2021 short film of the same name — embraces the ghoulish with infectious enthusiasm, creating a heightened cinematic world where songs emerge from moments of aching vulnerability, the grotesque becomes unexpectedly beautiful, and love flourishes in the unlikeliest of places.

Jodie Comer (TIFF ’23’s The End We Start From) is sensational as the fiercely independent Araminta. She is matched beat for beat by Harry Melling (TIFF ’23’s Shoshana), whose fearless performance transforms Bernie into one of the year’s most endearing screen oddballs. Under Rhys’ confident direction, the duo give the film its beating heart, grounding even its wildest flights of imagination in genuine longing, humour, and tenderness as the story spirals toward an unforgettable conclusion. Co-writer and composer Joss Holden-Rea's wonderfully idiosyncratic songs weave seamlessly into the narrative, creating a musical language as bold and adventurous as the film itself.

Bursting with gothic invention, Stuffed seems destined for cult status, introducing audiences to both a filmmaker with an original vision and to an offbeat love story they’ll never forget… and maybe want to preserve forever.
stuffed.teaser: Love, death, and taxidermy collide in this gloriously twisted musical, one of the year’s funniest, most original, and unexpectedly heartfelt romances.

the-debut.title: The Debut
the-debut.synopsis:
Mona Friedman (Academy Award winner Julianne Moore) feels stuck in her tedious suburban housewife life. When a role with a community theatre company arises, she jumps at the chance to try out. To her surprise, she lands a spot in the production.

Hard-headed theatre director Jerry (Paul Giamatti, TIFF ’23’s The Holdovers) sees a spark in Mona and pushes her to test the limits of what she can bring to the role. Which she does, obsessing over nailing her first performance.

Writer-director Jesse Eisenberg mines rich, dark comedy from the self-seriousness of community theatre, with every line change and beat scrutinized despite the relatively low stakes for all involved, including the audience.

Moore is tremendous as Mona, mirroring the depth and devotion Mona gives to the character she is portraying. Brilliantly riffing on the Constantin Stanislavski chestnut that “there are no small parts, only small actors,” The Debut examines just what that maxim looks like when taken to the extreme.

Giamatti leads a supporting ensemble of stellar performances, including Eisenberg himself. The Debut is hilarious and smart from beginning to end with no false notes.
the-debut.teaser: Jesse Eisenberg directs Academy Award winner Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti in a dark comedy about a bored suburban housewife who finds purpose acting in community theatre.

dorothy.title: Dorothy
dorothy.synopsis:
Set in the early 1990s, Dorothy follows Karthi and Subbu, two boys who grow up within an unforgiving landscape of rural Tamil Nadu. When a misfortune befalls Dorothy (Keerthy Suresh), a member of the household who always treated the childhood friends with gentleness, the story takes an unexpected turn, shifting from their mere survival into a harsh, scorched-earth reality shaped by rigid patriarchal hierarchies and everyday violence.

The loss profoundly affects Subbu (Sananth), who finds an unlikely community of people living outside society’s expectations, and vanishes. Karthi (Rishikanth) is sent on a mission across rural India to hunt Subbu, the person who once saved him from schoolyard fights. Conflicted and caught between the bonds of friendship and filial demands, the two embark on a journey of friendship, love, and the profound courage it takes to live honestly.

Director Karthik Subbaraj leaps across genres with his striking visual style, inviting viewers along on this wild ride, combining elements of noir thrillers, gangster films, and romances. With references to the action sequences of Bruce Lee and the physical comedy of Howard Hawks, Subbaraj writes a love letter to cinema where tenderness finds a way to thrive in the most unexpected places.

Dorothy offers not only an exhilarating and touching portrait of two individuals whose loyalty is tested by a legacy of violence but a celebration of friendship and a passionate critique of gender oppression.
dorothy.teaser: Set in a world shaped by caste, violence, and toxic masculinity, two childhood friends grow up inseparable in rural Tamil Nadu. Their lives are transformed by the arrival of Dorothy, a woman whose compassion quietly challenges the world around them.

inherit.title: Inherit
inherit.synopsis:
Beauty and youth are traits known to expire, but Grandma Woranart seems to be an exception. At over 80 years old, she still turns heads. Based on the Thai horror novel Tayard Asoon (translated in English as “The Demon's Heir”), Inherit brings the story of a character possessed by a centipede spirit onto the silver screen.

The Manasvanichs look like they have it all — a beautiful family, a mansion, power, and wealth — until an unexpected relative shows up at their door and unveils their dark secrets. Grandma Woranart’s (Davika Hoorne) striking beauty and youth aren’t the only things suspicious about her. Unnatural deaths happen wherever she goes, and it’s obvious she has an agenda for her visit — to find a new host for the centipede demon within her. Unfortunately, Oui (Baipor Thitiya Jirapornsilp), the youngest of the family, may just be the targeted heir.

Diverting from the renowned filmmaker’s previous box office horror hits, Banjong Pisanthanakun takes a different tonal approach in Inherit. Though the scares remain sleek and strong, heavier themes of corruption, exploitation, and social issues lie at its foundation. He reunites with his Pee Mak (2013) actress Hoorne, who breathes life into the iconic femme fatale, personifying the centipede demon embodying beauty and sinisterness with delicate perfection. Pisanthanakun’s adaptation weaves family drama with a chilling occult premise, resulting in a universally entertaining film that can be appreciated regardless of one’s familiarity with the original lore.
inherit.teaser: Davika Hoorne plays her most magnetic role yet as Woranart – a grandma possessed by a demon – in the latest chilling psychological thriller by Shutter director Banjong Pisanthanakun.

prima-facie.title: Prima Facie
prima-facie.synopsis:
Anchored by a powerhouse performance from Cynthia Erivo, the Oscar-nominated star of Wicked and TIFF ’19’s Harriet, this piercing legal drama examines what happens when an ambitious barrister who primarily defends those accused of sex crimes unexpectedly becomes the accuser. Adapted by Australian playwright Suzie Miller from her globally acclaimed one-woman show, and directed by Susanna White (Our Kind of Traitor, TIFF ’17’s Woman Walks Ahead), Prima Facie exposes the pitfalls of a legal system that places the burden of proof on the victim.

Having risen from a working-class background to a successful career in law, Tessa (Erivo) does not suffer fools. She is a formidable presence in the courtroom, expertly dismantling opposing arguments, uncovering vulnerabilities, and holding her adversaries to the highest standards of jurisprudence. For Tessa, the nature of a client’s alleged crime is irrelevant: she believes the legal system operates optimally when all parties are given the strongest possible representation. However, her life is turned upside down when she is sexually assaulted by a colleague, forcing her to experience first-hand just how merciless — and misogynistic — the law can be toward already-traumatized women who are merely seeking justice.

Backed by a magnificent supporting cast that includes Daniel Ings, Elizabeth Dulau, and Simon Russell Beale, Erivo is at once devastating and inspiring in this dauntingly complex role. “Prima facie” is a Latin expression meaning “based on first impression,” and this hard-hitting, intelligent film shows just how unreliable initial assessments can be.

Content advisory: strobing effects, sexual assault, sexual content, crude content, depictions of racism, explicit violence
prima-facie.teaser: Oscar nominee Cynthia Erivo (Wicked) stars in this adaptation of Suzie Miller’s globally acclaimed play that examines what happens when an ambitious barrister who primarily defends those accused of sex crimes unexpectedly becomes the accuser in a sexual assault case.

bas-book.title: Ba's Book
bas-book.synopsis:
Ba’s Book is a documentary recreation inside a documentary, inspired by a memoir. Fascinated by the idea that her quiet father has recently put his entire life story — including growing up in a Vietnamese village during the Vietnam war, and a brief foray into Iran — into a book, written as a series of letters to her, documentary filmmaker Ashley Duong gamely decides to adapt his written word for the screen.

After the stops and starts of convincing him and her mother to go back to Vietnam, they journey to his former village for a heartwarming reunion with his siblings. The family members are actively involved in bringing his memoir to life, helping to cast the younger versions of themselves, giving notes to the actors, and assisting in the building of the set (a recreation of the home they grew up in.) The doc cleverly uses the process of the recreation to pull out even more memories, particularly in a beautiful scene when the filmmaker’s father and the actor portraying him connect about the character.

Duong artfully creates enough space between their emotional trauma and the staging of the pre-production and production of a film to give her family the chance to breathe, as well as agency in their own stories. Produced by Ina Fichman (Fire of Love; Monsoon, TIFF ’14), Ba’s Book is an earnest look at memory and legacy.
bas-book.teaser: In a hybrid documentary retelling, documentary filmmaker Ashley Duong takes her father’s memoir and stages a recreation of it in Vietnam alongside her family.

like-magic.title: Like Magic
like-magic.synopsis:
“Cali is a magical place, but it’s also a dangerous one,” a young girl learns from her grandmother. It will take her years of pain and confusion to fully comprehend the meaning of such a warning and the profound contradictions that make up this city in Colombia. Here, a genuine joie de vivre and a deep disdain for life coexist in explosive ways, and it’s here where she grows to become a filmmaker in search of answers.

For her feature debut, Colombian filmmaker Melissa Saavedra Gil embarks on a journey that takes her as close as possible to confronting the story that shaped her life. Growing up in the 1990s, she experienced to some degree — as did many of her fellow countrypeople — the violence that permeated the social fabric of the city. As many ‘magicians’ dreamed of and fought to become obscenely rich overnight and as widespread corruption ensured justice became an abstract concept separated from reality, people suffered.

Weaving a vast trove of archival footage with testimonies from the time of the crime she investigates, Mela, as her grandma calls her, opens up cracks to shed light on both the personal and the collective stories that shaped the identity of her generation. In so doing, she finds a place where her relationship with the truth might just allow space for healing to take place.
like-magic.teaser: Blending archival footage, personal testimony, and a decades-long search for answers, Melissa Saavedra Gil transforms a childhood tragedy into a powerful exploration of memory, truth, and healing. An intimate and deeply resonant debut that illuminates both a personal story and a generation shaped by violence.

low-lies-the-land.title: Low Lies The Land
low-lies-the-land.synopsis:
In Northern Italy, the sun-dappled hills of Piemonte look like the setting of an escapist travel fantasy. Perhaps you’ve daydreamed about living on a vineyard in a place like this. Low Lies the Land allows us to vicariously experience the simple pleasures of working outdoors, harvesting fresh produce, hand-rolling pasta, and sampling new wines. But the film also plays like a slow-burn suspense over what changes might be coming.

Director Emanuele Gerosa immerses himself in the households of three families who have tended these vineyards for generations. Cinematographer Alvise Tedesco does impressive work shooting in a panoramic format with exquisite compositions. The film shares thematic and cinematic qualities with The Tale of Silyan and The Truffle Hunters, which won the hearts of TIFF audiences in recent years.

But this Garden of Eden has its own serpent in the form of a real estate broker. He represents an unnamed foreign investor who’s seeking to buy up properties and promising a once-in -a-lifetime price. That puts a heavy decision on the middle-aged growers who are simultaneously facing other pressures.

Rising temperatures and drought increasingly put each year’s crop at risk. And for a business largely handed down from father to son, it’s uncertain if the next generation wants the job. We follow the three families over the course of a year, from one pruning season to the next, as they contemplate whether they’ve reached the end of an era.
low-lies-the-land.teaser: Set in the breathtaking landscapes of Piemonte in Northern Italy, Low Lies the Land immerses us in the lives of three winemaking families facing an uncertain future.

rescue.title: Rescue
rescue.synopsis:
Rescue opens with a harrowing abduction in the waters of the Mediterranean close to the Libyan coast. Director Sine Plambech and her film crew are accompanying the Geo Barents, a rescue ship operated by Doctors Without Borders that’s trying to save a rubber boat packed with migrants in distress. Suddenly, a third vessel approaches, piloted by Libyan militia members. During a frantic scramble in the open water, some migrants are snatched by the militias, while others reach the Geo Barents. One of the rescued migrants, Hani, tells the film crew he has just been separated from his family. His wife Roro, his young son, and their two-month old daughter have been kidnapped by the militia.

That’s the start of an epic journey that Plambech continues to film over several months. The militias hold captives for ransom, while the European Union quietly funnels billions of euros to North African countries to halt migration. Normally, these tragedies take place beyond the reach of cameras. But in this case, Roro has managed to hide a cell phone in her baby’s diaper and is able to share what’s happening to her with Hani, who never gives up believing they can be reunited.

The story is so dramatic that you frequently need to remind yourself that it’s a documentary. That’s a credit to Plambech, who has honed her skills as an anthropologist and filmmaker over many years, and works here with an elite team. We are in their debt for the revelations that take place.
rescue.teaser: Director Sine Plambech (Heartbound, TIFF ’18) documents the kidnapping of a mother and her long quest to be reunited with her husband, illuminating a mass crisis experienced by migrants in the Mediterranean.

still-night-burning-house.title: Still Night, Burning House
still-night-burning-house.synopsis:
Filmmaker Carol Nguyen, whose short films Nanitic (TIFF ’22) and No Crying At the Dinner Table (TIFF ’19), earned a multitude of awards, has returned to the Festival with her much anticipated debut feature, a personal documentary on her paternal uncle’s tragic death.

With sensitivity and care, Nguyen, alongside her father, aunt and cousins, explores the story of her Uncle Thach. From his journey to Canada from Vietnam in 1983, they reveal the circumstances of his death a decade ago.

For Nguyen, whose memories of her uncle’s passing only include hushed mentions of suicide, her desire to create an understanding of him, and at the same time alleviate her father’s continued guilt, unites Thach’s loved ones. After reading thousands of pages of medical records to piece together his mental health issues and realizing how much his English comprehension exacerbated his situation, their grief is allowed to come to the forefront.

With the common goal to grieve him properly, the extended family travels to Vietnam from Toronto, and the bittersweet beauty of saying goodbye anew to Uncle Thach, in his homelands through their ceremonies, is palpable. Deeply affecting and visually stunning, this documentary allows a family to look back, come together, and see how their uncle continues to impact his young adult children’s lives today.
still-night-burning-house.teaser: A once-close family comes together to say goodbye to an uncle who struggled with mental health issues, in award-winning short filmmaker Carol Nguyen’s tender and emotional feature-length documentary debut.

tehran-under-the-skin.title: Tehran, Under the Skin
tehran-under-the-skin.synopsis:
Iran’s capital Tehran is one of the world’s epicenters for cosmetic surgery: nose jobs, tummy tucks, face lifts, liposuction, and more. Filmmaker Afsaneh Salari embeds herself in the offices of two thriving surgeons to understand the motivations of their patients. She brings curiosity, humour, and empathy to her queries. She’s tapping into global trends as social media makes the whole world body-conscious. But she’s especially attuned to local characters. She wonders how Iran has been shaped by political forces, including the restrictive mandatory hijab laws vs the resistant Woman, Life, Freedom movement.

Salari grew up in Tehran, but now lives in France. She’s both an insider and an outsider as she interviews plastic surgery clients (predominantly women) who describe what compels them to go under the knife. Previously, Salari produced the poignant TIFF ‘24 documentary A Sister’s Tale, exploring societal pressures on women.
