Her approach to filming in the operating room is sparing and stylish. She needs to acknowledge what it means to cut into the body, but she keeps it less gory than The Pitt. Plastic surgery might feel superficial in times when Iranians take to the streets to protest fundamentalism and suffer U.S. and Israeli bombardment. Those threats of violence lurk in the background. But one achievement of the film is to treat Iranians as individuals, not as the monolith portrayed in western media. They are as preoccupied with identity, agency, and pressures placed on the body as anyone else. Salari gets under their skin while holding up a mirror to any viewer.
tehran-under-the-skin.teaser: In an age of body anxiety, filmmaker Afsaneh Salari embeds herself in the offices of Iranian plastic surgeons to interview their clients with humour and empathy.

the-final-act.title: The Final Act
the-final-act.synopsis:
With growing access to medically assisted dying in jurisdictions worldwide, many of us are facing the kind of moral and ethical questions we may prefer to avoid lest they challenge us too deeply. And however we may answer those questions, there’s no denying the choices that we or our loved ones make about how to depart the world of the living carry profound weight.

In her extraordinary new documentary, filmmaker Sophie Deraspe approaches the subject with grace and sensitivity. Part of what makes The Final Act so remarkable is the balance that the director — whose films Antigone (TIFF ’19) and Shepherds (TIFF ’24) both won the Festival’s Best Canadian Feature prize — strikes between the film’s two carefully integrated components.

The first is a philosophical enquiry into humankind’s attitudes toward death and dying, with invaluable contributions by big thinkers like American social psychologist Sheldon Solomon. In the second, Deraspe’s film brings viewers into the lives and final moments of a variety of subjects who have decided to undertake medically assisted death.

Achieving an uncommon degree of intimacy while maintaining all the respect and reverence such moments deserve, Deraspe creates a space for contemplation. Yet for all the weight that The Final Act itself possesses, the film is suffused with great warmth, beauty, love, and lightness, too.
the-final-act.teaser: Quebec’s Sophie Deraspe returns to the Festival with a philosophical and intimate look at the many profound issues surrounding both death and medically assisted dying in an extraordinary documentary.

the-hummingbird-paints-fragrant-songs.title: The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs
the-hummingbird-paints-fragrant-songs.synopsis:
Though now in her seventies, Sara Flores is a rising star in the global art world. Her geometric-design paintings are celebrated in international galleries and were adapted by Dior for an exclusive handbag. It’s a rare opportunity for any artist, but it’s especially unique for Flores, a member of the Indigenous Shipibo-Konibo community from the Peruvian Amazon who has been perfecting her artistry since age 14.

Filmmakers Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi have been in creative collaboration with Flores for over a decade. They document her travels from the interior of the rainforest to the urban centres of New York and Paris. Her artistic practice is called Kené, an ancient and mesmerizing visual language, passed down through women. The work has a spiritual dimension to unravel harmful patterns in the world and replace them with orderly designs.

Alongside Ayahuasca, the íkaros — the mystical songs of the plants — are the agents that trigger the transformation. The phrase “the hummingbird paints fragrant songs” is a line from a shamanic song heard in the film, referring to the bird as a helper spirit.

The juxtapositions between the worlds Flores moves in are stark. At home, her community is waging an existential battle against illegal loggers. She joins local patrols armed with bows and arrows. When she’s being fȇted in art capitals, she quietly accepts praise from admirers while sipping champagne and making small talk. The filmmakers practice a poetic and experiential style, leaving viewers to draw their own interpretations. While honouring Flores’ talents, they’ve made their own work of art.
the-hummingbird-paints-fragrant-songs.teaser: The Indigenous painter Sara Flores gets discovered by the international art world in her 70s, setting her off on an adventure as she travels from her home in the Peruvian Amazon to be fȇted in galleries from New York to Paris.

turtle-island-rap.title: Turtle Island Rap
turtle-island-rap.synopsis:
Turtle Island Rap tracks the journey of three young Indigenous artists, Wiidaaseh, A$h Da Hunter, and Travis Thompson, from the hustle to the stage. In cinema verité style, the hard-won triumphs and trials are seen as their individual journeys are taken with warmth and humour, even when things are tough.

In documentary filmmaker Alexandra Lazarowich’s feature debut following her acclaimed short film Fast Horse, she boasts incredibly varied access, from backstage with the Snotty Nose Rez Kids to hunting on Nipissing territory.

Travis Thompson, a Navajo skater kid from a Seattle suburb, has a steady fan base thanks to a feature on the Macklemore song “Corner Store,” but still wonders if his community will show for a free concert.

A$h Da Hunter is from the Yavapai-Apache nation, now working as an indie rapper in Phoenix. Often seen with her mom, she divides her time between working on songs and booking gigs while selling burritos on the street.

Wiidaaseh is from Wiikwemkoong Unceded First Nation and lives in Toronto working as a rapper, producer, and chef and who performs wearing a beaded mask.

Each artist is incredibly candid, sharing their family issues, disappointments and more, surrounded by their support networks and communities.

The documentary’s music pedigree is strong, with several executive producers from the award-winning Hip-Hop Evolution on board, as well as The Halluci Nation’s Tim “2oolman” Hill and Bear Witness as creative producers.
turtle-island-rap.teaser: The bumpy road to success experienced by three aspiring Indigenous hip-hop artists is the focus of Alexandra Lazarowich’s (Fast Horse) verité-style feature documentary debut.

gentle-monster.title: Gentle Monster
gentle-monster.synopsis:
Can we ever truly know anyone else, even the people with whom we’ve chosen to spend our lives? This is the chilling question at the core of Austrian writer-director Marie Kreutzer’s follow-up to TIFF ’22’s Corsage. Featuring an emotionally intricate performance from Léa Seydoux (TIFF ’25’s Silent Friend; also at this year’s Festival in The Unknown) and an elegant cameo from Catherine Deneuve, Gentle Monster considers what monstrousness lies hiding in our very homes.

Experimental musician Lucy Weiss (Seydoux) crafts deconstructed pop songs on unconventional instruments. Her husband Philip (Laurence Rupp, TIFF ’25’s Rise of the Raven) is a filmmaker, though he has been working in television to pay the bills. After Philip suffers a breakdown, the couple, along with their nine-year-old Johnny (Malo Blanchet), relocate from Munich to the countryside.

But their bucolic idyll collapses when a sex crimes unit, led by officer Else Kühn (Jella Haase), arrives to seize the family’s digital devices — and to arrest Philip. As the case against him becomes increasingly difficult to deny, her attention shifts to her son Johnny — and the terrifying possibility that he might be involved.

Kreutzer’s measured handling of this freighted material allows us to identify with Lucy’s harrowing journey and also with Else, who has unspoken domestic concerns of her own. What emerges is a dual portrait of women trapped in moral maelstroms in their families. These are bracing stories of breaches of trust, but there’s hope in the profound humanity invested in the women’s experience.
gentle-monster.teaser: Featuring emotional performances from Léa Seydoux (TIFF ’25’s Silent Friend) and Jella Haase, writer-director Marie Kreutzer’s follow-up to TIFF ’22’s Corsage is a dual portrait of women trapped in moral maelstroms caused by men’s malfeasance.

happily-ever-after.title: Happily Ever After
happily-ever-after.synopsis:
Feng-I Fiona Roan made history with American Girl (2021) as the first woman to win Best New Director at the Golden Horse Awards. With countless accolades under her belt, anticipation has been building around her sophomore work. Effortlessly living up to expectations, Happily Ever After doesn’t disappoint. Delving into the themes of family relationships, generational expectations, and the definition of happiness, this is an engaging and approachable film with the perfect balance of humour and emotional tension.

Kitty (Shuhua Yeh) and Claire (Xuan Chen) are two very different sisters. Kitty, the younger of the two, is the textbook daughter and the mother’s favourite — she’s about to get a promotion and is engaged to a wealthy man. Meanwhile, Claire is far from traditional. She disappoints her parents in both career and love, but is working towards what she wants. One has it all, and one is on her way to freedom, but contrary to what meets the eye, their quest for fulfilment is complicated. When an abandoned cat enters their lives, it becomes the catalyst for unveiling their deep emotional wounds.

Roan’s strong script delicately unfolds the complexity of defining one’s own joy. Claire and Kitty’s uncertainty towards upcoming milestones and fear of breaking family expectations may seem ordinary, but they are battles that strike utterly real to many.

Despite Kitty being her first acting gig, Shuhua Yeh of K-pop group i-dle puts on a convincing and sincere performance alongside rising star Xuan Chen, and backed by seasoned actors Kuei-Mei Yang and Jack Kao — all as individuals searching for happiness in their own ways.
happily-ever-after.teaser: American Girl director Feng-I Fiona Roan’s sophomore film explores the definition of happiness through the lens of two sisters, backed by breakout performances from Xuan Chen and singer-turned-actress Shuhua Yeh of i-dle.

possible-love.title: Possible Love
possible-love.synopsis:
Award-winning filmmaker Lee Chang-dong’s (TIFF ’02’s Oasis, TIFF ’10’s Poetry, TIFF ’18’s Burning) heavily anticipated new film is a tale of deep yearning, envy, and grief. Every couple wants to find some sense of happiness. For Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu, Good News. TIFF ’25) and Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon, Good News. TIFF ’25) the hope is to move on from the trauma caused by the disastrous outcome of a labour dispute. When they are approached by young, ambitious documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, Parasite, TIFF ’19) to take part in her latest project, they become intimately intertwined with her and her business mogul husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung, Smugglers, TIFF ’23).

Revelations of interpersonal suffering come to light — both in front of and behind the camera — as the documentary develops, and tensions between the couples start to rise. Questions are asked around who gets to tell whose story, who speaks for whom, and what responsibilities observers have when taking on the perspective of the disenfranchised. As the lives of Ye-ji, Mi-ok, Sang-woo, and Ho-seok become increasingly entangled, tensions mount.

Through purposeful and layered storytelling, Possible Love quietly surfaces themes of social class and power. Small revelations of complex feelings ripple throughout accumulating into something profound and powerful.

Content advisory: explicit sex scenes, violence, themes of self-harm, nudity, coarse language, crude content
possible-love.teaser: Lee Chang-dong’s eagerly anticipated new film brings stories of relationships, generational and class divides, in this gripping tale of two couples playing games with themselves and one another.

the-idiots.title: The Idiot(s)
the-idiots.synopsis:
Sunday, September 17: This screening will be presented with open captions and live captioning for the onstage components.

The Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky is renowned as one of the greatest writers and most influential thinkers of his time. However, behind the monolithic image of the literary giant is a lesser-known story and next to the man through his most tumultuous times was the wife who supported him.

Fyodor (Johnny Flynn, & Sons, TIFF ’25) is a gambling addict, struggling to make money, delaying any type of creative spark, and generally lacking ambition to create his next work. The motivation he needs comes from Anna (Aimee Lou Wood, The White Lotus), who believes in him, his vision, and his art. With her backing he’s finally able to make something of himself and put out a new novel — The Idiot.

Adapting the literary biography The Gambler Wife by Andrew D. Kaufman, directors Małgorzata Szumowska and Michał Englert showcase a story of a troubled artist with many demons and the woman who did her best to lift him up in spite of himself. Wood and Flynn provide enigmatic and bold performances bringing depth and heartfelt honesty to two people consumed by art but entangled in a chaotic relationship. While Fyodor had more notoriety, this is a fully realized portrait of Anna, who went on to become a powerful figure in her own right.
the-idiots.teaser: Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn bring to life the story of Anna and Fyodor Dostoevsky, showcasing the troubled author and the woman who pushed him to write one of his greatest works.

bleeding-hearts.title: Bleeding Hearts
bleeding-hearts.synopsis:
Zella Day and Jesse Woods fell quickly and passionately in love, just like the lyrics of a classic country tune. Joined by musical collaborator Beau Bedford, they formed the alternative country band Chaparelle, a vibrant and harmonious trio. Over the course of a year, filmmaker Andrew Morgan captures their journey, shooting in black and white with vintage lenses to create a timeless visual language. We watch as they launch themselves as independent artists without the backing of a record label, pouring their hearts and souls into their debut album, Western Pleasure. Jesse explains the music as “a clever way of talking about a feeling that everyone has had, but explaining it in a way that you’ve never thought of before.”

This candid portrait doesn’t shy away from the messy parts of maintaining a relationship while making music. There’s enough professional and personal complications to fill a story arc of Nashville. Zella has the extrovert charisma of a rising star and is receiving music industry offers to pivot to a solo career. Jesse, 12 years older, is more introverted, facing a midlife crossroads on how to adapt himself to show business. Beau is giving up other opportunities to make Chaparelle work while friends question if that’s a good idea. Offstage can be chaotic. But when Zella and Jesse get on-stage together, the chemistry is as potent as any movie stars. Music documentaries are plentiful these days, but this one soars high above the rest.
bleeding-hearts.teaser: This real-life love story follows the charismatic musicians Zella Day and Jesse Woods as they team to create the alt-country band Chaparelle with collaborator Beau Bedford, in a documentary with as much drama as a season of Nashville.

cheyenne.title: Cheyenne
cheyenne.synopsis:
For the first time in nearly a century, the American rodeo circuit opened up a women’s competition for bucking “broncs,” the preferred term. Filmmaker Taimi Arvidson profiles four fearless cowgirls who embrace the opportunity to prove something to themselves and the naysayers. The goal in bronc riding is to stay in the saddle for eight seconds without getting thrown off. It’s a sport that teaches you how to take a hard fall and get back up again.

Each of these women enters the arena for different reasons. Bee, a seasoned veteran, is trying to provide for her son. Brooke, a relative newbie, is learning how to manage the pain that comes with the job. Lake seeks a distraction from past trauma. Ally wants the life-changing payout. We follow them for several months on the circuit as they push their physical and mental limits to win a coveted spot at the showdown known as the Daddy of ’em All: Cheyenne Frontier Days.

The milieu is a delectable mix of majestic animals, country music, Western clothing, and wide-open spaces. Cinematographer Nick Midwig does a stunning job of capturing the adrenaline-pumping rodeo action as well as the quieter moments when the women enjoy each other’s camaraderie and humour.

The double standards are ever present. Daryl, who trains women riders, sums it up: “A guy gets hurt and they hope he’s okay. A girl gets hurt and they’re like, ‘She shouldn’t have been out there.’” For these trail-blazing women, the only thing standing between triumph and defeat is their will to hold on.
cheyenne.teaser: Cheyenne follows a group of fearless cowgirls who compete at riding wild broncos on the rodeo circuit after nearly a century of being excluded because of their gender.

darlene-love-i-know-where-ive-been.title: Darlene Love: I Know Where I've Been
darlene-love-i-know-where-ive-been.synopsis:
The gulf between an artist’s impact on the world and the fame and adulation it generates can be vast and thoroughly unfair. For one such underappreciated musical icon, this high-spirited, warm-hearted portrait narrows that gap considerably.

Darlene Love generously shares her story in the latest of director Barry Avrich’s many engaging music docs, which include David Foster: Off The Record (TIFF ’19) and Oscar Peterson: Black + White (TIFF ’21).

Now in her eighties and still utterly magnetic on camera and on stage, Love recounts her journey, starting with her early days singing in a church choir in Los Angeles. Then came the many years she spent providing lead and background vocals, often uncredited, for some of the biggest hits of the 1960s while under contract to Phil Spector, the superstar producer who became her nemesis. Indeed, Spector’s machinations sparked decades of intense professional and personal struggles. Yet, despite every setback, Love weathered the storm to claim the centre-stage spotlight she has always deserved.

It all makes for an incredible story full of triumphs, heartbreaks, and inspirational demonstrations of resilience. It’s no wonder Love attracted so many friends along the way. Avrich assembles a who’s who of luminaries — Cher, Dionne Warwick, Bruce Springsteen, and David Letterman, among others — to express their admiration and affection.

Of course, there’s plenty of music to savour here, too. Along with a trove of archival clips, Avrich’s film features thrilling new sequences of Love and guest musicians like Paul Shaffer performing her most treasured songs, including “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” the holiday song that made Darlene Love the indisputable Queen of Christmas.
darlene-love-i-know-where-ive-been.teaser: Stars like Bruce Springsteen, Cher, and Dionne Warwick sing the praises of an underappreciated musical icon in this high-spirited and warm-hearted portrait from Canadian director Barry Avrich (Oscar Peterson: Black + White, TIFF ’21).

gail.title: Gail
gail.synopsis:
The titular character of Michael Maxxis’ documentary is a New York City subway station agent from the Bronx who, in her free time, is a dedicated superfan of the Canadian band Our Lady Peace.

A follower of the group since 1995, Gail is readying herself for their winter cross-country tour celebrating the 30th anniversary of making music. To every New Yorker she encounters during her preparation, which includes doctor and dental appointments and buying new shoes, she becomes an unofficial ambassador for both Canada and Our Lady Peace.

The doc tracks Gail as she journeys from Saskatoon VIP meet-and-greets with the quartet — lead singer Raine Maida, bassist Duncan Coutts, guitarist Steve Mazur, and drummer Jason Pierce, who rose to prominence during the late-1990s with songs like “Superman is Dead” and “Clumsy” — to their final Canadian tour stop in Halifax. Along the way, she wears her blind devotion like a badge of honour, which can sometimes lead to awkward exchanges.

Although this is an unconventional music doc, music is a key component. With an original score by Lesley Barber (Bonjour Tristesse, TIFF ’24) and orchestral arrangements by Eric Rosse (who produced Tori Amos’ groundbreaking album Little Earthquakes), music amplifies the dynamic soundscape of Gail’s Our Lady Peace experience.

A raw and resolute look at how music can impact one person, Gail is executive produced by Jason Reitman and Jason Blumenfeld (Saturday Night, TIFF ’24) and Our Lady Peace.
gail.teaser: This music documentary on an Our Lady Peace superfan follows her on the band’s 30th anniversary Canadian tour, and boasts an original score by Lesley Barber (Bonjour Tristesse, TIFF ’24), and orchestral arrangements by Eric Rosse (Tori Amos’ Little Earthquakes).

half.title: HALF
half.synopsis:
Since its 1970s heyday, the “curry western” has been a popular genre style across the Indian film industry. Indebted to American and Italian varieties of the form, these epics remixed the iconography and style of filmmakers like John Ford and Sergio Leone with culturally specific ingredients to fit a rural Indian frontier beset by roving gangs of bandits known as dacoits. In Samjad’s HALF, the subgenre further mutates with the introduction of vampires, a hallowed horror archetype that has previously permeated neo-Westerns like From Dusk Till Dawn and Near Dark. In this context, it bears down on those aforementioned bandits with a righteous fury and insatiable thirst for vengeance.

Following a wintery prologue that establishes our vamps Ethan (Ranjith Sajeev) and Ivy (Aiswarya Raj), twin siblings whose interspecies parentage (human mother, revenant dad) grants them supernatural abilities and spares them from the usual inconveniences, we catch up with the pair as they are traversing the desolate roads of the Rajasthan desert. Suddenly ambushed by local marauders who brutalize their bodies with a viciousness that recalls Mario Bava’s Rabid Dogs, brother and sister soon recover under cover of darkness and set out to maul, maim, and murder everyone responsible for the offense.

With action skilfully choreographed by Very Tri Yulisman — who conducted the martial mayhem of The Raid 2, The Night Comes for Us, and Headshot — HALF is a rousing cavalcade of guts and gore, set to the eclectic Malayalam soundtrack of the nonverbal Ivy’s cellphone playlist and the percussive pummeling of Ethan’s fists.
half.teaser: Twin half-blooded vampires (Ranjith Sajeev and Aiswarya Raj) wage war with desert highway hijackers in a gory martial arts curry western from writer-director Samjad and choreographer Very Tri Yulisman (The Raid 2, The Night Comes for Us).

re-pair.title: Re/Pair
re-pair.synopsis:
“I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that now we’re in a crisis around Black and Jewish community,” says Black Lives Matter co-founder Patrisse Cullors who sits in discussion with her former camp counselor, Rabbi Susan Goldberg. This is just one of many riveting talks that are staged in Re/Pair between members of American Black and Jewish communities.

Filmmaker Lacey Schwartz Delgado has a stake in both identities, a personal history she explored in her documentary Little White Lie. Here, she creates a lively format to foster communication, by pairing up prominent Black and Jewish personalities from across different disciplines in conversation with one another. They include writers W. Kamau Bell and Adam Mansbach; commentators Van Jones and Batya Ungar-Sargon; actors Harry Lennix and David Schwimmer — to name a few of the 19 different pairings. Their conversations are interwoven into a wide-ranging discourse characterized by respect, candor, and humour.

The flow of topics brings up historical moments both good and bad. The civil rights alliance between Martin Luther King Jr. and Rabbi Abraham Heschel reminds us of the common causes these communities once found. Now how do we process divisive moments that trigger deep hurt, including the polarizing debates around Israel and Palestine? Today, as hateful demagogues push ideas like “replacement theory,” we can see how racism and antisemitism are continually twinned together. Re/Pair doesn’t offer simple solutions. But it does demonstrate the need for us to move away from our social media feedback loops and hold our own dialogues where listening is as important as speaking.
re-pair.teaser: Lacey Schwartz Delgado (Little White Lie) explores the bonds and tensions between American Black and Jewish communities in a series of dialogues with prominent figures.

the-perverts-guide-to-utopias.title: The Pervert's Guide to Utopias
the-perverts-guide-to-utopias.synopsis:
If you love talking about movies, decoding a director’s intent or extrapolating on your own interpretations, then we’ve got the ultimate aphrodisiac for you in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias. Slavoj Žižek, a professor of philosophy and psychoanalysis, is an academic rock star renowned for riffing on cultural theory. Twenty years ago, he embarked on a collaboration with filmmaker Sophie Fiennes that started with The Pervert’s Guide to Cinema (TIFF ’06) in which they created a free-flowing essay interpreting film clips from a psychoanalytic perspective. They reprised the method in The Pervert’s Guide to Ideology (TIFF ’12). Don’t worry if you missed those; you can start fresh with this third installment that applies their lively approach to a new filmography that interweaves ideas about utopias, dystopias, faith, fascism, revolution, environmentalism, vampires, zombies, cloning, and more.

It’s a heady intellectual ride, infused with mischief and glee. Žižek starts by observing that cinema has the unique power to show us utopian views we don’t normally get in our daily life. “If aliens were to visit our Earth,” he says, “I would tell them to look at the movies and you will understand us.” One of the continuing delights in the Pervert’s series is that Fiennes stages Žižek in recreations of famous movie tableaus, framing him in iconic settings from Apocalypse Now, V for Vendetta, The Handmaid’s Tale, and others as he delivers his insights. If you look to movies as a chance to expand your mind, join the bandwagon of perverts.
the-perverts-guide-to-utopias.teaser: Twenty years after The Pervert’s Guide to Cinema, the renowned intellectual Slavoj Žižek reunites with director Sophie Fiennes for a fresh meditation on movies and ideas that crackles with energy.

the-spiral.title: The Spiral
the-spiral.synopsis:
On a dark and stormy night, Alice (Romana Maggiora Vergano) is surprised to answer the door to her estranged mother Anna (Jasmine Trinca) who has a sinister story to spin. Twenty years earlier, when their family seemed idyllic, a tragedy befell Alice; one whose consequences were circumvented by a bargain struck between Anna and an enigmatic stranger. But the pact came with a terrible price, and Anna found herself increasingly entangled with her Faustian benefactor. At first dismissing her mother’s confession as a desperate excuse to explain the erosion of their relationship, each tragic revelation brings Alice closer to uncovering the true and shocking reason for her mother's visit.

Skilfully turning the screws on its audience in tandem with his besieged characters, Paolo Strippoli directs this riveting psychological chiller with assured style and an appealing classicism that recalls Rod Serling’s ingenious mapping of high-concept horror on paranoid morality plays in The Twilight Zone. Divided across four chapters, Strippoli and Salvatore de Chirico’s elegant script perversely ratchets each episode with discomforting confrontations of decidedly bourgeois anxieties, revealing a canny critique of the lengths people will go to combat an undesirable destiny, and who they’re willing to have shoulder the burden

Enveloped in a sumptuously photographed but pervasive pall of unblinking dread, The Spiral further distinguishes its cautionary tale del momento from other recent popular treatises on the unintended side effects of supernatural wish fulfillment with the wicked personification of its devilish dealer, formidably portrayed by Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, whose icy calm and menacing stare will pervasively shudder the most steadfast soul.

Content advisory: suicide, self-harm, explicit violence, accident trauma, coarse language, scenes of surgery, mature themes
the-spiral.teaser: Director Paolo Strippoli turns the screws on a desperate mother (Jasmine Trinca) as she confesses a series of Faustian bargains to her estranged daughter (Romana Maggiora Vergano) in this riveting morality chiller.

vintage-violence.title: Vintage Violence
vintage-violence.synopsis:
Initially worlds apart, disgraced American urban explorer Carter (Cole Sprouse) and his Japanese online follower Izumi (Kiko Mizuhara) are drawn together in an impromptu business venture after Carter uncovers a cache of rare vintage jeans that could fetch a fortune in Japan’s collectors market.

But Izumi’s helpful overture masks a deceitful plot advanced by her boyfriend Hiro (Nijiro Murakami), who plans to steal the denim to repay a debt to a Levi’s-obsessed crime boss. The double-cross soon draws all parties into the path of Ko (Pierre Taki), an exiled Yakuza enforcer armed with a “speedball” drug spray for a middle finger and a resolve to wreak revenge on the criminal underworld. Chaos proceeds to reign, “like, comment, and subscribe” and the ol’ ultraviolence “follows” for more.

Recalling the freewheeling sensibilities of a Japanese V-Cinema exploitation film, Vintage Violence is the latest “chronically online” caper from internet-age satirist Eugene Kotlyarenko (Spree). Meshing his signature collage of digital screens and subjects with the stylized milieu of a Gakuryū Ishii or Takashi Miike movie, Kotlyarenko fashions a funny, hyper-contemporary comic thriller that seeds irreverence and romance with a candid authenticity, despite an elastic relationship with realism.

Sprouse and Mizuhara’s effortless charisma supports this high-wire tone, endearingly inhabiting a star-crossed pair whose connection is first sparked, and then literally propelled, by their digital devices. As does the film’s captivating aesthetic coherence, in part courtesy of Sean Price Williams’ visceral cinematography, which reliably captures all of its madcap hijinks through livestreams, pachinko parlours, and strikingly original, technology-driven foot chases through Tokyo.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.

Content advisory: explicit violence, accident trauma, coarse language, drug use, mature themes, sexual content
vintage-violence.teaser: In Eugene Kotlyarenko’s mixed-media caper, a livestreamer (Cole Sprouse) discovers a cache of vintage denim only to run afoul of the Yakuza when he is lured to Japan to sell the jeans by one of his subscribers (Kiko Mizuhara).

bunker.title: Bunker
bunker.synopsis:
Oscar winners Penélope Cruz (TIFF ’06’s Volver) and Javier Bardem (TIFF ’07’s No Country For Old Men) — together on screen for the first time since TIFF ’18’s Everybody Knows — play a couple whose bond becomes tested when a lucrative proposal prompts an ethical impasse. The latest from Oscar-winning writer-director Florian Zeller (TIFF ’20’s The Father) is an investigation into the limits of long-term partnership and an incisive exploration of class disparity.

In 17 years of marriage, literary agent Sofia (Cruz, also at this year’s Festival in La Bola Negra) has never resented her “starchitect” husband Miguel (Bardem, also at this year’s Festival in The Beloved) for uprooting the family from Madrid to London, where he rose to prominence. Fissures appear in their foundation, however, when a mysterious billionaire (Paul Dano, TIFF ’25’s The Wizard of the Kremlin) asks Miguel to design a luxury bunker where a tiny cluster of the ultra-wealthy can take shelter in an apocalypse.

The offer appeals to Miguel’s vanity as much as his pocketbook: this is an opportunity to furnish a pyramid for a modern-day pharaoh. But for Sofia, the proposal reeks of the gross inequality that is destroying the world. As tensions mount, Miguel becomes preoccupied by what he deems as a neighbour’s violation of his privacy, while Sofia seeks a promotion at work — and is disarmed by the attention of an attractive young author.

Supported by Stephen Graham (TIFF ’25’s Good Boy), Patrick Schwarzenegger (The White Lotus, also at the Festival with Love of Your Life), and Dano, Cruz and Bardem infuse their roles with complexity and vulnerability. In this tale of affluence, paranoia, and ambition, there is nothing more precious than love.
bunker.teaser: Oscar winners Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem play a couple whose bond is tested when a mysterious billionaire’s proposal prompts an ethical impasse in the latest from Oscar-winning writer-director Florian Zeller (TIFF ’20’s The Father).

a-good-little-soldier.title: A Good Little Soldier
a-good-little-soldier.synopsis:
Known for his portraits of individuals struggling against capitalism in films such as At War (2018) and The Measure of a Man (2015), Stéphane Brizé continues the tradition of French social realism with a story set within the skyscrapers and glass offices of the corporate world. Carla (Alba Rohrwacher, also at the Festival with A Common Story) is a high-powered executive in Human Resources with a successful career, having risen the ranks in the private sector by trading time at home with her son for long nights at work. Just recruited to a new position, she’s tasked by her demanding boss Arnaud (Vincent Lindon, Couture, TIFF ’25) with the responsibility of reconciling performance goals and employee well-being with a strategic campaign.

Brizé’s 11th feature expands upon the management side of labour, a perspective he first explored in Another World (2021). He captures how the corporate milieu has distorted policies of inclusion and subverted concepts like safe spaces to protect those already at the top of the hierarchy from discomfort or change. Faced with conflicting directives and the prospect of defending badly behaved high performers, Carla is pushed to assess her own humanity and that of her colleagues. With searing performances from returning collaborators Rohrwacher and Lindon, the film exposes the alienating, dehumanizing consequences of capitalist structures.
a-good-little-soldier.teaser: In Stéphane Brizé’s latest capitalist critique, Carla (Alba Rohrwacher) is pushed to her moral limits when she is recruited to rebrand a company’s image, compromising people for profit to serve her corporate supervisors.

kick-on.title: Kick On
kick-on.synopsis:
Torn between taking care of her sickly sister and tying one on with her mates, Eden (Markella Kavenagh) succumbs to peer pressure and embarks on an all-night rager. Looking to prolong their revelry with some recreational stimulants, they soon find themselves dropping in on Ray (Nikolai Nikolaeff), a notorious mobster’s volatile son, who runs a drug den atop a dilapidated high-rise in a malignant Melbourne neighbourhood. But what was supposed to be a simple score quickly plummets into paranoid pandemonium as a rash decision triggers a spot of homicide with far too many witnesses. Now, Eden and her friends must fight to survive the night in what transforms into a bloody ripper of a siege thriller.

Gorehounds can expect to be well fed as Phillip Klimek’s no-frills script constructs a mean machine of ultraviolence that director Nick Kozakis fulfills with aplomb. Visceral body-horror gags, from head to toe, recall the brutal cruelty of Jeremy Saulnier’s Green Room, and the tension is gleefully stretched as shotguns fire, glass shatters, bones break, and serrated cans are shoved into eyelids with a manic abandon.

It’s as if that drug-fueled nightmare of a scene with Alfred Molina from Boogie Nights was a movie unto itself, only soaked in kerosene and thrown on the barbie. And every time you think you’ve had your fill, Kick On cheekily retorts “ah c’mon, you just got here” and serves you an even gnarlier plate of seconds before smashing it over your skull.

Content advisory: strobing, extreme violence, accident trauma, coarse language, drug use, sexual content
kick-on.teaser: Looking to prolong their night of partying, four youths are plunged into paranoid pandemonium after crossing a mobster’s volatile son in Nick Kozakis’ bloody ripper of a siege thriller.

le-faux-soir.title: Le Faux Soir
le-faux-soir.synopsis:
The histories of the resistance movements in German-occupied Europe are full of courageous acts of heroism. Yet few are as cunning or surprising as the events captured in this fleet-footed and thoroughly entertaining thriller by Belgian director Michaël R. Roskam.

Inspired by the true story of a uniquely daring operation in Brussels in November of 1943, Le Faux Soir follows a group of resistance fighters as they proceed step-by-step through a scheme that the Nazis in charge most definitely did not see coming. These crafty conspirators’ goal: to turn the Germans’ propaganda tools against them by printing and distributing a spoof edition of the newspaper Le Soir.

Unlike most pranks, this one all but guarantees the execution of any perpetrator who gets captured. With every challenge and setback comes yet more risks for an unlikely array of allies that includes Marc “Yvon” Aubrion (Arieh Worthalter), an anarchist poet whose unruly ways may prove to be an advantage in a plan that demands so much improvisation and ingenuity.

A director who first broke out internationally with his Academy Award–nominated first feature Bullhead (2011) and who was last at the Festival with Racer and the Jailbird (2017), Roskam makes terrific use of a superb cast that also features Belgian and French stars Mélanie Thierry, Bouli Lanners, and Karim Leklou.

Together, they display the same grace under pressure as the real people who inspired them, delivering a historical drama that has all the pace and panache of a classic heist movie.
le-faux-soir.teaser: Inspired by a fact-based act of subversive irreverence in Nazi-occupied Brussels, Michaël R. Roskam’s thriller delivers a historical drama that feels more like a heist movie.

obsession.title: Obsession
obsession.synopsis:
Woe is Bear (Michael Johnston), who has long carried a torch for his childhood friend Nikki (Inde Navarrette). When another attempted profession of love fizzles, Bear wistfully wishes for romantic reciprocation, unfortunately doing so while in possession of a trinket with supernatural properties of The Monkey’s Paw variety.

Suddenly, Nikki is all over Bear, and he is quick to indulge in this long-desired turnabout while ignoring the ramifications of her intensifying fixation. Before long, Bear’s fantasy turns to nightmare as Nikki’s personality begins to twitch with a disturbing dysphoria that sinisterly suggests her autonomy has been usurped by a malignant entity that wants them both, body and soul.

“Be careful what you wish for” may be a staple in the horror genre, but writer-director Curry Barker enlivens this well-worn premise by lacing its inherent irony with a wickedly wry tone and an anxious tension that’ll plummet the stomach of even hardened Midnighters. Having honed high-concept absurdism and creeping dread from his online productions, Barker deftly demonstrates a savvy command of tone and terror reminiscent of fellow sketch comedian Zach Cregger’s Barbarian.

As with that auspicious debut, Barker’s first feature preserves an uncomfortable relatability in its hyperbolic scenario. Though literally featuring a customer service call from (and possibly to) Hell, Obsession cuts to the quick as it lays bare the innate violence in romantic objectification with an unforgiving candidness. That's made all the more disarming, thanks to exceptionally nuanced performances, particularly from Navarrette whose “Freaky Nikki” oscillates between doe-eyed desire and devastating torment that will chill you to the bone.
obsession.teaser: When a hopeless romantic makes a wish that his long-time crush falls in love with him, a sinister enchantment ensues in writer-director Curry Barker’s freaky and frightening feature debut.

river.title: River
river.synopsis:
In his acclaimed 2018 short film In Sound, We Live Forever, writer-director Joshua Giuliano shrewdly split the sound and image of a slasher scenario, so that the violence was heard before its consequences were observed. This eerie dissonance laid bare an insidious undertow inherent to the horror genre, a current that, once one is caught up in it, carries its victims toward a seemingly grisly inevitability from which there is no escape. Such is the current that three siblings find themselves adrift upon in River, Giuliano’s audacious nerve-shredder of a feature debut.

Having convened to scatter the ashes of their late father from a family motorboat, embittered sisters (Jane Levy, TIFF ’14’s Bang Bang Baby, and Jessica Rothe, TIFF ’23’s Boy Kills World), and their younger brother (Max Mattern, television’s Cape Fear) stall out beneath a derelict bridge along a rural waterway. Familial wounds are provoked, and fingers are pointed, first at each other, but soon at the sudden appearance of a strange man (Dane DiLiegro, Prey) eerily staring from the shoreline. Tall and statuesque, the figure’s face is seemingly without features or emotion, just a palpable, anonymous malevolence. And when he stops merely staring, the family must come together and start surviving.

From that anxious fulcrum, the open water becomes oppressively claustrophobic. And as a pastoral surrealism seeps into this dire strait, the suspense is wound with such austere starkness that its naked machinations are wickedly weaponized to play with the expectations of even the savviest slasher scholar. Conducted with the canny confidence of a Carpenter — John to be precise — Giuliano has carved a whole new “Shape” in terror.

Content advisory: explicit violence, accident trauma, coarse language, mature themes, strobing effects
river.teaser: Joshua Giuliano makes an audacious debut with a suspenseful slasher that sets three embittered siblings adrift along a rural waterway, and in the sights of a masked killer.

the-unknown.title: The Unknown
the-unknown.synopsis:
A moody, existential body-swap puzzler, drenched in atmospheric dread, L’Inconnue is a rare film that directly activates cinema’s innate capacity to haunt. Propelled by superlative performances, intelligent writing, and an audacious style in which the uncanny bleeds into a fierce naturalism, this third feature by acclaimed French filmmaker, actor, and Academy Award–winning screenwriter Arthur Harari (co-writer of TIFF ’23’s Anatomy of a Fall) was a highlight of the 2026 Cannes Competition.

After David (Niels Schneider), a withdrawn photographer, attends a raucous party and tries a mysterious pill, he locks eyes with a woman he vaguely recognizes (Léa Seydoux), leading to a backroom hookup. The next morning’s hangover, however, reveals that he has somehow come to occupy the woman’s body, setting him on a frantic search for answers. He manages to learn that she is a German actor named Eva, and discovers that rather than a traditional swap, a young terrified woman named Malia (Lilith Grasmug) is, in fact, now housed in David’s body. As David/Eva and Malia/David are forced to grapple with the psychological toll of a disembodied existence, the film’s daring narrative grows evermore labyrinthine and unsettling.

Based on a graphic novel by Harari and his brother Lucas, L’Inconnue is heady and vertiginous, with the crepuscular, constantly surprising cinematography provided by a third talented brother, Tom Harari. Other key contributions include a terrific supporting role by Romanian filmmaker Radu Jude (also at the Festival with Diary of a Chambermaid). While garnering deserved comparisons to the likes of Antonioni, Rivette, Lynch, and De Palma, the film’s ambiguity and sense of despair feel uniquely attuned to the multiplicities of our present day.

Content advisory: accident trauma, drug use, sexual content, nudity, mature themes
the-unknown.teaser: A highlight of this year’s Cannes Competition, the third feature by acclaimed French filmmaker, actor, and screenwriter Arthur Harari (co-writer of Anatomy of a Fall) is a moody, existential body-swap puzzler starring an extraordinary Léa Seydoux and a near-unrecognizable Niels Schneider.

a-long-winter.title: A Long Winter
a-long-winter.synopsis:
Sunday, September 17: This screening will be presented with open captions and live captioning for the onstage components.

Following the extraordinary emotional resonance of 2023’s All of Us Strangers, Andrew Haigh returns with a period drama occupying the liminal space between hope and acceptance. Adapted by Haigh and Colm Tóibín from the acclaimed Irish novelist’s short story, A Long Winter follows Mike (Fred Hechinger), a young man on the cusp of adulthood whose life is upended when his mother disappears during the first blizzard of the season. As the search stretches from days into weeks, the onset of winter becomes inseparable from the family’s slow reckoning with the possibility that she may never return.

While Mike’s emerging sexuality forms part of his journey, Haigh’s gaze remains fixed on something broader: the emotional fault lines that open within a family when normalcy is ruptured. Set in the mountains of Colorado and filmed in the breathtaking Canadian Rockies, the vast landscape is both beautiful and unforgiving, mirroring the emotional distance between Mike and his stoic father. Haigh’s patient, intimate filmmaking finds an ideal companion in Tóibín’s measured storytelling, where every silence, glance, and gesture carries extraordinary weight.

Hechinger (The White Lotus) embodies Mike’s evolution with remarkable sensitivity. Ebon Moss-Bachrach (The Bear) is superb as an aging father struggling to express his own grief, while Caitríona Balfe (Belfast, TIFF ’21) leaves a profound impression as the absent mother whose disappearance shapes every moment that follows. With memorable support from Kit Connor (Heartstopper) and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai (Reservation Dogs), A Long Winter is beautifully observed work from one of contemporary cinema’s most compassionate filmmakers.
a-long-winter.teaser: After his mother disappears during the first blizzard of the season, a young man refuses to give up hope as one long Colorado winter reshapes his relationship with his father and his understanding of the man he is becoming. From Andrew Haigh, the acclaimed director of All of Us Strangers.

i-play-rocky.title: I Play Rocky
i-play-rocky.synopsis:
There is no greater movie about beating the odds through sheer determination than Rocky. But the story behind that box-office smash — which turned its unknown writer-star Sylvester Stallone into a phenomenon — is just as unlikely and inspiring. Helmed by Oscar winner Peter Farrelly (TIFF ’18 People’s Choice Award winner Green Book) and featuring a career-making performance from Anthony Ippolito, I Play Rocky vividly recreates a paradigm-shifting moment in Hollywood history and chronicles the meteoric rise of one of cinema's preeminent multihyphenates.

Sylvester (Ippolito) dreams of being an actor, but he grew up poor, shuttled from home to home, and at one point lived on the street. Now in his twenties, the closest he's come to the big screen is acting in a porno and working as an usher. Then he sees Muhammad Ali fight Chuck Wepner, and inspiration hits: in a few fevered days, he writes a screenplay about an underdog boxer who goes the distance. Studio executives love it — but they balk at Sylvester’s stipulation that he play the hero. The production of this ambitious indie film will prove more arduous than anyone could have imagined.

In an uncanny echo of the legend he’s embodying, Ippolito is a revelation as the young Stallone: the stance, the cadences, that air of gravitas and diligence. He's supported by a dream cast that includes Tracy Letts (TIFF ’17’s Lady Bird), Stephan James (TIFF ’18’s If Beale Street Could Talk), and Oscar nominee Matt Dillon. I Play Rocky soars with sweat and spirit.
i-play-rocky.teaser: Featuring a career-making performance from Anthony Ippolito, the latest from Oscar winner Peter Farrelly (TIFF ’18 People’s Choice Award winner Green Book) vividly recreates the story of how an unknown named Sylvester Stallone got Rocky produced — and became a superstar.

the-stunt-driver.title: The Stunt Driver
the-stunt-driver.synopsis:
Jay Baruchel and director Michael Dowse re-team for a raucous yet heartfelt comedy about a Canadian stuntman who dared to dream big and fly (very) high.

Even when compared with his fellow mavericks, misfits, and adrenaline junkies who wowed audiences with their high-speed stunts during the 1970s golden age of daredevils, Ken Carter was one of a kind. Known as “The Mad Canadian” and immortalized in Robert Fortier’s 1981 NFB documentary The Devil At Your Heels — a film whose creation is very much woven into this successor’s gonzo tapestry — Carter repeatedly risked his life for a series of car stunts that culminated in the most ambitious project of all: a historic jump in a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental across a mile-wide expanse of the St. Lawrence River. What could go wrong? In short: everything.

Powered by Jay Baruchel’s all-out performance as the man behind the wheel, Michael Dowse’s endearingly scrappy comedy honours its inspiration by portraying all the steps and missteps over the course of Carter’s years-long quest. The fact that The Stunt Driver frequently matches the anarchic energy of Baruchel and Dowse’s previous teaming on Goon (TIFF ’11) is no surprise. What’s more unexpected is the poignancy that the actor brings to his take on a man whose displays of bravado conceal a welter of fears and insecurities. It’s easy to see why he relies on steadfast allies like his wife Gloria (Laurence Leboeuf) and his car designer and technician Dick Keller (Ed Helms) — and why he’s so easily undermined by the machinations of his American nemesis, the legendary Evel Knievel (Ben Foster).

All this makes for a thoroughly mad and Canadian mostly-true-life tale that will reintroduce a new generation of viewers to Carter’s wild story and his reckless determination to tell the laws of gravity to shove it.

Content advisory: coarse language, drug use, sexual content (innuendo, language), violence
the-stunt-driver.teaser: Jay Baruchel and director Michael Dowse re-team for a raucous yet heartfelt comedy about a Canadian stuntman who dared to dream big and fly (very) high.

villeneuve-the-rise-of-a-legend.title: Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend
villeneuve-the-rise-of-a-legend.synopsis:
This adrenaline-charged biopic chronicles the career of one of Canada’s foremost athletes. Directed by Yan Lanouette Turgeon (Rock Paper Scissors) and written by Daniel Roby (TIFF ’04’s White Skin) and Guillaume Lonergan (also at this year’s Festival with Alice), Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend stars Rémi Goulet as the kid from Quebec who changed the way Formula One was done.

Born to a piano tuner in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Gilles Villeneuve (Goulet) came from a humble background, but his passion for speed and precision was evident from a young age. He started out snowmobile racing before entering drag-racing events with his modified 1967 Mustang.

In 1970 he marries Joann (Rosalie Bonenfant), with whom he will go on to have two children, but Gilles is not one to settle down. While the upper echelons of competitive racing seem elusive, the exclusive domain of the elite, Gilles persists. He finally makes his Formula One debut at the 1977 British Grand Prix, where he impresses famed entrepreneur and driver Enzo Ferrari (Frank Crudele, TIFF ’04’s Saint Ralph), who helps Gilles take the fast track to his dreams.

In his too-short life, Villeneuve achieved a dizzying roster of triumphs: six wins, two pole positions, eight fastest laps, and 13 podiums in Formula One. The Rise of a Legend shows us what he overcame to get there, through a fusion of rare talent, extreme discipline, the support of his loved ones, and a devil-may-care attitude that left others in the dust.
villeneuve-the-rise-of-a-legend.teaser: Chronicling the exhilarating career of Gilles Villeneuve, one of Canada’s foremost athletes, this biopic from director Yan Lanouette Turgeon stars Rémi Goulet as the kid from Quebec who changed Formula One.

your-mother-your-mother-your-mother.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
your-mother-your-mother-your-mother.synopsis:
A showcase for the immense range and singular magnetism of Oscar winner Mahershala Ali (TIFF ’18 People’s Choice Award winner Green Book), the latest from writer-director Bassam Tariq (Mogul Mowgli) is an audaciously inventive Texas-set action thriller in which the line that separates religious devotion from righteous bloodshed evaporates in a cloud of mayhem.

Latif (Ali) is a devout Muslim and a loving family man who also happens to be a contract killer. He has a strict code: he never uses guns and he only accepts targets the world would be better off without.

After his beloved wife dies, Latif resolves to end his criminal career and focus on caring for his three children — but his longtime employer Mike (Laith Nakli, TIFF ’25’s Lucky Lu) has other plans. Latif is having a hard enough time finding breast milk for his baby girl and wants no part in Mike and cowboy Haun Yoon’s (John Cho) rapidly escalating feud but, as his bloodstained past comes back to haunt him, he may have no choice in the matter.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother — its title a reference to an Islamic hadith — is a wild ride, overflowing with spectacle and suspense, tenderness and violence. As Latif navigates a minefield of viciousness and fanaticism, he’s also forced to confront his own moral hypocrisies. Only Ali could embody such a delicate balance of menace and grace.

Content advisory: explicit violence, sexual content, coarse language, mature themes
your-mother-your-mother-your-mother.teaser: Oscar winner Mahershala Ali (TIFF ’18 People’s Choice Award winner Green Book) stars as a devout Muslim, loving family man, and contract killer in this audaciously inventive Texas-set action thriller from writer-director Bassam Tariq (Mogul Mowgli).

brace-your-heart.title: Brace Your Heart
brace-your-heart.synopsis:
With each film, Amanda Kernell further establishes herself as a defining voice in contemporary Nordic cinema. Returning to Sápmi for her third feature, Kernell crafts an intimate, layered love story in which the rhythms of reindeer herding shape every aspect of life, from family and community to identity, desire, and belonging.

When Ejva inherits her late father’s reindeer herd, mounting expectations push her toward accepting the romantic advances of Heaika, a powerful local leader whose courtship gradually gives way to mistreatment. Falling unexpectedly for his cousin Nejla offers the possibility of another life, but it’s one that threatens Ejva’s future and her place with her people and the land that has always defined her. What begins as a personal story gradually reveals itself to be something more expansive, as questions of autonomy and tradition become inseparable from the realities of life in northernmost Europe.

Kernell has a remarkable gift for creating fully realized characters from the smallest of gestures and imbuing landscapes with emotional power. As both writer and director, she brings a singular cinematic vision to every frame while leads Elli Sara Valkeapää and Vincent Niia — both actual reindeer herders like much of the cast — deliver extraordinary performances as Ejva and Nejla.

Without losing sight of its deeply moving story, Brace Your Heart becomes a richly observed portrait of what Sámi women are sometimes asked to endure to hold onto what is rightfully theirs.
brace-your-heart.teaser: Amanda Kernell’s luminous third drama is a richly observed portrait of love, resilience, and the enduring strength of Sámi women in northernmost Europe.

djinn-wedding.title: Djinn Wedding
djinn-wedding.synopsis:
Djinn Wedding follows four siblings through three distinct stages: childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Since their occupation of the house they live in is considered unlawful, a kind of curse hangs over the family’s fates. Deniz (İlhan Şen), the eldest son, is able to leave the village to study in the city. His beloved sister Ceren (Demit Özdemir) has no other way out but marriage, while their younger brother, Halit (Kaan Yildirim), is forced to remain in the village to take care of their disabled brother, Yasin (Sarp Bozkurt). During Ceren’s wedding, long-buried memories begin to resurface.

Carried by its superb cast, Djinn Wedding has just the right amount of mystery to make you want to delve deeper, while using numerous narrative devices to ensure it never reveals too much. The wedding scene — the film’s centrepiece, which lays bare all the family tensions — is a captivating sequence following multiple characters as different events unfold simultaneously, reminiscent of some of the more memorable long takes in other great movies.

The weight of customs, patriarchy, family responsibilities (including the rifts between those who evade them and those who bear them), and societal expectations (exemplified by the village imam, who is criticized for buying a car) are skilfully explored. Ferit Karahan’s atmospheric family drama, swinging between beliefs, hopes, and dissolution, is a fantastic piece of work.
djinn-wedding.teaser: Set in a remote Anatolian village, Ferit Karahan’s Djinn Wedding is an impressive family drama that unravels family secrets and conflicts across three periods of time.

the-smell-of-apples.title: The Smell of Apples
the-smell-of-apples.synopsis:
In John Trengove’s relentless third feature, a sheltered 11-year-old white South African boy gradually comes to realize the horrors of the apartheid system.

In 1974, in an insulated and sunny white apartheid South Africa, 11-year-old Marnus (Dawian van der Westhuizen) lives his best life. His amazing father (Hilton Pelser) plays a lot with him, his beautiful mother (Maude Sandham) is a devoted spouse, his friend Frikkie (Wian Carstens) is almost a brother and his nanny Doreen (Celeste Matthews Wannenburgh) discreetly takes care of everyone.

But when Mr. Smith (Alejandro Goic), a secretive Chilean colleague of his father, turns up at their home, the peaceful harmony of Marnus’s idyllic life is suddenly shattered. In just five days, his wonderful world begins to crumble. Realizing that the beauty around him is actually tinged with cruelty and oppression, Marnus comes to see that everything he once believed was nothing more than a mirage.

Adapted from South African writer Mark Behr’s 1993 bestselling novel, The Smell of Apples offers an intimate and radical insight into the apartheid regime from the perspective of those who benefited from it — whether they were aware of it or not. Behind every privilege and advantage lies a sordid truth that everyone prefers to ignore. By facing that reality head-on, director John Trengove offers us not only a brilliant exploration of human baseness, but also a stark reminder that responsibility is shared with those who pretend it does not exist.
the-smell-of-apples.teaser: In John Trengove’s relentless third feature, a sheltered 11-year-old white South African boy gradually comes to realize the horrors of the apartheid system.

conversation-with-the-sea.title: Conversation With The Sea
conversation-with-the-sea.synopsis:
Set in Jerusalem, Muayad Alayan’s fourth feature sensitively explores the relentless situation in which Kamal, a Palestinian father (a stunning Kamel El Basha), finds himself trapped.

Convicted by an Israeli court, Kamal must repay the overdue social security contributions owed by his son, who died twenty years earlier in the Red Sea. With no evidence but the name of an Israeli woman found in a report, Kamal must prove his son’s death while re-establishing contact with his circle of friends and family, who haven’t seen him in years and hold a deep grudge against him. In a highly safeguarded society, his investigations reveal numerous tensions between communities, and the difficulty of proving his son's innocence.

How does one mourn a loved one whose body one has never seen? Film after film, Alayan depicts the lives of Palestinians in Israel and the complexities of their coexistence. The strength of this screenplay lies in the development of its main character: at 60, Kamal carries a heavy past that is revealed only through the encounters he has as the film unfolds. A remorse-ridden antihero caught between police violence and everyday racism, he moves through the city with determination, in an almost futile struggle to clear his son’s name.

Based on true events, with a fantastic lead actor and meticulous direction, Conversation With The Sea is both a social commentary and a personal quest.
conversation-with-the-sea.teaser: Condemned to pay the social security contributions owed by his son, a father (Kamel El Basha) desperately tries to prove his death in the moving drama Conversation With The Sea.

man-in-motion-the-rick-hansen-story.title: Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story
man-in-motion-the-rick-hansen-story.synopsis:
All screenings will be presented with open captions, with live captioning for the onstage components during the screenings on September 11 and September 12.

This portrait of a true Canadian icon takes us back to the roots of the disability rights movement and the building of a more accessible world. Produced by homegrown star Ryan Reynolds (TIFF ’25’s John Candy: I Like Me) and helmed by documentarian Adrian Buitenhuis (I Am Burt Reynolds, Anne Murray: Full Circle), Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story is a vital celebration of the magic that arises when athleticism meets activism.

Rick Hansen grew up playing sports, but a car accident at age 15 paralyzed him from the waist down. Remarkably, Hansen turned this life-altering event into a catalyst. He became the first student with a disability to graduate from the University of British Columbia with a degree in physical education, captured national championships in wheelchair volleyball and basketball, and went on to win six Paralympic medals in wheelchair racing. In 1985, galvanized by his friend Terry Fox’s Marathon of Hope — the subject of fellow Gala Presentation Run Terry Run — Hansen undertook the 26-month Man in Motion World Tour, traversing 40,075 km across 34 countries in his wheelchair, raising $26 million for the removal of barriers, forever changing public perception of people with disabilities, and inspiring David Foster and John Parr’s massive hit “St. Elmo's Fire (Man in Motion).”

Incorporating original interviews, personal audio recordings, and rare archival materials, Buitenhuis’ documentary chronicles Hansen’s era-defining tour, as well as his life and activism in the decades since. Man in Motion is about more than overcoming challenges — it’s about meeting life wherever it takes you, and becoming the best version of yourself.
man-in-motion-the-rick-hansen-story.teaser: This galvanizing portrait celebrates Rick Hansen, the great Canadian athlete and activist. It chronicles his 26-month Man In Motion World Tour: a 40,000-kilometre wheelchair journey that raised millions to eliminate accessibility barriers and transform public perception of people with disabilities.

marie-madeleine.title: Marie Madeleine
marie-madeleine.synopsis:
In the follow-up to her 2021 narrative feature debut Freda, Gessica Généus boldly reimagines the Biblical tale of Mary Magdalene set in vibrant Jacmel, Haiti. Marie Madeleine (played by Généus), a fiercely independent sex worker, carries a razor in her mouth during dates with clients and lives a bohemian lifestyle alongside the other women in her brothel.

After Marie collapses in the street, she is rescued by Joseph (Béonard Monteau), the dutiful and sexually repressed son of an evangelical preacher. He attends to her while harried nurses casually call her “whore” in the hospital hallway.

The city itself becomes a character, its constant soundscape underscoring the island’s conflicting rhythms of lapping waves, boisterous street festivals and parades, radio broadcasts of religious sermons, and parties spilling out into the streets.

Généus interjects moments of sublime surrealism as Marie and Joseph become closer — and she inspires him to pursue desires that his stern pastor father does not condone. All of their worlds collide explosively when the pastor opens a church directly across from Marie’s brothel and aggressively campaigns its madam to close up shop.

Shot in gorgeously saturated colours by Canadian cinematographer Nicolas Canniccioni (How to Have Sex, TIFF ’23), Marie Madeleine — named, in fact, for the protagonist’s grandmother — revels in the spirituality and daily lives of the island’s people. It celebrates forms of expression: dance, poetry, song, and sexuality in all the ways that they lead one back to their true self.

Content advisory: mature themes, sexual content, some violence, homophobic content
marie-madeleine.teaser: Géssica Généus directs and stars in this vibrant reimagining of the biblical tale of Mary Magdalene, following a free-spirited Haitian sex worker whose serendipitous involvement with a repressed preacher’s son opens each to possibilities.

misty-green.title: Misty Green
misty-green.synopsis:
Featuring a career-making performance from Slow Horses’ Rosalind Eleazar and supporting turns from Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver, and Anna Kendrick, Chris Rock’s latest as writer-director brilliantly satirizes the bigotry and hustle at the heart of Hollywood.

Superstar comic Chris Rock’s latest as writer-director is a hilarious, scathing satire of the institutional bigotry and soul-draining hustle that dominate the movie industry. Featuring a career-making lead performance from Rosalind Eleazar (TIFF ’19’s The Personal History of David Copperfield) and supporting turns from Oscar winner Daniel Kaluuya plus Oscar nominees Adam Driver and Anna Kendrick (also at this year’s Festival in Babies), Misty Green chronicles the extremes one Black actor goes to to keep both her career and brother alive.

Misty (Eleazar) is on the verge of a comeback, if only she could curb her worst habits. In a narcotic-fuelled mania, she went from winning an Emmy to losing a big project helmed by ace director Jordan (Rock). Jordan, however, is ready to give Misty another chance with his forthcoming remake of Dreamgirls. It’s a coveted opportunity, but Misty has competing concerns, such as her looming eviction and her brother (Kaluuya), navigating life with bipolar disorder, who gets into serious trouble. As pressure to procure funds mounts, Misty finds herself considering an offer by her former flame (Driver) that’s simultaneously heinous and lucrative beyond her wildest dreams.

In the tradition of such Black cinema milestones as Robert Townsend’s Hollywood Shuffle and Spike Lee’s TIFF ’00 feature Bamboozled, Rock’s searing portrait of Tinseltown exposes just how deeply racism, classism, and misogyny contaminate the motion picture ecosystem. Misty Green is one of the best LA movies in years — and its best jokes sting with the insight only a veteran wit like Rock could deliver.

Content advisory: strobe lighting, themes of sexual violence, sexual content, drug use, coarse language
misty-green.teaser: Featuring a career-making performance from Slow Horses’ Rosalind Eleazar and supporting turns from Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver, and Anna Kendrick, Chris Rock’s latest as writer-director brilliantly satirizes the bigotry and hustle at the heart of Hollywood.

rehearsals-for-a-revolution.title: Rehearsals for a Revolution
rehearsals-for-a-revolution.synopsis:
Celebrated Iranian actor Pegah Ahangarani’s breakout performance came at a young age in The Girl in the Sneakers (1999). Her career flourished over the years, appearing in approximately 40 films before pivoting to stepping behind the camera. Ahangarani’s debut feature is grounded in the Iranian concept of yād — mining memory — through an essayistic form, weaving together home movies, family photographs, and news broadcasts to construct a vivid portrait of Iran’s modern history in the four decades since the revolution.

Balancing the personal with the political, the film unfolds in five chapters, each devoted to a figure who shaped Ahangarani’s life: her revolutionary filmmaker father, Jamshid Ahangarani; her beloved teacher, Shermin Sarra; her uncle, Rashid; her close friend, Amir; with the final section dedicated to her young daughter, Lily. Each chapter confronts seismic turning points in Iranian history — moments when hope and the promise of change were palpable — from the 1997 election of Mohammad Khatami and the 2009 protests to the persistent oppression of the current regime and the ongoing destruction from U.S. and Israeli missiles.

Now living in exile, Ahangarani grapples with her role in the ongoing struggle — one that is resolute and unwavering. She clings fiercely to hope and to the “people who didn’t give up, who rehearsed for the revolution,” remaining steadfast in the fight for justice and freedom.

The winner of Cannes’ L'Œil d'Or documentary prize, Rehearsals for a Revolution skillfully fuses the political with the personal, resonating powerfully with current events.
rehearsals-for-a-revolution.teaser: Acclaimed actor-turned-documentarian Pegah Ahangarani draws on a trove of archival material to skillfully weave her personal narrative with Iranian politics over the past four decades.

run-terry-run.title: Run Terry Run
run-terry-run.synopsis:
This intimate and inspiring portrait from veteran filmmaker Sean Menard (TIFF ’17’s The Carter Effect) reveals the vulnerable human being behind the great Canadian icon. Drawing upon never-before-seen footage, Run Terry Run walks us through the arduous process and profound commitment that fostered Terry Fox’s magisterial Marathon of Hope.

It’s a story every Canadian child learns at school: in April 1980, 21-year-old Terrance Stanley Fox set out from St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, to raise awareness and funding for cancer research. Having an amputated right leg due to osteosarcoma, Fox was forced to use a poorly fitted, off-the-shelf artificial limb (advanced running prosthetics did not yet exist). Nevertheless, over 143 days, he ran a full marathon every day, traversing more than 5,000 kilometres. Fox made it all the way to Thunder Bay, Ontario, where unfortunately, the cancer had spread to his lungs, forcing him to stop. Fox died ten months later. Every year since, the Terry Fox Run honours his legacy and inspires millions of participants, now in upwards of 60 countries, to continue running for the cause.

The material the Fox family entrusted to Menard allows us to really get to know this charming, philosophical, good-humoured hero. Illness robbed Fox of many aspects of his youth but, in return, it gave him preternatural wisdom — and a vision of what it takes to enact real change. In an era marked by stark divisions, Fox’s activism continues to unite us with that most durable of all resources: hope.
run-terry-run.teaser: This intimate and inspiring portrait from filmmaker Sean Menard (TIFF ’17’s The Carter Effect) draws upon never-before-seen footage to reveal the arduous process and profound commitment behind Terry Fox’s Marathon of Hope to raise awareness and money for cancer research.

the-city-of-the-living.title: The City of the Living
the-city-of-the-living.synopsis:
Known for millennia as the Eternal City, Italy’s capital includes neighbourhoods — and underbellies — rarely seen by flocking tourists. In one such locale, La Storta, a 23-year-old car mechanic of modest means named Luca Varani (depicted by the talented Emanuele Di Stefano) made his way through the world with the support of loving parents (eloquently portrayed by Simona Senzacqua and Valerio Mastandrea, last at the Festival with 2014’s Pasolini) and his high school sweetheart, Marta (played with grace by newcomer Gaia Merlonghi).

At an age when everything feels possible yet also somehow lost, Luca led a double life. One night, after a seemingly chance encounter, Luca’s trajectory was set on a path of senseless violence. His young life, most of which would still have been on the horizon, ended in March 2016 at the hands of two privileged men who, on this drug-fuelled occasion, were fixated on murder.

The City of the Living is an anti-true crime film based on Nicola Lagioia’s bestselling literary chronicle of the same name. Director Edoardo Gabbriellini takes great care to honour Varani, whose life began in the besieged city of Sarajevo.

Skilfully shot by Amine Messadi (who also lensed Gabbriellini’s Holiday, which screened at TIFF ’23), the film delicately explores the social, cultural, and emotional dynamics behind the tragic true events. In doing so, it exposes the fractures in contemporary Roman life — reflecting the historical weight and rhetorical artifice of Italian politics — and serves as a mirror to society as a whole.
the-city-of-the-living.teaser: The City of the Living is Edoardo Gabbriellini’s (Holiday, TIFF ’23) gripping yet respectful anti-true crime film based on Nicola Lagioia’s bestselling literary chronicle about the senseless 2016 murder of a young man that rocked Rome.

the-secret-lives-of-baba-segis-wives.title: The Secret Lives of Baba Segi's Wives
the-secret-lives-of-baba-segis-wives.synopsis:
Based on Lola Shoneyin’s 2010 debut novel, which was later adapted for the stage, Daniel Oriahi’s The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives is a sharp, funny, and often devastating portrait of polygamous family life in contemporary Nigeria.

Baba Segi (Odunlade Adekola), a wealthy and haughty patriarch, has spent years building a household, marrying several women in the process: first wife Iya Segi (Iyabo Ojo), second wife Iya Tope (Mercy Aigbe), third wife Iya Femi (Bimbo Ademoye), and the most recent and youngest, university-educated yet naïve Bolanle (Omowunmi Dada). The new wife upsets the tentative balance struck by the first three wives, who have been locked into rivalries, secrets, and mutual survival strategies, each trying to solidify their own status. When Bolanle fails to conceive, Baba Segi enlists doctors to find out what is wrong with her, setting off a chain of revelations that unravel the fragile order holding the household together.

Oriahi shifts between the women’s perspectives with compassion, tracing each one’s past to dismantle the standard stereotypes that would typically define them as materialistic, subservient, or venomous. Using humour, the narrative exposes deep wounds caused by infertility, sexual exploitation, and tested loyalties.

The film features many of Nollywood’s finest talents, including a spectacular lineup of cameo appearances. Omowunmi Dada’s empathetic performance gives Bolanle’s plight real emotional stakes. The tale lingers as a critique of misplaced patriarchal pride and a tender study of the hard choices women make to meet impossible expectations.
the-secret-lives-of-baba-segis-wives.teaser: A wealthy patriarch’s fragile household unravels when the youngest of his four wives fails to conceive. Blending sharp Nollywood wit with tenderness, this deeply satisfying drama explores topics of infertility, gendered inheritance, and shifting family power.

thirteen-in-gaza.title: Thirteen in Gaza
thirteen-in-gaza.synopsis:
Raghad (Mary Ziyara), a 13-year-old girl, has lost her home and most of her family in a bombing in the Gaza Strip. She now lives with her father (Firas Al-Masri) in a displacement camp, where she’s entering puberty in a crowded environment devoid of safety, privacy, and care. Meanwhile, her father faces hard choices and a moral dilemma involving Khalil (Ghassan Salem), the local boss, in order to ensure their survival.

Palestinian director Hosam Abu Dan and his crew are all based in Gaza and have decided to show us humanity rather than destruction and survival rather than despair. How do parents manage to protect children in exceptional conditions imposed by a prolonged conflict? What does it mean to grow up in an unstable environment? And what are the long-lasting consequences of such an upbringing?

Puberty is a universal phase marked by physical changes and a shift in how others perceive us and how we understand ourselves. By using a coming-of-age formula to explore daily hardships, Hosam Abu Dan offers us an insider’s intimate view rather than an outsider’s sensationalistic gaze. For this, Thirteen in Gaza not only pays tribute to those living in unacceptable conditions by celebrating their humanity, it also questions our collective failure to protect those who are most vulnerable.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
thirteen-in-gaza.teaser: Palestinian director Hosam Abu Dan makes his narrative feature debut with a nuanced and deeply human portrait of a father and his teenage daughter navigating everyday life in a refugee camp in the Gaza Strip.

trees-are-watching.title: Trees are Watching
trees-are-watching.synopsis:
Darya (Eva Green), a writer obsessed with the spiritual resonance of trees, returns to her hometown of Mardin with her deaf daughter and grows haunted by past memories of Spin and Nihal, twin sisters she knew as a child.

Residing in their former family home — which is bordered by mass deforestation save for an ominous pair of trees planted for each sister — Darya’s unease is suddenly exacerbated by nightly visitations of a malignant entity that takes a seemingly benign form: a chair made from local timber. Soon ruminating on her checkered relationship with Spin and Nihal, the latter of whom claimed to be terrorized by a similarly fearsome fixture, specifically a maternal witch said to lurk in the home’s noisy toilet, Darya’s sanity begins to wane.

Cannily blending psychological horror with local myth, Kurdish-Iranian new wave auteur Bahman Ghobadi explores humanity’s often unharmonious relationship with the natural world with his signature emotional humanism, but also a remarkably playful proclivity for the tropes and traditions of supernatural horror. Across surreal set pieces that ebb with heightened phantasmagoric stylization and sometimes full-blown Grand Guignol spectacle — particularly in a thrilling sequence that recalls the American Final Destination series — Ghobadi conjures a unique flavour of terror, enriched with nuanced philosophy and a deeply personal dimension.

Elevated by an extraordinary performance by Green, who is further supported by an exceptional cast of child actors expertly directed by Ghobadi, Trees are Watching is a mesmerizing confluence of a total filmmaker’s propensity for both the provocative and poignant, as well as the funny and frightening.
