trees-are-watching.teaser: Iranian Kurdish auteur Bahman Ghobadi blends psychological horror and ecological allegory as he depicts the eerie haunting of a writer (Eva Green) reckoning with past misdeeds under the ominous gaze of a pair of trees and a malignant wooden chair.

viva-carmen.title: Viva Carmen
viva-carmen.synopsis:
In his follow-up to The Girl Without Hands and Chicken for Linda!, director Sébastien Laudenbach returns for his third animated feature with a reimagining of Bizet’s opera Carmen. Told through the eyes of Sevillian children, the tragic story — in which the free-spirited Carmen is killed by the soldier Don José in a jealous rage — has the opportunity to be rewritten when the youngsters try to stop her fatal conclusion. Despite the vibrance of this world rendered with expressive brushstrokes, the weight of the original material is still deeply felt, providing a striking contrast to the violence of the narrative.

In addition to the presence of the children, the film’s intervention also offers a feminist perspective, interrogating the logic of patriarchy and calling for solidarity among women. A vision of hope and persistence, childhood is represented as a period of great potential to demand societal change and alternative ways of living in the world.

With a notable absence of the opera’s full musical numbers, the score — composed by Amine Bouhafa and the director’s sister Isabelle Laudenbach — interpolates Bizet’s patterns to craft a minimalist composition. The result is a worthwhile entry in the sea of Carmen adaptations that appeal to adult and child viewers alike, introducing a new generation to one of the most performed, timeless operas in the world.
viva-carmen.teaser: A vibrant reframing of Bizet’s famous opera through the lens of a pack of Sevillian street children who are determined to subvert Carmen’s tragic fate. With an intimate approach to music and bold brushstrokes that dance, this animated feature sings brightly.

woman-unknown.title: Woman Unknown
woman-unknown.synopsis:
A woman with secrets to hide desperately tries to avoid mob justice in postwar Copenhagen in May el-Toukhy’s bracing third feature.

In this gripping third feature by Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy, the citizens of Copenhagen are eager to reclaim the city as their own with the end of the five-year Nazi occupation. Yet those with previous ties to the occupiers live in terror of their fellow Danes, with some of the most vicious forms of retribution exacted upon women accused of past involvement with Germans.

For Marie (Mathilde Arcel), the possibility that her secrets may be discovered instills her with a dread that’s palpable in all her actions, no matter how hard she works to conceal it. A young housekeeper and nanny, Marie is poised to take a significant step above her social station by marrying Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund), the wealthy widower who’s also her employer. But a chance encounter with a man from her past initiates a series of events that put Marie in grave jeopardy. Over the next three days, she makes an increasingly desperate effort to avoid the same ordeal experienced by the unnamed women seen in the film’s most harrowing sequences.

As she did in her bold first feature Queen Of Hearts (2019) — remade by Catherine Breillat as Last Summer (TIFF ’23) — el-Toukhy applies a keen intelligence and an equally sharp rigour to the story of a woman who risks the wrath of a society eager to punish her for any act it deems transgressive. Yet there’s no hint of didacticism in Woman Unknown, only a fierce empathy for its heroine, an ever-escalating sense of tension, and abundant proof of el-Toukhy’s fearlessness as a filmmaker.

Content advisory: coarse language, crude content, sexual content, nudity, violence
woman-unknown.teaser: A woman with secrets to hide desperately tries to avoid mob justice in postwar Copenhagen in May el-Toukhy’s bracing third feature.

in-waves.title: In Waves
in-waves.synopsis:
Grief comes in waves, a universal truth that is especially true here. For her debut feature, director Phuong Mai Nguyen adapts AJ Dungo’s graphic novel to tell a personal tale of friendship, love, and loss. AJ (Will Sharpe), a young skater, meets Kristen (Stephanie Hsu), a young surfer living with cancer, and the two bond over a passion for the ocean during their brief time together. Tracing the Hawaiian origins of surfing, the film renders water as a sacred element with spiritual depth, offering a joy and strength that the two find solace in as they confront her illness.

Through a mix of 2D animation and 3D tools, Nguyen skilfully brings the intimate memoir to the big screen with a visual language that embodies all that water can be: still and turbulent, clear and murky, restorative and devastating. Her extensive research — a trip across the Pacific coast in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Portland, and Hawaii — pays off greatly, bringing beauty and texture to the skate parks, beaches, and multicultural landscape of America that serve as backdrops to our protagonists' emotional journey. Just as Dungo keeps the memory of Kristen alive through his drawings, Nguyen continues her legacy through a gentle coming-of-age story that depicts a relationship between teenage lovers who find their place in the universe through surfing.
in-waves.teaser: Set under the confectionery pink and blue skies of California, this animated film narrates the love story between a young skater and a surfer who share a mutual passion for the ocean.

in-the-heart-of-the-south.title: In the Heart of the South
in-the-heart-of-the-south.synopsis:
A crackling criticism of how the art world in Canada treats Indigenous artists, this psychological thriller stars Inuit actors from the series North of North.

In the Heart of the South is a surprising and exciting swerve away from director Nyla Innuksuk’s debut feature Slash/Back, the 2022 sci-fi film in which teen girls fight off an alien invasion in Nunavut. Here, she reteams with her co-writer Ryan Cavan to turn her focus on less obvious enemies, like a long-lost childhood friend who suddenly reappears on the doorstep.

Anna Lambe leads as Yura Ivalu, the latest darling of the Toronto art world, whose virtual reality piece promises to blow your mind. Presented with a new opportunity to develop a film, she offers to lean into a traumatic story from her youth, which involves a friend who believed she was a shaman. But when that friend, Sesi, re-enters her life, Yura’s sheen of perfection in this polite society begins to show cracks.

Played with a raw menace by actor Zorga Qaunaq, Sesi isn’t as willing to play the perfect Inuk as Yura is. Sesi infiltrates her home, her art show openings, and her social circle. As the tension builds between the two old friends, Yura’s psychological state begins to falter, as she senses that Sesi is there to replace her, expose her, or worse.

This second feature from an exciting directorial voice is thrilling, stylish, funny, and sharply critical of the fallibility of human perception.
in-the-heart-of-the-south.teaser: In the Heart of the South is what Single White Female would be if it were set in Toronto, with an Inuk protagonist and a dash of supernatural elements, starring North of North’s Anna Lambe.

carrie.title: Carrie
carrie.synopsis:
Stephen King’s 1974 novel Carrie is a cultural touchstone for good reason. The routine indignities of high school create a rich environment for stories about outsiders, hidden truths, and horror. After several previous collaborations including TIFF ’24’s People’s Choice Award winner The Life of Chuck, King and director Mike Flanagan bring Carrie to life five decades after the book’s debut.

As Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) walks the halls of her high school for the first time, her peers barely make eye contact, staring instead at the devices in their hands. Sheltered Carrie doesn’t have a smartphone, the parameters of her young life constricted by her paranoid and fervently religious mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan, Midnight Mass). Encouraged by the kindness of Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard), Carrie hopes school will offer some freedoms. But her initial excitement is tempered by the wariness of her classmates Chris (Alison Thornton), Sue (Siena Agudong), and Tommy (Joel Oulette, Can I Get a Witness?, TIFF ’24; also at this year’s Festival in Seventeen). As pressure mounts, Carrie feels something growing inside her that she may not be able to control.

Grounded in the reality of high school as humiliation ritual, Carrie has resonated with readers for decades because of its vivid scenes: the locker room, the prom stage, the vulnerable teenage girl standing in the spotlight. Flanagan unearths new terrors from a familiar story, ensuring there is more to be afraid of, and more to feel.
carrie.teaser: Vanguard of character-driven horror Mike Flanagan (Life of Chuck, TIFF ’24) returns to episodic storytelling with this kinetic adaptation of Stephen King’s classic novel, about the cruelty faced by a sheltered young girl entering high school.

the-lost-children-of-tuam.title: The Lost Children Of Tuam
the-lost-children-of-tuam.synopsis:
Some discoveries can change everything. Frank Berry’s deeply humane drama — based on a tragic true story — chronicles Catherine Corless’ tireless search for the truth after the amateur historian uncovered the recorded deaths of 796 infants and children without corresponding burial records at the former Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home in Tuam, Ireland. Driven by an unwavering sense of moral justice, Corless exposed one of the darkest chapters in modern Irish history and sparked a profound national reckoning.

Berry mines compelling dramatic tension from Corless’ painstaking archival work, patient persistence, and determination to ensure the deceased children would not remain invisible. As Corless’ inquiries were met with indifference, skepticism, and even resistance, she refused to abandon the evidence until it proved impossible to ignore. Monica Dolan (also at the Festival in Elsinore and Onwards and Sideways) delivers a magnificent, deeply restrained performance, carrying the film with a quiet conviction worthy of her compassionate, intelligent real-life subject.

While rooted in Irish history, The Lost Children of Tuam speaks to universal questions of institutional accountability, historical memory, and how we treat children deemed “undesirable.” It is a moving tribute to the power of perseverance, and a reminder that extraordinary change can begin with one person who simply refuses to stop asking difficult questions.
the-lost-children-of-tuam.teaser: A quietly powerful true story of an amateur historian’s quest to uncover a long-buried injustice. By exposing what rightly became a national scandal, Catherine Corless changed Ireland forever.

2-6-seconds-death-in-the-outback.title: 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback
2-6-seconds-death-in-the-outback.synopsis:
The fatal police shooting of a 19-year-old Warlpiri man, Kumanjayi Walker, in the remote Northern Territory community of Yuendumu reverberated across Australia, exposing deep and unresolved questions about race, justice, and policing that continue to shape the nation today. In his remarkable directorial debut, acclaimed producer Darren Dale brings extraordinary cinematic ambition to the story behind one of Australia's defining contemporary events.

Structured with the precision and emotional sweep of a feature film, this gripping four-part docuseries (episodes one and two are presented) reconstructs the events surrounding the shooting, tracing the lives of Walker and police officer Zachary Rolfe before their paths collided in just 2.6 seconds. Refusing simplistic answers and familiar true-crime conventions, Dale instead examines the broader systems that brought these two men together, revealing how history, place, and institutional power converged in a single, irreversible moment.

The series does not look away. It includes the police body-camera footage of Walker's death, presented with the support of his family and community who believe the world needs to witness what happened. The result is confronting, but never exploitative. Instead, it becomes an act of truth telling and a profound expression of collective grief.

While this is an Australian story, its echoes will be deeply familiar to audiences in Canada and elsewhere, where Indigenous communities continue to confront the enduring legacies of colonial policing. Urgent, insightful, and unforgettable, 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback is ultimately a testament to the power of documentary to bear witness, and to demand that difficult truths be confronted.
2-6-seconds-death-in-the-outback.teaser: A gripping, cinematic documentary series that reconstructs one of Australia’s defining contemporary events, exposing the enduring legacies of race, justice, and colonial policing.

all-of-a-sudden.title: All of a Sudden
all-of-a-sudden.synopsis:
At the centre of Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s latest film, his first shot largely in French, is an extended exchange between Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira, TIFF ’25’s A Private Life), the newly appointed director of a Parisian elderly-care facility, and Mari (Tao Okamoto), a Japanese theatre director living with terminal cancer. Their conversation moves across languages and ideas — from capitalism, demographic decline, and social exhaustion, to illness, caregiving, and art itself — yet Hamaguchi uses dialogue less as exposition than as an ethical practice: a way of listening, testing thought, and reaching toward another person.

Theatre is crucial to this encounter, and to Hamaguchi’s poetics. Mari’s play, Up Close, No One Is Normal, brings into the film the vision of Italian psychiatrist Franco Basaglia, whose radical challenge to institutional confinement echoes through Marie-Lou’s efforts to rethink care. As in Hamaguchi’s earlier work, performance is never closed fiction: it becomes a space where body, thought, and relationships are tested.

Drawing inspiration from a book of letters between a terminally ill philosopher and a medical anthropologist, Hamaguchi expands his cinema of words while exposing the limits of speech. Marie-Lou and Mari often converse in languages that are not their own, and the leads give extraordinary performances shaped by precision, vulnerability, and emotional generosity.

Shot in a working care facility, with professional actors alongside real patients, All of a Sudden allows chance and fragility into its rigorous structure. What emerges is a profound vision of care — as a measure of time, risk, and renewed contact with others and the world.
all-of-a-sudden.teaser: Ryûsuke Hamaguchi brings Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto together in a poignant drama about friendship, illness, art, and the responsibilities of care, creating a film that makes the world seem gentler, more open, and more humane.

anchors-aweigh.title: Anchors Aweigh
anchors-aweigh.synopsis:
When an overeager artist (Matt Barats) proposes to his Broadway-bound girlfriend, her perturbed appeal that they “take space” sends him spiralling into a reverie of desperate nostalgia and pitiable self-reflection. Impulsively moving into a sailboat moored by a New York airport, our jilted lover seeks solace by sifting through a stack of home movies, only to be confronted by his own arrested adolescence and the creeping dread that he might indeed be a loveless loser. Such anxiety festers across a series of increasingly surreal vignettes, which Barats stoically narrates with incisive comic precision as his persona wrestles with all the ennui, alienation, and cringe that comes with existence.

Oscillating between a self-deprecating essayistic form that parodies Ross McElwee’s Sherman’s March, and shrewdly shaggy comedy sketches whose deadpan punchlines hit with the hysterically awkward tenor of a Nathan Fielder bit, writer-director Barats refines the alt-comedy sensibility previously savoured in his award-winning underground film Cash Cow and his collaborations with Anthony Oberbeck and Graham Mason (the Reveries trilogy).

Producers Allie Viti and Whit Conway are frequent collaborators of comedians John Wilson and Joe Pera, known for gently amusing observations that give way to disarming profundity. Barats similarly achieves a wholesome resonance with his practiced non sequiturs, despite a more satirically entitled and serrated disposition.

Buoyed by Simon Hanes’ dreamy jazz score, Anchors Aweigh is a laugh-out-loud plea for human connection. Simultaneously sardonic and sincere, it is sure to be a source of constant quotation from any Midnighter who sets sail on its delightfully absurd wavelength.
anchors-aweigh.teaser: After a thwarted marriage proposal, alt-comedian Matt Barats spirals into an existential crisis in this semi-autobiographical blend of deadpan absurdism and unexpected poignancy told in a first-person, confessional style à la Ross McElwee or John Wilson.

bitter-christmas.title: Bitter Christmas
bitter-christmas.synopsis:
Riddled with intrigue, personal entanglements, and stories within stories, the latest from Oscar-winning maestro Pedro Almodóvar, last at the Festival with TIFF ’24’s The Room Next Door, follows a pair of filmmakers vying against the hazards of sustaining a meaningful artistic career — and the alliances that sometimes get compromised in the process.

Elsa (Bárbara Lennie, TIFF ’22’s El Suplente) gave up art-house filmmaking for gainful employment as an advertising director long ago, but the urge to craft something personal and creative comes creeping back: she begins writing a new screenplay, drawing upon the misfortunes of her friends for material. Parallel to Elsa’s endeavour, revered auteur Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia, who featured in Almodóvar’s thematically related TIFF ’19 drama Pain and Glory) is also using the personal hardships of his inner circle to concoct character arcs for his new project. Both artists seek to rejuvenate their respective practices through autofictional devices that threaten to dismantle their most cherished relationships.

Bitter Christmas invites us into an entrancing house of mirrors as only Almodóvar can construct. Alter egos, seductions, and betrayals abound, as do memorable characters and performances — such as Elsa’s firefighter/exotic dancer boyfriend (Patrick Criado) and longtime Almodóvar alum Rossy de Palma in a buoyant cameo — and sequences that fuse the director’s characteristically sumptuous use of colour with evocative locations. With noirish hues and telenovela twists, it’s a captivating exploration of grief, love, and the perils of unchecked artistic licence.
bitter-christmas.teaser: With noirish hues and telenovela twists, the latest from Oscar-winning maestro Pedro Almodóvar (TIFF ’24’s The Room Next Door) follows a pair of self-centred film directors exploring grief, love, and the perils of unchecked artistic license.

rogue-trooper.title: Rogue Trooper
rogue-trooper.synopsis:
Blue-skinned and bred to fight, die, and repeat in an interstellar forever-war, 19 (Aneurin Barnard, Radioactive, TIFF ’19) is the sole survivor of a genetically engineered platoon tasked with liberating the toxic planet Nu-Earth. Accompanied by the consciousnesses of his fallen squadmates — stored inside military biochips embedded in his gun (Jack Lowden, Benediction, TIFF ’21), helmet (Daryl McCormack, Wake Up Dead Man, TIFF ’25), and backpack (Reece Shearsmith, A Field in England, TIFF ’13) — 19 searches for a way to restore them while uncovering a traitor within military command.

If any aspect of this premise sounds familiar, you’ve either pored over the panels of Gerry Finley-Day and Dave Gibbons’ iconic issues (a.k.a. “progs”) of the legendary 2000 AD comics anthology, or enjoyed the plethora of movies and games indebted to them. From Warhammer 40K to Star Wars: The Clone Wars and James Cameron’s Avatar, Rogue Trooper’s aesthetic and thematic tendrils have long infiltrated the military science-fiction subgenre.

Their exploits are now authentically rendered through an innovative synthesis of live-actor performance-capture and computer-generated animation. Writer-director Duncan Jones’ shrewdest creative decision, though, is embracing the comics’ unabashed Britishness.

Drawing from Gibbons’ gritty “The War Machine” reboot and the original 1980s run, and featuring nigh every accent from the British Isles and beyond across a stellar ensemble that further includes Matt Berry, Jemaine Clement, Diane Morgan, Sean Bean, and Hayley Atwell — plus a pixel-chewing Peter Serafinowicz as a snooty francophone sniper — Jones preserves the playful, satirical, and surreal personality that distinguished the original comics with an infectious zeal and attention to psychotronic spectacle.

Content advisory: explicit violence, accident trauma, coarse language, crude content, scenes of surgery
rogue-trooper.teaser: Directed by Duncan Jones (Moon, Warcraft), this outlandish animated adaptation of the influential British comic book follows a clone soldier bred for an interstellar forever-war and his fallen comrades whose personalities live on within his gun, helmet, and backpack.

always-lalisa.title: Always Lalisa
always-lalisa.synopsis:
K-pop idol–turned–global superstar Lisa stars in this intimate and transformative documentary tracing her journey from childhood ambition through BLACKPINK stardom into the artist she is today.

Few artists have achieved the same level of global reach and recognition as Lisa. In fact, there’s no other superstar quite like her.

Born in Thailand and trained in the fast-paced Korean entertainment industry, Lalisa Manobal spent years becoming the mononymous Lisa we know today. Her debut in the girl group BLACKPINK captured the world’s attention and, as the only Thai artist signed to hit factory YG Entertainment, she carved out a path that was unmistakably her own.

Always Lalisa follows that journey with an intimate and effortless insider’s fluency, moving through Lisa’s milestones — her childhood dance competitions, breakout K-pop debut, and the creation of her own label — while acknowledging that the superstar is navigating uncharted terrain as she aims to break into the Western market.

Documentary filmmaker Sue Kim (TIFF ’24 Official Selection The Last of the Sea Women) is no stranger to the glossy world of K-pop — she was an executive producer on Apple TV’s docuseries K-Pop Idols, profiling established artists navigating rigorous training and demanding industry pressures. Over the course of a year, Kim followed Lisa through ambitious new forays, including a monumental performance at Coachella. Similarly, her role in HBO’s The White Lotus announced Lisa’s clear desire to explore creative territory beyond music.

Drawing on interviews, incredible performances, and behind-the-scenes footage, the film showcases Lisa’s relentless dedication to becoming a versatile artist. For faithful Lillies who have followed Lisa’s journey from the start, this is the ultimate reward. For those learning about her for the first time, it’s an irresistible introduction to her world.
always-lalisa.teaser: K-pop idol–turned–global superstar Lisa stars in this intimate and transformative documentary tracing her journey from childhood ambition through BLACKPINK stardom into the artist she is today.

everybody-wants-to-fck-me.title: Everybody Wants to F*ck Me
everybody-wants-to-fck-me.synopsis:
Taron Egerton gives a gleefully committed performance as Adam in Jonathan Schey’s darkly comedic debut, riffing on the dating scene and the self-proclaimed “nice guys” who litter it. Adam has mastered all the trappings of enlightened masculinity: listening more than speaking in meetings with women coworkers, reading feminist literature, practicing yoga, and offering a soupçon of self-deprecation when chatting up women at bars or on dating apps. Adam’s longtime friend who once provided cover for his behaviour is growing up and growing weary of being an accomplice.

Adam has had a lifetime of f*ck around, but his find out is just around the corner when he meets Jessica Henwick’s Sofia. Intriguing and sharp, she proves to be a challenge calling out his behaviour. The encounter shakes Adam and, stranger still, everybody (but mostly women) start responding to his carefully studied charms, first with mild interest, then flat-out stalking, then vigorous pursuit — even when he’s appropriately dressed.

Audacious, with genuinely intense moments, Schey takes aim at the absurd realities of modern relationships, the self-mythologizing of online profiles, and the way in which many men have learned to signal virtues they may not possess. At the end of the day can the f*ckboy change his swipes? Everybody Wants To F*ck Me does not offer any easy redemptions but there’s a lot of fun to be had in watching the tables turn.
everybody-wants-to-fck-me.teaser: Taron Egerton gives a gleefully committed performance as a man determined to be viewed by potential paramours as the ideal catch in director Jonathan Schey’s darkly comic appraisal of modern dating and how some men signal virtues they don’t possess.

angh.title: Angh
angh.synopsis:
Set in the early 1960s in a remote jungle near the Indo-Burma border, Angh follows Anghba, the last surviving chief of a Nagaland village that has been deserted by its people. He remains behind with his ailing wife and non-speaking young son, holding on as the world around them shifts irrevocably.

The arrival of an American missionary (Douglas Henshall, Shetland) sets the region’s transformation in motion, leaving Anghba to guard the beliefs and customs that have been passed down through generations. What emerges is a haunting and intimate story of a father and son, the latter increasingly seduced by the comforts of the mission. The film avoids sentimentality, instead observing how conversion operates deliberately by offering gifts even as the local culture is reframed as deficient.

Theja Rio’s debut feature — strikingly photographed and built on a richly spatial sound design — follows the success of his short film of the same name, which won a special jury award at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival in 2021. Shot on 16mm, the film’s grain seems to hold the passage of time. Texture is drawn from the spiritual and storytelling traditions of the Naga people.

Nagaland, an Indigenous region of Northeast India, has rarely been depicted on screen. Rio views the film as an offering, “A gesture of remembrance, of pride, and of presence. A way of saying that we are here, that we have always been here, and that our stories deserve to stand alongside the rest of the world.”
angh.teaser: In a deserted Nagaland village in the early 1960s, a chief must choose between his family and a transforming world embodied by an incoming American missionary in filmmaker Theja Rio’s gripping feature-length adaptation of his award-winning 2021 short.

hombre-al-agua.title: Hombre al agua
hombre-al-agua.synopsis:
The latest directorial feature from superstar multihyphenate Gael García Bernal (TIFF ’19’s Chicuarotes) is a psychologically astute comedy of manners for the modern age. Exploring class, ambition, and the delicate art of social advancement, Hombre al agua follows an ensemble of eclectic characters from across the Americas, each seeking to become something more than who they are.

Everything changes the day Cuban lifeguard Camilo (García Bernal) rescues Mexican businessman Abel (Jorge Salinas, García Bernal’s co-star in TIFF ’00’s Amores Perros) from drowning. A night of drinking at Havana’s best tourist spots leads to an invitation for Camilo to come work for Abel’s seal manufacturing business, which leads to Camilo wooing, wedding, and having a child with Abel’s daughter Juana (Esmeralda Pimentel), and residing in Abel’s luxurious Yucatán country manor.

But paradise soon gets complicated. Camilo is tasked with discreetly looking after Abel’s pregnant Argentine mistress Silvina (Natalia Oreiro), while Juana teams up with a Brazilian film star (Débora Nascimento) to make a movie about her life.

Written by García Bernal and Mariano Pensotti, Hombre al agua creates a world of ambiance and intrigue: everyone seems to be playing a character or reinventing their past. The more money and power at stake, the harder it is to know who to believe. The beauty and humour of this sophisticated film lies in its reflection of hidden truth.
hombre-al-agua.teaser: The latest directorial feature from Gael García Bernal (TIFF ’19’s Chicuarotes) is a psychologically astute comedy of manners for the modern age, following an ensemble of eclectic characters seeking to become something more than who they are.

everytime.title: Everytime
everytime.synopsis:
Sandra Wollner, who garnered the prestigious Un Certain Regard Prize at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, doesn’t believe in an afterlife but deeply envies those who do. According to the Austrian writer-director, the images of the people we love stay with us and somehow inscribe themselves into the world.

Jessie (Carla Hüttermann) is packing for an upcoming Spanish vacation with her single mother, Ella (played by the mesmerizing Birgit Minichmayr, Jack, TIFF ’15), and her younger sister, Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling). On the eve of the trip, Jessie sneaks out to be with her boyfriend Lux (Tristan Lopez) and this, unfortunately, ends in tragedy. One year later, despite their persistent heartbreak, Ella and Melli cling to a fragile routine and on the surface, appear to get by. But when Lux re-enters the family portrait, the wounds are reopened and, while the matriarch can’t seem to concede to her unspoken blame, Lux can’t seem to cope with his longing for forgiveness. Driven by a strange impulse, Ella takes Lux and Melli to Tenerife on the holiday that never happened. Under the blazing sun, the newly formed unit wades through rough emotional waters, as if in a hallucinatory state. Perhaps because they have no choice, perhaps because it’s the only way to survive.

Shot with precision by Gregory Oke (whose previous work as a cinematographer includes Charlotte Wells’ Aftersun, TIFF ’22) and masterfully edited by Hannes Bruun (who previously collaborated with Wollner on her lauded 2020 feature The Trouble with Being Born), Everytime is a film that lingers well beyond its runtime.
everytime.teaser: A grieving mother and her late daughter’s boyfriend explore questions of guilt, grief, and forgiveness on a family holiday, in Sandra Wollner’s bold and haunting Un Certain Regard winner.

flies.title: Flies
flies.synopsis:
Olga (Mexican contemporary indie cinema mainstay Teresita Sánchez) is a mature, single woman who leads a mostly unhurried — but rather lonely — life in a middle-class apartment complex across from a big, busy hospital. To support herself she decides to rent out a room in her apartment to a father (Hugo Ramírez) who has a relative at the hospital. Unexpectedly, she forms an unlikely bond with his nine-year-old son, Cristian (Bastian Escobar), whose quiet resilience gradually disrupts her routines and opens the door to a profound emotional transformation she didn’t anticipate.

Fernando Eimbcke returns to the Festival following Duck Season (TIFF ’04), Club Sandwich (TIFF ’13), and his 2025 opus Olmo, this time exploring how apathy can give way to connection, and even lead to action for the sake of the well-being of others. Presenting Olga’s predictable, measured world in stark black and white while maintaining a natural rhythm and understated mise en scène, the film tenderly unfolds to reveal uncomplicated, yet deeply resonant characters and situations.

With remarkable sensitivity, Eimbcke finds moments of humour, grace, and quiet revelation in the everyday, creating an intimate portrait of chosen family, empathy, and the unexpected ways in which caring for another person can restore one's own sense of purpose. Suddenly confronted with her own pain through the mirror of strangers, Olga takes the leap to nurture a child at the moment he needs it most.
flies.teaser: When a lonely woman rents a room to a father with a hospitalized relative, she forms an unexpected bond with his young son, in Fernando Eimbcke’s tender story about care, connection, and quiet transformation.

intermission.title: Intermission
intermission.synopsis:
A brilliant feast for the eyes, Yonfan’s Intermission distills the essential meaning of cinema as the collective experience of pursuing a dream by following a beam of white light projected onto a screen in a darkened space.

Neither a documentary nor a conventional film-on-film essay — and conceived almost like a musical compilation — Intermission draws from the wealth of beauty, elegance, and the extraordinary constellation of stars populating Yonfan’s 15 films spanning nearly 40 years.

Maggie Cheung, Sylvia Chang, Chow Yun Fat, Cherie Chung, Daniel Wu, Shu Qi, Stephen Fung, Rie Miyazawa, and many others are captured at defining moments in their careers which collectively made Yonfan’s cinema so singular.

Here, he creates a cinematic portrait of his work and an alternative history of Hong Kong cinema shaped by his unmistakable artistic vision. Images, music, dance, and memory flow into one another through virtuoso editing evoking the graceful, circular movement of tai chi: beginnings become endings, and every ending opens onto another dream.

The romanticism and complex female protagonists of his early works, and the later explorations of queer desire, eroticism, social marginality, and artistic liberation, all gather in Intermission, a meeting place where intimacy and spectacle, memory, and fantasy coexist in harmony.

Intermission resists easy classification. It is at once memoir, reverie, and act of preservation and an exquisitely fluid celebration of cinema itself, of the vanished faces, places, and desires that continue to live whenever light reaches the screen.
intermission.teaser: Yonfan transforms excerpts from his 15 films into a brilliant, genre-defying meditation on cinema, memory, beauty, desire, and his own singular body of work, featuring Maggie Cheung, Chow Yun-fat, Sylvia Chang, Shu Qi, Daniel Wu, and many, many more.

atonement.title: Atonement
atonement.synopsis:
Grounded in emotionally layered performances from Boyd Holbrook (TIFF ’18’s The Predator), Hiam Abbass (TIFF ’25’s Palestine 36), and Oscar winner Kenneth Branagh (TIFF ’21’s Belfast), this searing real-life story follows the lives of several characters in the years following a horrifying event. Based on Dexter Filkins’ 2012 New Yorker essay of the same name, the feature debut from Oscar-nominated writer-director Reed Van Dyk (DeKalb Elementary) considers the consequences of war long after the last shots are fired.

In Baghdad, in 2003, US Marine Lou D’Alessandro (Holbrook) and his unit open fire on two ostensibly hostile vehicles. Three passengers are killed before it’s revealed that those vehicles were carrying three generations of a civilian family. A decade later, following a dishonorable discharge, Lou is back in San Diego, haunted by the incident, unsupported by Veterans Affairs, and unable to continue the life he started before the war.

Meanwhile, Mariam (Abbass), the matriarch of the family torn apart on that fateful day, has begun a new life in Glendale with her daughter’s young family. She’s profiled by journalist Michael Reid (Branagh), who was also in Baghdad when the tragedy unfolded. Desperate to explain his side of the story, Lou asks Michael to broker a meeting with Mariam. Though terrified of reopening old wounds, Lou believes this might be everyone’s best chance to finally heal.

Atonement asks difficult questions about reconciliation and trauma while acknowledging that everyone seeks out different means of moving on. This is a story about reckoning with unimaginable pain en route to catharsis and, just maybe, atonement.
atonement.teaser: Boyd Holbrook (The Bikeriders), Hiam Abbass (TIFF ’25’s Palestine 36), and Oscar winner Kenneth Branagh star in Oscar-nominated writer-director Reed Van Dyk’s searing story of trauma and forgiveness following a horrifying event during the Iraq War.

diary-of-a-mad-old-man.title: Diary of a Mad Old Man
diary-of-a-mad-old-man.synopsis:
This captivating adaptation of Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s novel from director Wayne Wang (TIFF ’93’s The Joy Luck Club) follows an aging widower drawn into an unnervingly intimate relationship with his caregiver daughter-in-law.

This captivating chamber drama from versatile auteur Wayne Wang (last at the Festival with 2019’s Coming Home Again) draws us into the troubled psyche of an aging widower whose sudden onset of disability coincides with the development of an unnervingly intimate relationship. Featuring a brilliantly graded performance by veteran actor Lily Franky (familiar to TIFF audiences from Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Shoplifters and Chie Hayakawa’s Renoir), this adaptation of revered Japanese author Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s eponymous novel ushers us into a realm of beguiling signals and unruly desire.

The night before his 69th birthday, Utsugi (Franky) had a stroke that paralyzed the left side of his body. Since then, he’s been cared for by his sister-in-law Hana (Yūki Kudō, star of Jim Jarmusch’s cult classic and TIFF ’89 Official Selection Mystery Train) and his daughter-in-law Susu (Fan Bingbing, TIFF ’16’s I Am Not Madame Bovary). When the family is set to go on holiday for the summer, Utsugi insists on staying home — with Susu as his sole caregiver. While Utsugi believes his stroke has reduced him to a wretched state, he becomes convinced that Susu is flirting with him. Left alone together, Utsugi and Susu bond over suspicions, extravagances, and increasingly erotic gestures.

As evidenced in beloved films such as Smoke and TIFF ’93’s The Joy Luck Club, Wang expertly stages tales of unlikely alliances and complicated family dynamics. With Diary of a Mad Old Man, he’s fashioned his most delicate depiction of the schism between our inner worlds and outer realities.
diary-of-a-mad-old-man.teaser: This captivating adaptation of Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s novel from director Wayne Wang (TIFF ’93’s The Joy Luck Club) follows an aging widower drawn into an unnervingly intimate relationship with his caregiver daughter-in-law.

elsinore.title: Elsinore
elsinore.synopsis:
Ian Charleson is widely known as the real-life star of TIFF ’81’s Chariots of Fire, the first People’s Choice Award winner to receive the Oscar for Best Picture. Its piano-led ubiquity in pop culture follows the Scottish actor everywhere, making him yearn less for Hollywood and more for his theatre roots. When Daniel Day-Lewis walks off stage as Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, the role of a lifetime appears for Charleson — but so does an AIDS diagnosis. Dream and nightmare collide as Charleson strives to command the stage and survive as long as possible.

Andrew Scott (TIFF ’25’s Blue Moon and Wake Up Dead Man) delivers a career-best performance in Elsinore, wondrously celebrating both Charleson and Hamlet on screen. Through Scott, each real and fictional man’s confrontation with death becomes visceral, profoundly moving, and resoundingly answers Shakespeare’s famed question with “to be.”

Olivia Colman brings a wellspring of empathy as a doctor treating Charleson and fellow gay men during the HIV epidemic, including a supporting turn from Heartstopper’s Joe Locke. Harnessing warmth and even wit, Queer Palm and BAFTA-winning screenwriter Stephen Beresford (TIFF ’14’s Pride) and director Simon Stone (TIFF ’15’s The Daughter) effectively fortify Charleson’s legacy in Elsinore, a courageous testament to the meaning of life and art.
elsinore.teaser: Andrew Scott (TIFF ’25’s Blue Moon and Wake Up Dead Man) delivers his strongest performance honouring the real-life story of Ian Charleson, the Chariots of Fire actor who courageously pushed through AIDS to play Hamlet at London’s National Theatre.

its-my-time.title: It's My Time
its-my-time.synopsis:
Led by Michelle Yeoh, Oscar-winning star of Everything Everywhere All at Once, TIFF ’00 People’s Choice Award winner Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, and fellow TIFF ’26 feature The Surgeon, this inspired comedy from director Bai Xue (TIFF ’18’s The Crossing) tells a story of galvanizing gamesmanship and ageless defiance.

The rebellious Zhao Yanhong (Yeoh) was not meant for life in a nursing home — so she causes a commotion every chance she gets. Her days of mind-numbing routine and placating caregivers get a welcome shake-up when she meets Gen-Z slacker Wu Youwei (Liu Haoran), a one-time magic-cubing champion now reduced to performing cheap tricks in night markets. Determined to learn the art of the magic cube, Zhao enlists this humbled whiz kid as her mentor — and the pair discover an unlikely chemistry. With every leap in skill, however, Zhao unexpectedly finds herself confronting a personal history freighted with unfinished business and regrets. As she readies herself for the World Cubing Championship, our hero will have to bring all her inner resources to the stage — which means reckoning with the past as a means of mastering the present.

Trading martial arts heroics for warmth and deep emotion, Yeoh is the perfect actor to embody Zhao on her journey from forced languor to cube-twisting glory. It’s My Time is a great time for spectators of all ages — and a reminder that any point in life can yield a colourful surprise.
its-my-time.teaser: Led by Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh (Everything Everywhere All at Once), this inspired comedy about a woman on the road to magic-cube mastery is a story of galvanizing gamesmanship and ageless defiance.

the-housewife.title: The Housewife
the-housewife.synopsis:
Grounded in memorable performances from Oscar nominee Naomi Watts (TIFF ’01’s Mulholland Drive), Tye Sheridan (TIFF ’13’s Joe), Luke Evans (Dracula Untold), and The Sopranos alum Michael Imperioli (TIFF ’24’s Oh, Canada), this psychological historical drama depicts the complexities of seeking justice in the long shadow of Nazism. Based on a true story, and brilliantly scripted by Alyssa Hill, director Ben Shirinian’s feature debut conveys this troubling tale with intelligence, suspense, and unexpected twists.

The year is 1964. A very proper Hermine (Watts) and her hardworking husband Russel (Evans) enjoy a seemingly normal life in New York City — until the fateful day Hermine meets The New York Times journalist Joseph Lelyveld (Sheridan). Following a tip from a Holocaust survivor, Joseph is investigating the possibility that Russel might be a Nazi in hiding. As his inquiry deepens — and his exchanges with Hermine become increasingly intimate — Joseph discovers a series of revelations far stranger and more complicated than he could have imagined.

As it shifts from tense thriller to courtroom drama, The Housewife gradually emerges as a complex study in complicity and accountability. History may pass but the question remains as to whether some crimes can be forgotten, forgiven, or washed away. With this feature debut, Shirinian not only raises timely questions, but does so with impressive craft and polished storytelling, positioning himself as a director to watch.

Content advisory: themes of antisemitism, violence, self-harm, coarse language, mature themes
the-housewife.teaser: Grounded in artful performances from Oscar nominee Naomi Watts (TIFF ’01’s Mulholland Drive) and Tye Sheridan (TIFF ’13’s Joe), this salient historical drama depicts the complexities of seeking justice in the long shadow of Nazism.

the-liberation.title: The Liberation
the-liberation.synopsis:
For Rita, a workaday life as an assistant bank manager, wife, and mother of two approaching empty-nest status has just collided with the re-emergence of a very painful chapter of her family history. She finds various ways, all frustratingly temporary, to cope with her anxieties — that is, until a mysterious new client, Ricki, walks into Rita’s bank.

In addition to making a large deposit, Ricki tenders a more interesting offer: to join a group of women that night in a sunset ritual and perhaps find the gateway to newfound purpose. Much to her family’s dismay, Rita immerses herself into an organization with many skeletons in its proverbial closet and eventually leaves to help Ricki establish a rural all-woman commune.

Carrie Coon (His Three Daughters, TIFF ’23) gives an incredibly powerful performance as Rita, who is inspired by filmmaker Guy Nattiv’s own grandmother. As Ricki, Lily James (Swiped, TIFF ’25) embodies cunning and charm. Ricki's remarkable ability to quickly read the insecurities of potential recruits allows her to exploit their vulnerabilities with unsettling precision. Bella Ramsey (Catherine Called Birdy, TIFF ’22) and Odessa Young (Mothering Sunday, TIFF ’21) play Rita’s daughters, who search for their mother and find themselves dangerously entangled in the rituals and delusions of the cult. The Liberation is a devastating look at how easily seemingly ordinary people can succumb to physical and psychological manipulation when running from grief and anxiety.
the-liberation.teaser: Carrie Coon soars in the riveting story inspired by filmmaker Guy Nattiv’s grandmother, whose humdrum day-to-day life is upended by a mysterious and entrancing young woman (Lily James) offering the promise of escape to something better.

clarissa.title: Clarissa
clarissa.synopsis:
Six years after their debut feature Eyimofe: This Is My Desire, brothers Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri have produced and directed a wonderful adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s classic 1925 novel Mrs. Dalloway. Set in contemporary Nigeria, the film chronicles a high-society couple portrayed by the magnetic Sophie Okonedo as the titular Clarissa Dalloway and Jude Akuwudike as her husband Richard.

While preparing for a big reception, Clarissa recalls her teenage years (with the younger Clarissa played in these scenes by India Amarteifio). At that time, her heart was torn between Richard and Peter, a promising young writer (Toheeb Jimoh and touchingly played as an older man by David Oyelowo) who has suddenly reappeared in Clarissa’s life.

The harmful impacts of World War I are ingeniously transposed onto the fight against Boko Haram, which has been ravaging northern Nigeria since 2009. Septimus (Fortune Nwafor, impressive), a soldier suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, crosses paths with one of Clarissa’s guests who is distraught over what happened to him.

Abetted by Jonathan Bloom’s magnificent 35mm cinematography and meticulous attention to detail, and written by Chuku Esiri, who also scripted Eyimofe: This Is My Desire, Clarissa immerses us in a suspended moment in time — a time of introspection, existential crisis, and re-examination of the past. By choosing to focus on individual destinies rather than collective ones, the Esiri brothers offer us precious portraits in a unique and impressive style.
clarissa.teaser: Led by a stellar cast including Sophie Okonedo and David Oyelowo, filmmaking brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri’s second feature is a beguiling adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway set in contemporary Lagos.

in-alaska.title: In Alaska
in-alaska.synopsis:
Across the frozen Arctic tundra, an unlikely and misunderstood vandal is doggedly pursued by federal agents in this riveting drama co-directed and co-written by North of North actor Vinnie Karetak (The Grizzlies, TIFF ’18) and Dutch filmmaker Jaap van Heusden.

Woody (Leo Matthew Temela, in his first starring role) is a young, depressed Inuk teen whose life is upended by a single, desperate mistake. When his attempt at self-harm fails and an errant bullet pierces the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, there are huge ramifications: he’s suddenly labelled an eco-terrorist and forced to go on the run. Abandoning the small Alaskan village he grew up in, he sets out towards Nunavut, where he has family he doesn’t know but who he hopes will take him in.

Hot on his trail is the FBI, led by Agent Susan Tarheel. Played with the appropriate world-weary coolness by Noomi Rapace, best known for the Girl with the Dragon Tattoo films, is battling with mental health demons of her own. Laser-focused in her pursuit, she knows that catching her target will require getting inside the mind of the fleeing boy.

The beautiful northern landscapes quickly turn hostile for Woody, making nature as much of a threat as the federal manhunt. A tense and darkly humorous coming-of-age story, In Alaska offers viewers a thoughtful and thrilling ride.
in-alaska.teaser: When a suicidal Inuk teen accidentally pierces an oil pipeline with a bullet, the FBI launches a full-scale manhunt across the northern wilderness in this drama starring Noomi Rapace (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo) and newcomer Leo Matthew Temela.

it-will-happen-tonight.title: It Will Happen Tonight
it-will-happen-tonight.synopsis:
Louis Garrel (last at the Festival with TIFF ’25’s Couture) and Jasmine Trinca (Simple Women, TIFF ’19) lead a charming ensemble cast in the latest from Italian auteur Nanni Moretti (TIFF ’01’s The Son’s Room). Unfolding across many years, the characters in It Will Happen Tonight encounter passionate interludes of love and loss, unexpected beginnings and endings, that will restore your faith in romantic destiny and the wild logic of the heart.

Matteo (Garrel) first meets Greta (Trinca) in Rome. He’s playing tennis and — en route to her own wedding — she stops for a round with this stranger. Greta wipes the floor with Matteo and, with a beguiling smile, dashes off to be married. Matteo is lovestruck, but what can he do?

Years later, Matteo, in San Sebastián to attend a Bruce Springsteen concert, sees Greta searching for her missing daughter. Their paths cross. Later still, Matteo spots Greta once again in a Rome café. She’s still with her husband, deeply focused on motherhood, and Matteo has a new wife.

Based on a short story collection by Eshkol Nevo, It Will Happen Tonight is an exuberant celebration of moments when the universe comes knocking with a glimpse of another possible life.
it-will-happen-tonight.teaser: Louis Garrel (TIFF ’25’s Couture) leads a charming ensemble in this decades-spanning divine dramady from Nanni Moretti (TIFF ’01’s The Son’s Room) that will restore your faith in destiny and the wild logic of the heart.

la-bola-negra.title: La Bola Negra
la-bola-negra.synopsis:
At the cusp of the Spanish Civil War, a young man confronts his ideology and sexuality as he is conscripted into the fascist army where he becomes fascinated by a prisoner of war. Another young man in pre-dictatorship Spain finds himself blackballed from his father’s prestigious social club due to rumours about his sexuality. Finally, a young gay historian manoeuvres through his complicated family history and a unique inheritance decades after the dictatorship has ended.

A celebration of famed Spanish writer Federico García Lorca’s enduring legacy, La Bola Negra reimagines vignettes of his works that centred on repressed identity and sexuality, specifically his last, unfinished work that featured an openly gay protagonist in the context of extreme societal oppression. Academy Award winner Penélope Cruz (also at the Festival in Bunker), Academy Award nominee Glenn Close (The Wife, TIFF ’17), and Julio Torres (Problemista) star alongside stunning debut performances by musician Guitarricadelafuente and Milo Quifes.

The seamlessly converging storylines make for a sweeping and operatic romantic drama, punctuated by the lasting tragedy of Lorca’s execution at the hands of fascists. Directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo present a bold and ambitious narrative that delicately balances collective memory with deeply emotional personal histories. With these interconnected arcs, combined with stunning cinematography and a grand score, falling in love with La Bola Negra is inevitable.
la-bola-negra.teaser: Los Javis’ ambitious and captivating homage to Federico García Lorca sees the lives of three men intertwined in love and loss across eras. Featuring powerful performances by Guitarricadelafuente, Carlos González, and Miguel Bernardeau.

the-age-of-goodbyes.title: The Age of Goodbyes
the-age-of-goodbyes.synopsis:
Based on the award-winning novel by Li Zi Shu, Edmund Yeo’s The Age of Goodbyes is a multifaceted story about how memories are inherited through generations.

Jumping between different timelines, the film follows Kai (Troy Liu), a boy who finds a book called The Age of Goodbyes. The novel begins on page 513, a poignant reference to May 13, 1969, one of the darkest and most defining days in Malaysian history. As Kai reads, he enters the world of Du Li An (Vivian Sung).

In Ipoh in 1969, Du Li An falls in love with Lin Sang (Stanley Yau). He confides in her about a dark curse that plagues his family, then, shortly after, he disappears without a trace. Years pass, and Du Li An finally moves on, until one day Mong Sang (Stanley Yau) appears before her — and he is the spitting image of her unforgettable love. The more Kai turns the pages, the more he uncovers the ties between himself and those in the book.

Once considered unfilmable, the story’s non-linear timeline could make it challenging to follow. But this is a unique and visually stunning cinematic experience that will reward multiple viewings. Malaysian filmmaker Edmund Yeo infuses his adaptation with his personal fascination with the way experiences turn into narratives. As stories are passed down through generations, they take on lives of their own, intertwining history and myth. And, similarly, as Du Li An’s story gets passed along through screenings of The Age of Goodbyes, so shall it take on a life of its own.
the-age-of-goodbyes.teaser: Vivian Sung stars as the ravishing Du Li An in a breathtaking cinematic adaptation of Li Zi Shu’s The Age of Goodbyes, a story about memory, loss, love, doppelgängers, and hidden truths.

the-road-not-taken.title: The Road Not Taken
the-road-not-taken.synopsis:
The latest work from acclaimed filmmaker Peter Ho-Sun Chan is a polished and emotionally charged family drama that explores the horror of early-onset Alzheimer disease, as the boundaries of a once-familiar reality dissolve into an alien dimension that’s impossible to trust.

Jia Jia (Zhou Xun) is a successful television host whose professional life appears completely under control even as her marriage to a wildlife conservationist is falling apart.

When, during a public discussion about AI, she struggles to remember the term, calling it “artificial talent” instead, she blames work-related exhaustion. Soon, however, these lapses become increasingly disturbing.

The film’s narrative structure combines Jia Jia’s emerging symptoms with domestic crises involving the deeply fractured relationship with her daughter and the complex rapport she has with her father. The relentless takeover of the disease provides a distinctive rhythm, like an accelerating heartbeat that punctuates the disappearance of intellectual certainties as they are gradually replaced by a raw and frightened emotional state. Social roles, old arguments, and carefully constructed identities slowly begin to fall away.

Illuminated by Zhou’s extraordinary performance, the film is further strengthened by Wen Qi’s convincing portrayal of Jia Jia’s daughter and by celebrated Fifth Generation filmmaker Tian Zhuangzhuang’s warm and generous performance as her father.

Rooted in Chan’s artistic sensibility and exceptional command of storytelling, The Road Not Taken combines intimate, character-driven drama with strong emotional and commercial appeal, offering a powerful reflection on family and what remains of us when the structures through which we understand the world begin to disappear.
the-road-not-taken.teaser: Peter Ho-Sun Chan directs Zhou Xun, Wen Qi, Tian Zhuangzhuang and Wang Xiao in a drama about early-onset Alzheimer disease. Combining expert storytelling with commercial appeal, The Road Not Taken reflects on what remains when our understanding of the world begins to disappear.

whatcha-want.title: Whatcha Want
whatcha-want.synopsis:
From her winsome TIFF ’94 feature debut Double Happiness onward, writer-director Mina Shum has been chronicling myriad aspects of the Asian-Canadian experience with humour, grace, and a heartfelt universality. With Whatcha Want, Shum tells the story of a young woman whose marriage to an affluent businessman is beginning to resemble a gilded cage.

Yin (Isabella Wei) hasn’t seen BT (Hugh Tran) in five months. While he claims to be under great professional stress back in their native Hong Kong, she spends her days in their new hometown of Vancouver, where she is chauffeured by the charming Ming (Tzi Ma, TIFF ’16’s Arrival) and kept company by her older and wiser friend (Ming-Na Wen, Joy Luck Club, TIFF ’93), who advises Yin to stop worrying about her less than ideal marriage and enjoy her life of privilege.

But Yin longs for more than designer shopping and spas, and when she spots a high-energy dance class happening across the street from her apartment, her love of dance as a child comes flooding back. Yin joins the dance group and rediscovers what’s been lost.

Shum exudes a confident light touch while exploring themes of gender and class in a cross-cultural landscape. With nods to Crazy Rich Asians and Flashdance, it’s a classic tale with a Canadian twist.
whatcha-want.teaser: The latest comedy from writer-director Mina Shum (Double Happiness, TIFF ’17’s Meditation Park) tells the story of a young woman from Hong Kong whose marriage to an affluent businessman is beginning to resemble a gilded cage.

all-about-corinne.title: All About Corinne
all-about-corinne.synopsis:
Paris Follies writer-director Marc Fitoussi reteams with the inimitable, Oscar-nominated Isabelle Huppert (TIFF ’16’s Elle) for this delectable comedy about the obstinance of dreams — and the ubiquity of seemingly impenetrable cliques.

After decades spent struggling to make advances in her country’s notoriously inaccessible film industry, Corinne Maclou (Huppert) remains a background actor. While being known as a dependable extra has its perks, Corinne still aspires to strut her stuff among the stars. She spies her chance when she meets Sandrine Kiberlain (TIFF ’24’s Meet the Barbarians) and, little by little, uses her eccentric charms to befriend the celebrated actor. But will friendship alone provide Corinne with the tools necessary to break into the fickle family of le cinéma français?

Playful, absorbing, and rife with insider wit, All About Corinne allows us to root for the underdog while rubbing elbows with royalty. Echoing the meta-hijinks of hit satire Call My Agent! (Dix pour cent), for which Fitoussi directed six episodes, the film features a grand assemblage of beloved stars — Kiberlain, Emmanuelle Bercot, Anne Marivin, Ana Girardot, Vincent Dedienne, and Thomas Jolly — playing themselves. This makes the irony of casting Huppert, one of the world’s boldest and most versatile actors, as a cinematic minion that much more delicious. If she can’t make it, no one can.
all-about-corinne.teaser: Paris Follies writer-director Marc Fitoussi re-teams with the inimitable, Oscar-nominated Isabelle Huppert (TIFF ’16’s Elle) for this delectable comedy about a veteran background actor who spies a belated chance to break into the fickle family of le cinéma français.

all-that-she-wants.title: All That She Wants
all-that-she-wants.synopsis:
Annie Murphy (Schitt’s Creek) stars in this effervescent, tender-hearted, refreshingly modern rom-com that chronicles a casual encounter between a millennial and a Gen Zer — and the life-altering consequences that result.

Schitt’s Creek star Annie Murphy and Cha Cha Real Smooth’s Cooper Raiff come together in this effervescent, tender-hearted, refreshingly modern spin on the romantic comedy. Written by Schitt’s Creek executive producer David West Read and directed by Scarlett Bermingham and Andrew Rhymer (Plus One), the Toronto-set All That She Wants chronicles a casual encounter between a millennial and a Gen Zer — and the life-altering consequences that result.

Reeling from a painful breakup, thirtysomething Emma (Murphy) decides to nurse her wounds with a night out clubbing. That’s how she meets the cute, charismatic, and notably younger Luke (Raiff). It isn’t until the next morning that the pair’s age gap fully hits: Emma, it turns out, was once Luke’s babysitter.

After this emphatically one-off hookup, Emma turns a page, forging a new career path and deciding, regardless of her relationship status, that she wants children. Luke, meanwhile, has a funny way of reappearing in Emma’s life on a semi-regular basis. Might he be a sperm donor? Might he be something more?

All That She Wants has all anyone could want in a rom-com: it’s sexy, hilarious, and disarmingly perceptive about long-term entanglements and the trickiness of balancing independence and attachments. It features a superb supporting cast that includes Girls’ Zosia Mamet and Mamma Mia!’s Christine Baranski, and works as a welcome showcase for Murphy — one of Canada’s most remarkable talents.

Content advisory: strobe lighting, sexual content, coarse language, crude content
all-that-she-wants.teaser: Annie Murphy (Schitt’s Creek) stars in this effervescent, tender-hearted, refreshingly modern rom-com that chronicles a casual encounter between a millennial and a Gen Zer — and the life-altering consequences that result.

closing-night.title: Closing Night
closing-night.synopsis:
Naomi Watts, Sarah Paulson, and Odessa A’zion deliver powerhouse performances in Cody Fern’s sensational feature debut, where a hardened movie star reunites with the deliciously messy family she left behind decades earlier.

Actor Cody Fern (American Horror Story, The Great Darkened Days, TIFF ’18) makes a sensational directorial debut with this sharp, emotionally astute story about family bonds and buried truths. When an internationally renowned movie star (Sarah Paulson) invites her estranged family to the opening night of her Broadway play after decades of silence, old wounds resurface almost as quickly as old habits. Her emotionally fragile sister (Naomi Watts, The Friend, TIFF ’24) remains determined to hold onto a lifetime of resentment, while her nephew (Toby Wallace, Finestkind, TIFF ’23) sees an opportunity to forge a relationship with his famous aunt.

Co-written by Fern and fellow actor Devon Bostick, the film's terrific screenplay offers its exceptional ensemble richly layered roles that continually surprise. Paulson, Watts, Wallace, Odessa A'zion (Marty Supreme), and the incomparable Dianne Wiest (I Care A Lot, TIFF ’20) relish every deliciously barbed exchange, creating a family that is equal parts chaotic, exasperating, hilarious, and all too recognizable. Fern has enormous fun with relatives who know exactly how to wound one another, yet can't quite stop showing up when it matters most. Every confrontation crackles with wit, and every insult conceals an old hurt.

But just when you think you're settling into a wickedly entertaining family drama, Closing Night quietly reveals another heart beating beneath the surface. Without ever losing its acerbic edge, the film evolves into a compassionate reflection on love, sacrifice, and the difficult choices we sometimes make for those we cherish most, asking whether even the deepest fractures can be mended when everything is finally laid bare.
closing-night.teaser: Naomi Watts, Sarah Paulson, and Odessa A’zion deliver powerhouse performances in Cody Fern’s sensational feature debut, where a hardened movie star reunites with the deliciously messy family she left behind decades earlier.

club-kid.title: Club Kid
club-kid.synopsis:
For Peter Green (Jordan Firstman), a promoter and purveyor of… shall we say… stimulating party favours in the queer New York club scene, the party never stops. Each revelry blurs into the next, with restraint and responsibility perpetually foisted upon others, especially his fed-up business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingne). But on the precipice of losing another decade to the rhythm of the night, reality bites in the form of his surprise parentage to 10-year-old Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the result of a half-remembered hookup. When his mother unexpectedly dies, the boy is thrust straight into Peter’s carousing care.

Firstman’s spirited debut feature as writer and director bops to familiar beats as his affably incorrigible Peter tackles fatherdom, first with trepidation, and soon with enthusiasm as his precocious child’s propensity for DJ mixing becomes a springboard to endearing if precarious father-son bonding, though this is later threatened by encroaching custodial factors.

What distinguishes this trajectory from mere stock sentimentality is the care taken in depicting Peter’s queer community as they accept and invite Arlo into their world. Supported by Adam Newport-Berra’s intimate cinematography, Firstman authentically renders the lives of his characters with an effervescence that is both subtle and captivating. Special shout out to the excellent Diego Calva who portrays both Arlo’s therapist and Peter’s romantic foil with an affectionate calm.

A sensation at Cannes, where comparisons were drawn to TIFF ’24’s Anora (the films share producer Alex Coco), Club Kid boldly brings its affecting story home with sobering shifts, but an emotional catharsis that makes it a consummate crowd pleaser.

Content advisory: strobing, sexual content, nudity, mature themes, drug use, coarse language
club-kid.teaser: In his exuberant debut feature, writer-director Jordan Firstman stars as a carousing New York City club promoter whose lifestyle is upended by the unexpected responsibility of raising a 10-year-old son he never knew he had.

faith.title: Faith
faith.synopsis:
For single mother Gina (Erin Doherty, The Crown), every day is a balancing act. Raising her young son Jamie (Smylie Bradwell) while working shifts at a local factory, she does everything she can to build a comfortable home from modest means. When Gina meets the enigmatic and charming Michael (James McAvoy, California Schemin’, TIFF ’25) — a volunteer at the local food bank — his easy companionship offers the possibility of something she has long denied herself: the chance to envision a brighter future.

With remarkable rigour, writer-director Paul Andrew Williams (Song for Marion, TIFF ’12) explores both the unimaginable weight of grief and the fragile hope that can survive even our darkest moments. Known for his powerful portraits of ordinary lives under extraordinary pressure, Williams brings a new tenderness to Faith, blending grounded realism with subtle touches that expand the emotional world of the film. Doherty delivers a staggering performance, palpably capturing love, despair, and resilience while McAvoy commands a character whose true motivations remain elusive.

Heartbreaking yet filled with grace, Faith is a moving reflection on the fragile threads that keep us connected to life when everything else seems lost. Williams reminds us that hope rarely arrives all at once. Sometimes it begins with a simple kindness and with the possibility that there may be more connecting us than we can fully understand.
faith.teaser: The spark of romance offers a hard-working single mother (Erin Doherty, The Crown) the chance to imagine a different future. But after tragedy strikes, she discovers that the man she may be falling for (James McAvoy) is hiding a truth she couldn’t have imagined.

love-of-your-life.title: Love of Your Life
love-of-your-life.synopsis:
Featuring a beautifully understated performance from Margaret Qualley (TIFF ’24’s The Substance), this sweeping romantic character study from director Rachel Morrison (TIFF ’24’s The Fire Inside) is an exhilarating testament to loving fully, making amends, and moving on.

By turns soulful, heartbreaking, and wise, this complex character study from director Rachel Morrison (TIFF ’24’s The Fire Inside) and screenwriter Julia Cox (TIFF ’23’s Nyad) provides the perfect showcase for the talented Margaret Qualley (TIFF ’24’s The Substance). Following a young woman’s romantic adventures and relationships over several years and continents, Love of Your Life is a contemporary portrait of love, loss, and letting go.

Maya (Qualley) is a 26-year-old Boston nurse when she falls in love with Charlie (A House of Dynamite’s Gabriel Basso). Emotions deepen quickly, the couple marries, but all things fall tragically apart with the onset of the pandemic. Maya abruptly flees her life in the US, severing all her connections — including her best friend Jason (Patrick Schwarzenegger, TIFF ’26’s Bunker). She becomes a digital nomad in Portugal, where she meets Felix (Aaron Pierre, TIFF ’22’s Brother), who revives her capacity for intimacy and prompts a move to England. But can any amount of transformation or new beginnings stave off the ghosts Maya seems determined to run from?

The film spotlights Qualley’s beautifully understated performance, and is supported by powerful moments from Oscar nominee Catherine Keener (TIFF ’05’s Capote), Directed with an assured and authentic hand by Rachel Morrison, Love of Your Life speaks to what it means to be a young woman and alive in the world today.
love-of-your-life.teaser: Featuring a beautifully understated performance from Margaret Qualley (TIFF ’24’s The Substance), this sweeping romantic character study from director Rachel Morrison (TIFF ’24’s The Fire Inside) is an exhilarating testament to loving fully, making amends, and moving on.

report-to-mother.title: Report to Mother
report-to-mother.synopsis:
A daring clarion call and one of the most significant works of Indian political cinema, John Abraham’s extraordinary final film Amma Ariyan (Report to Mother) follows a young man in 1970s Kerala as he journeys — with a progressive swell of companions — to inform a mother of her son’s death, amid widespread unrest.

A legendary figure in Indian parallel cinema and protegé of Ritwik Ghatak, John Abraham (1937–1987) is known for his modest, yet visionary and iconoclastic body of work. His final film, the Malayalam cult classic Amma Ariyan (Report to Mother, 1986) — now resuscitated in this meticulous, handsome 4K restoration — is one of the most significant works of political cinema from the subcontinent.

In 1970s Kerala, Purushan is set to leave for Delhi. His trip is cut abruptly short, however, when he encounters the dead body of a young man who has tragically taken his own life. Investigating the dead man’s identity by way of his friends — including doctors, activists, and musicians — he learns that the deceased is Hari, a young tabla player and revolutionary. Purushan then journeys — initially travelling on foot with a small group that progressively swells — to inform Hari’s mother. Along the way, they traverse both the geography and social stratum of Kerala, mapping out the state’s political unrest in a form of collective ritual.

Shot in black and white with all natural light and seamlessly incorporating cinéma vérité reports of ongoing and historical workers’ struggles in the region, the film is a rich mix of documentary realism and fiction, with structural rhythms that emanate a moving lyricism. Independently produced by the Odessa Collective, an itinerant cinema club that screened films with a 16mm projector and radically challenged the systems of film production, exhibition, and community outside of the capitalist industry, Amma Ariyan’s spirit of rebellion and solidarity is also reflected in the conditions of its making — and remains a timely inspiration today.

Restored by Film Heritage Foundation at L’Immagine Ritrovata laboratory and Digital Film Restore Pvt. Ltd. in association with Odessa Collective. Special thanks to cinematographer Venu ISC and editor Bina Paul. Funding provided by Film Heritage Foundation. Amma Ariyan was restored in 4K from one of the only two surviving prints: the first-generation 35mm release print preserved at the NFDC – National Film Archive of India.
report-to-mother.teaser:
North American Premiere of 4K restoration!

A daring clarion call and one of the most significant works of Indian political cinema, John Abraham’s extraordinary final film Amma Ariyan (Report to Mother) follows a young man in 1970s Kerala as he journeys — with a progressive swell of companions — to inform a mother of her son’s death, amid widespread unrest.

spirit-guardians-the-last-secret-of-the-.title: Spirit Guardians: The Last Secret of the First Emperor
spirit-guardians-the-last-secret-of-the-.synopsis:
The largest production in the history of Vietnamese cinema, this sweeping epic from director Nguyễn Phan Quang Binh (The Floating Lives) transports us to the era of the Đinh dynasty, when a diverse band of fearless warriors set out on a secret mission to safeguard a sacred mystery. Featuring an ensemble cast led by Tuấn Trần (Mai), Johnny Trí Nguyễn (Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods), and Đỗ Thị Hải Yến (TIFF ’02’s The Quiet American), Spirit Guardians: The Last Secret of the First Emperor is a spectacular tale of heroism and sacrifice.

Following a period of chaos and violence between warlords vying for territory, Đinh Bộ Lĩnh (Lê Vũ Long, TIFF ’24’s Don’t Cry, Butterfly) emerges as the first emperor of a newly independent Vietnam. Stability under Đinh’s reign is fragile, however, and when the emperor’s earthly life reaches its end, the sanctity of his tomb is under threat. Spanning class and gender, a team of seven warriors is dispatched to escort 99 coffins through enemy territory as part of a mission to ensure that Dinh’s resting place remains an eternal secret.

Reminiscent of the grand, engrossing period films of Akira Kurosawa and punctuated with breathtaking martial arts choreography, Spirit Guardians is at once bracingly visceral and flooded with sumptuous pageantry. Windswept locations, intricate production design, and exquisite, handmade costumes vividly evoke the rugged splendour of 10th-century Vietnam. This is epic storytelling, and a shining example of Vietnam's surging new film scene.
spirit-guardians-the-last-secret-of-the-.teaser: The largest production in Vietnamese history, this sweeping epic from Nguyễn Phan Quang Binh (The Floating Lives) transports us to the Đinh dynasty, when a band of fearless warriors set out on a secret mission to safeguard a sacred mystery.

spring-in-a-small-town.title: Spring in a Small Town
spring-in-a-small-town.synopsis:
Crowned the greatest Chinese film ever made by the Hong Kong Film Critics Society, director Fei Mu’s poetic, romantic 1948 masterpiece observes a bored wife enlivened by a surprise visit from an old flame, whose presence threatens to upend the matrimonial home.

Yuwen (Wei Wei) has spent six of her eight married years nursing Liyan (Shi Yu) through vague, undefined illnesses, possibly compounded by a hypochondriac neurosis. Yuwen is an ideal wife — she also looks after her husband’s younger sister — but she is terribly bored. Into this stasis comes Liyan’s old friend Zhichen (Li Wei), now a doctor. It is revealed that he and Yuwen were once adolescent sweethearts. Urbane and vital, Zhichen awakens something in Yuwen. But Liyan’s dawning awareness of the romantic history between Yuwen and Zhichen creates tension, jarring the couple from their romantic fever dream.

Despite the time period — the film was released in 1948 and is set just prior — Yuwen is no passive figure, driving the film’s quiet current of desire. The evolution of her feelings is traced through a delicate visual style of long takes, careful framing, and suggestive lighting that communicates what the characters cannot.

Performances are understated and often strikingly modern, with Li Wei — who would go on to play the cruel dye-house owner in Zhang Yimou's Ju Dou decades later — a particular standout as Zhichen. When resignation finally settles over the characters, it lands softly, as each of their emotional sacrifices have been witnessed and honoured.

A study of repressed desire and duty, renowned director Wong Kar-wai has cited Spring in a Small Town as an inspiration for his film, In the Mood for Love. Frequently topping the lists of greatest Chinese films, Fei Mu’s masterpiece went against the grain upon its release, eschewing the melodramatic stylizing of the era’s popular, nationalist films. It is essential viewing in the canon of cinema of yearning.

Restored from the 35mm nitrate camera-original negatives, this 4K restoration by the China Film Archive honors the 120th anniversary of director Fei Mu’s birth. A highlight of this project was the discovery of a pre-mix music soundtrack negative, which was confirmed as part of the original 1948 theatrical soundtrack. The original balance and ambient depth were restored, and the audio was remastered into 5.1 surround sound.
spring-in-a-small-town.teaser:
World Premiere of 4K restoration!

Crowned the greatest Chinese film ever made by the Hong Kong Film Critics Society, director Fei Mu’s poetic, romantic 1948 masterpiece observes a bored wife enlivened by a surprise visit from an old flame, whose presence threatens to upend the matrimonial home.

ten-dark-women.title: Ten Dark Women
ten-dark-women.synopsis:
In the stylish, satirical, and ahead-of-its-time Ten Dark Women (Kuroi jûnin no onna, 1961), by legendary Japanese director Kon Ichikawa, 10 women discover they are sharing the same pathologically unfaithful man, and temporarily abandon jealousy to meticulously orchestrate a collective revenge.

In Ten Dark Women (Kuroi jûnin no onna, 1961) by legendary Japanese director Kon Ichikawa, 10 women discover they are sharing the same pathologically unfaithful man, and temporarily abandon jealousy to meticulously orchestrate a collective revenge. Kaze (Eiji Funakoshi) is the pathetic cad at the centre of all of the hoopla, a philandering television producer who falls so easily in love that he can’t keep track of how many times he has cheated on his long suffering wife, Futaba (Fujiko Yamamoto), a successful restaurateur who has reached her limit. Refusing to remain a victim, Futaba forms a pact with nine of her husband’s mistresses (played by an unparalleled ensemble of studio divas) to kill him off — though she has a secret plan of her own that leads to unexpected twists.

With a brilliant, before-its-time script by Natto Wada (Ichikawa’s wife and collaborator, with whom he arguably made his greatest films, writing under a pseudonym), the film transforms both the codes of noir and the classic melodrama through a feminist inversion, going so far as to blur, reject, and reassign gender roles. Shot in widescreen DaieiScope in stunning chiaroscuro, the film is teeming with long shadows, close-ups, modernist jazz, terrific set pieces, formal precision, and some zesty dialogue, balancing its cynicism with sardonic humour and sharp social critique.

Avant-garde in the true sense of the word, Ten Dark Women was largely misunderstood and deemed too progressive at the time of its release, only gaining in importance since, making this gorgeous 4K restoration imperative viewing.

Restored in 4K in 2026 by KADOKAWA CORPORATION at IMAGICA Entertainment Media Services laboratory, from the original 35mm negatives. Grading supervised by Masahiro Miyajima and Chizuko Osada.
ten-dark-women.teaser:
North American Premiere of 4K restoration!
