In the stylish, satirical, and ahead-of-its-time Ten Dark Women (Kuroi jûnin no onna, 1961), by legendary Japanese director Kon Ichikawa, 10 women discover they are sharing the same pathologically unfaithful man, and temporarily abandon jealousy to meticulously orchestrate a collective revenge.

tender-loving-care.title: Tender Loving Care
tender-loving-care.synopsis:
Academy award nominated writer-director and Palme d’Or and BAFTA winner Mike Leigh (Mr. Turner, TIFF ’14; Hard Truths, TIFF ’24) returns to the Festival with another astute portrait of ordinary lives, examining the complexities of aging, family, and learning to embrace life’s inevitable changes. Amy (Kate O’Flynn, Widow’s Bay) is a devoted social service worker who puts her heart and soul into her job to care for those in need. At home, however, she finds herself confronting new challenges as her beloved father begins to have issues, and she and her mother must begin to make peace with their new reality. Through it all, Amy finds comfort, perspective, and plenty of laughter through sips of wine with her lifelong friend Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), whose warmth and wit become a vital anchor as both women navigate the shifting rhythms of approaching middle age.

Few artists understand the emotional texture of everyday life quite like Leigh. Renowned for his singular collaborative process with actors, he once again elicits performances of remarkable honesty from his talented ensemble, capturing the quiet moments, awkward conversations, and small acts of kindness that define our relationships. O’Flynn and Bailey Johnson give compellingly authentic performances, creating an enduring friendship that feels lived-in and familiar. Poignant without ever becoming sentimental — and unflinchingly real without becoming grim — Leigh’s latest is a gently uplifting celebration of resilience, compassion, and the people we surround ourselves with. In the hands of the incomparable filmmaker, Tender Loving Care is another masterclass in finding the extraordinary within the ordinary.
tender-loving-care.teaser: Seven-time Academy Award nominee Mike Leigh returns with an uplifting story of family and how to deal with grief, featuring remarkably emotional performances from Kate O’Flynn and Alice Bailey Johnson.

the-julia-set.title: The Julia Set
the-julia-set.synopsis:
For Julia (Chase Infiniti, One Battle After Another), mathematics has always come naturally. But growing up, she learned to downplay her abilities to draw attention away from her high-needs sibling and perhaps not disrupt the expectations of others. Before long though, her intellectual talents are recognized by a teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney, The Summer I Turned Pretty), who recruits her into an elite group of student prodigies training for a highly prestigious undergraduate mathematics competition, The Putnam Exam.

Julia is thrown into the deep end, training with an infamously tough professor (Nina Hoss) who has already picked her favourites. Among them is Pascal, whose father (Jason Isaacs) is a giant in the field of mathematics. Unfortunately, his way of passing the baton is through intimidation. As the competition nears, tensions rise, sending Pascal spiralling but bringing out the best in slow and steady Julia.

Niki Byrne’s insightful debut explores how we decide who is groomed for genius and who is expected to be in a supporting role in ways that often come down to the body one is born into and the means of the family raising them. Infiniti is strong as the quietly capable Julia, aided by Chloe Bailey as her spirited best friend and Gillian Anderson in a powerful performance as a talented thinker in her own right watching Julia stand at a familiar crossroads.
the-julia-set.teaser: Chase Infiniti stars as a gifted university student who becomes romantically involved with a teaching assistant as they both prepare for the Putnam Exam, the most challenging math competition in North America. Gillian Anderson and Jason Isaacs co-star.

the-man-i-love.title: The Man I Love
the-man-i-love.synopsis:
Friday, September 18: This screening will be presented with open captions and live captioning for the onstage components.

The protagonist of Ira Sachs’ new drama, The Man I Love, is an actor and performance artist in 1980s New York who’s dying of AIDS. His diagnosis is central to the plot, but, just as Jimmy (Rami Malek, TIFF ‘25’s Nuremberg) remains the defiant author of his own life, Sachs eschews the familiar beats of a story about illness, instead excavating a naturalistic portrait of a group of artists in a very particular time and place.

As is fitting for such a mesmeric character, we hear about Jimmy before we see him. After a recent hospital stay, he feels more alive than ever, and is ready to concentrate his energy on a starring role in an adaptation of a work by Québécois playwright Michel Tremblay. The Man I Love lingers on impromptu performances, conversations around the dinner table, and long, grounded theatre rehearsal scenes: the communal act of creation remains central. The film's visual language is warm and inviting, prioritizing rich textures and intricate details over strict medical precision.

But this collective also carries the potential for destruction. Jimmy can be selfish and capricious, taking up all the air in the room. As well, the spectre of the disease is always present, though it often weighs more heavily on Jimmy’s devoted partner Dennis (an unshakeable Tom Sturridge, TIFF ‘23’s Widow Clicquot) and his sister Brenda (Rebecca Hall, TIFF ‘24’s The Listeners) than on Jimmy himself. The Man I Love is an idiosyncratic portrait of an artist who above all aches to create.

Content advisory: strobing effects, sexual content, nudity, mature themes, coarse language
the-man-i-love.teaser: Ira Sachs’ vision of New York artists living under the spectre of AIDS in the ’80s focuses on the joy and salvation of creativity.

a-common-story.title: A Common Story
a-common-story.synopsis:
Erika and Mauro are accustomed to their quotidian routines and live a simple life in provincial central Italy. Erika (portrayed by the incomparable, shapeshifting Alba Rohrwacher, also at the Festival with A Good Little Soldier) works as a cashier at the local market while Mauro (Guido Caprino, last at the Festival in 2017 with Godard Mon Amour, in a heartfelt performance) works as a day labourer. When their adored daughter leaves home to study — far from the reach of her doting parents — the house empties and, in a heartbeat, the two are left alone together.

Having always defined herself by caring for others, Erika is suddenly adrift. Mauro, raised by an authoritarian father who is still in the picture, meanders through the newly created void, encountering long-hidden vulnerabilities around every corner. But as they still have many years ahead of them, the nascent empty nesters must adapt to a new way of life, refocus their worlds, and find balance.

Co-written with Tania Pedroni and Matteo Ferri, Anna Foglietta’s debut feature is an intimate exploration of making peace with the passage of time, welcoming the possibility of transformation, and finding a new compass with which to navigate an unknown future.

Elegantly shot by Andrea Benjamin Manenti, the film vividly captures a complex spectrum of difficult emotions, lingering in each gesture and every moment of silence. With their truths finally laid bare, the couple must face one another and, most critically, themselves. A Common Story is certain to resonate with singles and couples alike.
a-common-story.teaser: Starring Alba Rohrwacher (Three Goodbyes, TIFF ’25) and Guido Caprino, writer-director Anna Foglietta’s heartfelt debut feature follows nascent empty nesters who encounter old desires while seeking new meaning in their lives.

arne-goes-to-space.title: Arne Goes to Space
arne-goes-to-space.synopsis:
Earth can be an odd and confounding place even for its regular inhabitants, never mind an interplanetary traveller like the one who enters the lives of two brothers in Arne Goes To Space. The chance to see our planet from this unusual perspective makes for a delightfully odd yet warm-hearted film by Sweden’s Lars Vega.

Arne (Lennart Jähkel) and Stefan (Rolf Lassgård) are two elderly siblings still living on the farm where they were raised by their parents in a sleepy rural community in the northern Swedish province of Norrbotten. Though the personality differences between the talkative, sunny Arne and the taciturn, crotchety Stefan become stark over the course of their daily and nightly routines, it’s just as clear how well the brothers complement each other.

Yet along with some worrying news about Arne’s health, another development threatens to upset the household’s longstanding order when an alien spacecraft crash lands in the woods nearby. That the brothers and their neighbours are so unfazed by the presence of a three-foot-tall extraterrestrial (played by Hollywood veteran Kiran Shah) — who Arne names “Roland” in a characteristically friendly gesture — is one of the many rich sources of comedy in Vega’s debut feature.

Boasting the same flair for small-town surrealism and affection for his characters that the director displayed in his award-winning shorts, Arne Goes To Space blossoms into a charming and utterly distinctive ode to the value of family and community, and to the challenges of facing uncertainties at any stage of life.
arne-goes-to-space.teaser: An extraterrestrial visitor upends the lives of two elderly brothers in northern Sweden in Lars Vega’s disarming blend of sci-fi fable and small-town comedy.

bedford-park.title: Bedford Park
bedford-park.synopsis:
This powerful and raw feature debut from writer-director Stephanie Ahn explores the complexities of diasporic experience through a chance encounter between two thirtysomething, second-generation Korean Americans. Tracking their relationship as it moves from circumstantial to friendly to romantic, Bedford Park brings deeper insight to what it means to self-actualize between cultures.

Eli (Son Sukku, My Liberation Notes) and Audrey (Moon Choi, Now, We Are Breaking Up) meet when Eli gets into a car accident with Audrey’s mother. They come to know each other when Audrey, as a way to make amends, volunteers to drive Eli to work. On the surface, their lives couldn’t appear more different: Eli was adopted by a white woman, raised with little connection to his roots, and works as a mall security guard, while Audrey grew up in a tumultuous household with her Korean-born parents, and is a physical therapist. Yet both characters seek to make peace with their present lives by reckoning with their respective pasts. For Eli, this means facing fatherhood, while Audrey struggles to free herself from her mother’s unreasonable expectations.

Ahn brings great sensitivity to her protagonists’ disparate needs, balancing the weight of personal identity and generational trauma. Bedford Park is not afraid to look at the darker, more painful wounds from cultural displacement and shows us that sometimes we need to parent ourselves to break harmful cycles.
bedford-park.teaser: Writer-director Stephanie Ahn’s feature debut explores the complexities of diasporic experience through a chance encounter between two thirtysomething, second-generation Korean Americans, tracking their relationship as it moves from circumstantial to friendly to romantic.

children-untold.title: Children Untold
children-untold.synopsis:
War may be over, but for the children of Miwa Nishikawa’s latest film — adapted from her forthcoming novel — survival has only begun.

Set amid the ruins of postwar Tokyo, this piercing portrait of childhood stolen by war follows 12-year-old Kotoko, who loses her family, disguises herself as a boy, and joins a group of orphans surviving through odd jobs, theft, black-market trading, and the fragile protection of a local gang. Meanwhile, her former teacher, Sone, burdened by poverty and guilt, sets out to find Kotoko, the student she failed to protect.

Nishikawa develops the story with remarkable sensitivity, never overlooking the realities of abandonment, abused childhoods, and the compromises forced upon children and adults alike, all without slipping into sentimentality. The film recalls Italian neorealism, particularly Vittorio De Sica’s Shoeshine, in its attention to children surviving amid postwar devastation, social neglect, and moral uncertainty — yet feels entirely contemporary in its acute gaze at youth denied.

The young ensemble is remarkable. Ami Koyae is astonishing in her first leading role, capturing Kotoko’s transformation from model student to street survivor with extraordinary complexity and emotional control. The other actors are equally convincing, while Fumi Nikaido brings depth to Sone and Koji Yakusho is, as always, magnetic and commanding in a small but pivotal role.

Children Untold carries particular urgency today. As children continue to bear the consequences of conflicts around the world, the film asks what war does to the young and what responsibility adults and society bear toward those left unprotected.
children-untold.teaser: Acclaimed filmmaker and author Miwa Nishikawa adapts her forthcoming novel into a compassionate and clear-eyed postwar drama about a 12-year-old orphan who disguises herself as a boy, featuring a striking performance by newcomer Ami Koyae and a memorable supporting turn by Koji Yakusho.

head-to-head.title: Head to Head
head-to-head.synopsis:
Bahar (Mehrnoosh Satari) is an acclaimed Iranian director, having made numerous films selected in international festivals. So when she casts actors and asks them to wear women’s outfits for her latest film, they agree in the hope of an international career — or even a visa to leave the country. But wearing skirts and headscarves under the heat is harder than they expected … as is the hit to their pride.

In this "film within a film" structure, Ghasideh Golmakani tackles not only the way women are portrayed by her fellow male directors but also their place in Iranian society. Using all the questions she had, Golmakani makes a brilliant use of humour to depict the relationships between men and women. “I’m not torturing you,” says Bahar to an uncooperative actor. “We’re recreating a perfectly normal situation with costumes used in our cinema.”

Then censorship intervenes, and the film crew steps outside its original setting to confront its own ambivalences with those of the outside world. The mockery rises to a whole new level, in which an old woman appears as the guardian of traditions, and thus an accomplice to the oppression experienced by women.

At a time when women filmmakers are fighting harder than ever to gain recognition in film industries where they remain a minority, Golmakani’s voice resonates as a cry from the heart, and Head to Head as a necessary and salutary act of rebellion.
head-to-head.teaser: Iranian filmmaker Ghasideh Golmakani’s absurd and sharply satirical debut feature explores what happens when a female director forces male actors to wear skirts and headscarves.

i-am-mario.title: I Am Mario
i-am-mario.synopsis:
Mario (Oustin de León) is a gentle forty-year-old transgender taxi driver working in a big city in present-day México. He has bonded with his colleagues and has a relationship with his family — his mother and two sisters — that is caring and mostly stable. When he unexpectedly becomes pregnant, he finally has the opportunity to fulfill a long-held and intimate desire to become a father. But the news also shakes what he thought were the solid foundations of many of his own beliefs and expectations, particularly those regarding his masculinity. Mario’s questioning leads him to painful decisions and a sense of being completely cornered by life. Before exposing himself to his colleagues and facing social prejudices, he must confront himself.

Writer and director Sharon Kleinberg — making her directorial debut after a long career as both an actor and playwright — conducted extensive research for her feature film debut, which led her not only to cast a trans man — and untrained actor — as her lead, but to crystallize a deeply moving and dignified narrative. I Am Mario is a film that challenges moral, social, and religious principles and assumptions surrounding pregnancy, which is traditionally associated solely with women. Faced with a circumstance that is hard to fathom, Mario finds courage and strength in the vulnerability he thought wasn’t a part of him anymore.

Content advisory: homophobic, racist, and transphobic language; explicit sex scenes
i-am-mario.teaser: A transgender taxi driver’s dream of fatherhood becomes a reality when he gets pregnant, forcing him to confront his own notions of masculinity while navigating unexpected social, moral, and emotional consequences.

idda.title: Idda
idda.synopsis:
In director Irene Dionisio’s simmering and sensual Idda, a physical act becomes imbued with emotional magnitude. A children's dance teacher, Sofia (Romana Maggiora Vergano), returns to her hometown to meet her childhood friend Adele (Tecla Insolia), who works as a photographer and tends to her father's shop. After years of aspiration, the pair plan to finally climb Mount Etna, an active volcano on the Eastern Coast of Sicily.

As Sofia enjoys the seemingly uncomplicated ease associated with the reunion, Adele quietly occludes her own feelings of resentment, until they have no other outlet but to erupt. As the pair make their way up the mountainside, both aided and impeded by a veritable mountain man (Giuseppe De Domenico), the physical strain pales in comparison to the emotional weight they carry as they navigate the winding terrain. In this languidly mysterious portrait anchored by ubiquitous fears about the perils of change, secrets of the past and the present bubble up, culminating in a loss that neither woman could have imagined.

Following her 2016 debut Le ultime cose, Dionisio’s sophomore feature, which she co-penned alongside Marco Borromei, takes an epic approach to unearthing the packed layers of a stewing friendship. Cinematographer Gergely Pohárnok’s portentous camera acts as the perfect complement to Dionisio’s sublime style and singular voice, meandering through paths loaded with personal strife, confused tactility, and an undercurrent of divinity. The diffident performances pulse with the understated violence of the volcano on which they tread, a reminder of nature's immortalism and humanity's inevitable finality.
idda.teaser: When two childhood friends meet after years to fulfill the broken promise of climbing Mount Etna, Adele and Sofia realize that like the mountain, old wounds loom over everything.

in-conversation-with-andrew-scott.title: In Conversation With... Andrew Scott
in-conversation-with-andrew-scott.synopsis: Here at TIFF ’26 with one of the standout performances of the year in Elsinore, Andrew Scott proves once and for all that he’s one of the most versatile and captivating performers of our time. While his role as the charismatic priest in Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag introduced Scott to a wider audience, devoted fans had been following his work for years, including his electrifying turn as Moriarty in Sherlock, where he transformed the iconic villain into a captivating force of chaos. Scott first came to the Festival in 2014 with Matthew Warchus’ Pride, as part of an ensemble cast celebrating the history of LGBTQ+ activism in the UK, and returned most recently in 2025 as part of the acclaimed Knives Out franchise with Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery and Richard Linklater’s celebrated Blue Moon. Scott has emerged as one of the leading actors bringing complex queer experiences to the screen — from Andrew Haigh’s All of Us Strangers, an intimate meditation on longing, grief, family, and memory, to his chilling transformation in Netflix’s Ripley, a dark reimagining of The Talented Mr. Ripley. In Elsinore, a film he also produced, Scott delivers a deeply personal and powerful performance as actor Ian Charleson, who in his final years summons exceptional courage to overcome immense physical challenges and deliver a defining performance of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre while living with AIDS. The conversation will explore the remarkable range of Scott’s career and celebrate this extraordinary new performance.
in-conversation-with-andrew-scott.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

in-conversation-with-chris-rock.title: In Conversation With... Chris Rock
in-conversation-with-chris-rock.synopsis: As he presents the TIFF ’26 World Premiere of his latest film Misty Green, Emmy and Grammy Award–winning director, writer, actor, producer, and comedian Chris Rock joins us for a conversation about his multi-faceted career in front of and behind the camera. After his breakthrough on Saturday Night Live in the early 1990s — as part of an iconic cast that included Adam Sandler, Chris Farley, and David Spade — Rock re-defined the landscape of stand-up comedy with his sharp, incisive special Bring the Pain (1996). The groundbreaking set catapulted him to superstardom and earned him two Emmys. Tackling socio-political issues like race relations, class division, and the justice system with piercing fervor, Rock has crafted an indelible onstage persona over the past three decades. Beyond stand-up, his career spans Hollywood blockbusters, hit television series, and acclaimed independent filmmaking. He produced and starred in the lauded documentary Good Hair (TIFF ’09), which won the Special Jury Prize Documentary at Sundance, and later moved into the director’s chair for the deeply personal Top Five (TIFF ’14). He returns to the Festival with Misty Green, a film destined to further cement his status as one of Hollywood’s most original creative voices.
in-conversation-with-chris-rock.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

krux.title: Krux
krux.synopsis:
In the final days of the Second World War, rumours of heavy losses and an advancing Soviet force — brutal and bloodthirsty for revenge — were making waves westward through what remained of the Third Reich. Set in a remote east German village, unluckily located on the side facing the front and in the Red Army’s path, and based on true events, Krux depicts a shocking point in history when right-wing terror was directed against its own people.

While the men are away on the frontline, 28-year-old Greta (Jella Haase), 30-year-old Anni (Frida-Lovisa Hamann) and the remaining villagers — women, children, the elderly, the mayor (Lukas Miko), and men who, like the priest (Martin Wuttke) and local headmaster (Clemens Schick), were deemed unfit for service — try to preserve a semblance of life. But, mounting corpses along the riverbank signal defeat, and soon, fear gives way to hysteria, culminating in chilling and brutal commands from afar: leave no Germans alive for arriving Russians.

With haunting visuals from celebrated director of photography Piotr Sobociński Jr. (Corpus Christi, TIFF ‘19) and balanced by Lorenz Dangel’s resonating original score, the fortified debut of writer-director Tony Vahl delivers a stark portrait of moral collapse, societal panic, and the consequences — mostly to be endured by those who bore no arms — of standing on the wrong side of history. As humanity frays and propaganda spills beyond borders, Krux leaves little space for moral quandary, where the so-called perpetrators await their fates like lambs to the slaughter.
krux.teaser: The feature debut of writer-director Tony Vahl delivers a powerful and stark portrait of moral collapse, societal panic, and the consequences of being on the wrong side of history.

memories-of-a-forest.title: Memories of a Forest
memories-of-a-forest.synopsis:
Frieda (Julia Windischbauer) is on deadline to finish her doctoral dissertation by the end of summer, after which she’ll be offered a prestigious position at the University of Vienna. However, the sudden death of her beloved grandmother heralds her return to the Lower Austrian village in which she was raised, where, unlike Frieda, not much has changed. And, as the famous adage goes, you can’t go home again.

When the estate is being settled, everyone is surprised to learn that the prized 15 hectares of forest — once purchased as an investment in the future, and which could now be sold to relieve the family’s financial difficulties — have been left to the city-dwelling student. Frieda’s laconic mother Joahanna, in the footsteps of the late family matriarch, whose life was marked by responsibilities and physical labour, has always subordinated her needs to farm and family, and harbours strong feelings about their resources. However, upon evaluating the landscape of her inheritance, which, due to a rampant bark beetle infestation may be worthless, the bewildered granddaughter, bearing a sense of obligation to her legacy and to the forest that bore witness to generations of sacrifice, must now make a choice between her origins and her envisioned future.

Shot by Jacob Kohl and co-penned alongside Karla Cristóbal, director Katharina Rabl’s stunning debut toggles between loyalty and a sense of duty to what’s come before and the desires to fulfil one’s own wildest dreams and what might lay ahead. When the time comes, Freida must choose what for her is a road less traveled.
memories-of-a-forest.teaser: Katharina Rabl’s stunning debut feature toggles between loyalty and longing for independence, centring a doctoral student who must choose between carrying on her family’s legacy or forging her own path.

nosotros.title: Nosotros
nosotros.synopsis:
When Romero (Jozef Coxaj), a thirtysomething man from rural Guatemala, leaves his Indigenous wife and young child behind in their remote village, he promises them he will return just as soon as he’s earned enough money to ease their economic struggles. Moving to the city to work as a security guard, he finds himself facing estrangement, loneliness, and the performative macho milieu that surrounds him in this unfamiliar environment. His journey is further complicated when he falls fast and hard for Nubia (Lola Vásquez), a transgender small business owner with a shop in the mall he patrols.

In his feature directorial debut, director Joaquín Ruano carefully deploys a cinematic language of nuance, restraint, and clarity. As Romero and Nubia’s developing relationship blooms in the midst of perils and tensions, Ruano quietly opens new ways to witness this unexpected intimacy. Romero finds refuge where he least expected — and even without knowing he was desperately searching for it — and discovers an affection that is as fragile as it is tender. Inside the safe space Nubia creates for both of them, Romero finds a version of himself he wasn’t aware had previously existed. The harsh world around them may never truly leave them alone.

Content advisory: homophobic and transphobic language, explicit sex scenes, bullying, course language, mature themes
nosotros.teaser: After leaving his Indigenous family for work in Guatemala City, a lonely security guard falls for a business owner at the mall he patrols, discovering an unexpected refuge and a new sense of self in a world not yet ready to make space for them.

on-behalf-of-my-son.title: On Behalf of My Son
on-behalf-of-my-son.synopsis:
Featuring a standout, affecting turn from Rejane Faria, Gabriel Martins’ compassionate drama is a moving meditation on guilt, grief, and the elusive possibility of forgiveness. With remarkable feeling and restraint, the film explores the devastating aftermath of tragedy, asking whether redemption can ever ease the weight of unbearable loss.

The story begins with a shocking accident: a public transit bus plunges from a bridge, claiming multiple lives. In the wake of the disaster, Vicentina (Faria), the mother of the driver, is consumed by the fear that her son may have deliberately caused the crash. Determined to confront the consequences of what happened, she embarks on a difficult journey to meet the victims’ families, seeking forgiveness while searching for answers that may never come.

Faria delivers a performance of extraordinary depth and understated resilience. She inhabits Vicentina with profound empathy, conveying immense sorrow without ever surrendering her character’s dignity or determination. Every encounter and every mile travelled carries the weight of a woman trying to survive an impossible burden.

Leonardo Feliciano’s cinematography heightens the film’s intimacy, capturing grief in all its subtle, shifting forms while immersing viewers in Vicentina’s emotional landscape. Following his acclaimed Mars One, Brazil’s official submission to the Academy Awards in 2023, Martins takes another significant step as a filmmaker. With tenderness and honesty, he crafts a humane portrait of mourning, revealing how loss transforms lives while leaving just enough room for hope to emerge from even the darkest moments.
on-behalf-of-my-son.teaser: Anchored by a deeply affecting performance from Rejane Faria, Gabriel Martins’ moving drama follows a grieving mother seeking forgiveness from the families of a tragic bus accident. What unfolds is a profound meditation on guilt and whether forgiveness is possible.

seventeen.title: Seventeen
seventeen.synopsis:
Seventeen follows the intersecting lives of three young, queer, Indigenous sex workers in gritty downtown Vancouver over 17 hours as they face significant challenges. First-time feature director and writer Justin Ducharme handles each character with care and sensitivity, and the authenticity radiates off the screen.

A cast of relative newcomers play the three lead characters. The drama is not about the work each of them do, but instead about important deadlines they are racing to meet: Tamara (Nizhonniya Austin) must track down a passport before she’s kicked out of the country, Aiden (Taio Gélinas) has to find the money for a deposit on a new apartment, and December (Aalayna) needs to acknowledge a pressing family situation back home on her reserve. Also appearing in pivotal smaller roles are some of today’s leading Indigenous actors, such as Kaniehtiio Horn (Seeds, TIFF ’24) and Joel Oulette (Can I Get a Witness? TIFF ’24, also at this year’s Festival in Carrie).

As the clock ticks down on each of their deadlines, chosen family members step in — and up — to do whatever they can but, crucially, Tamara, Aiden, and December need to do the work themselves. This is an impressive debut from Ducharme, one that gives viewers a glimpse into the complex realities of queer Indigenous people living on the margins in the urban spaces around us.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
seventeen.teaser: Three young queer Indigenous people’s lives intersect and overlap over the course of 17 hours in downtown Vancouver.

silenced-nights.title: Silenced Nights
silenced-nights.synopsis:
One night, in a dark Manila alley, Andoy (Nico Antonio) witnesses the police executing a teenage boy. It’s a near-nightly occurrence with the ongoing anti-drug operations, and its dangers prompt Andoy to lay low. He quietly returns to his daily routine of fixing gadgets and taking on odd jobs until he crosses paths with the dead boy’s distraught mother, Marissa (Lotlot de Leon). Seeing her struggle to discover the truth, Andoy finds the courage to break his silence.

With an enthusiastic journalist (Ina Feleo) on their side, Andoy and Marissa attempt to trace the events of that bloody evening, determined to reclaim the boy’s innocence and hold his killers accountable. But brick walls keep appearing, thwarting the group’s best efforts.

Award-winning filmmaker Lawrence Fajardo’s bleak drama gives an unapologetic glimpse into the sociopolitical realities and harsh experiences of the Filipino people. Shot on location in the Manila slum known as Happyland — derived from its original Visayan name “Hapiland”, which means “dump siteing ground” — the film takes a cinema verité approach to capture the raw authenticity of its setting.

As with many of his previous works, such as the buzzy 2024 Cinemalaya title The Hearing, Fajardo once again dissects social injustice to amplify the voices of the silenced.
silenced-nights.teaser: For some, staying silent is the only way to survive. Lawrence Fajardo’s bleak sociopolitical drama Silenced Nights follows a witness to an extrajudicial killing in a Philippines slum as he seeks to make the truth known.

sisters.title: Sisters
sisters.synopsis:
Intergenerational trauma and guilt encircle sisters Chelo (Emma Suárez) and Marta (Elena Anaya) when a celebratory holiday weekend outside Madrid heralding the beginning of summer is overshadowed by a real-life nightmare.

In the middle of the night, Chelo’s tween daughter Sofia awakens her mother, terrified, to confide that she has been sexually assaulted by her 18-year-old cousin, Lucas. While Chelo leaps into action, expertly managing the bureaucracy of hospitals and police statements while trying to stay afloat in caring for her catatonic daughter, Marta refuses to believe that her son would commit such an abhorrent crime.

Ione Hernández’s stunning fiction debut examines a shattered family to investigate the intertwined complications of personal bias, hazardous contrition, and lingering envy, with an intuitive lens and a careful consideration of truth and justice.

Hernández’s unique observational approach exchanges detachment for compassion, highlighting her journalistic eye and expansive tonal control. Each sister stands in mirrored contrast, as Chelo’s reliance on therapeutic resolution contends with Marta’s panicked denial. Suárez embodies a measured sadness that combines grief with strength, while Anaya’s Marta swells, emotionally spent and psychologically bruised.

As the starkly charged trial looms, Marta’s desperation and anxiety mounts, rearing long-suppressed wounds shared with older sister Chelo. With Sofia’s testimony echoing through the courtroom, the sisters must once again struggle through an impossible reality.
sisters.teaser: Outside of Madrid, two sisters unite their families on a summer weekend, celebrating milestones and the solstice-heralding San Juan Festival. However, joy quickly turns to horror when a serious allegation of sexual abuse surfaces from one of their children.

strong-son-2.title: Strong Son
strong-son-2.synopsis:
For all the hours he spends in the gym pumping iron and working hard to transform his physical form into a well-honed ideal of power and masculinity, the bodybuilder hero of Ian Bawa’s Strong Son can never feel strong enough.

Instead, Harvinder “Harvey” Singh (Mandeep Sodhi) is trapped in a quagmire of anxiety and insecurity. Worse yet, this painful experience has intensified since he returned to his family home in Winnipeg to take care of his aging father, Jagdeep (Amrit Parbhakar).

Stressed out by his caregiver role and further undermined by Jagdeep’s very vocal opinions about what a man ought to do and be, Harvey is barely hanging on. If Harvey has any hope of decreasing the frequency of his teary public breakdowns, it may depend on his burgeoning connection to his co-worker Caitlin (Michaela Kurimsky of Sweet Angel Baby, TIFF ’24) and his promising foray into pro wrestling, Jagdeep’s favourite sport.

With his perceptive and affecting debut feature, Bawa takes several confident steps deeper into the explorations of masculinity, identity, and Sikh family dynamics that he began with his shorts Strong Son (TIFF ’20) and The Best (TIFF ’24), both of which premiered at the Festival. Sodhi — who served as Bawa’s on-screen alter ego in those similarly autobiographical films — again brings a keen vulnerability and a bounty of nervous energy to the central character, a man struggling to discover a new way of defining himself and managing the welter of emotions he feels inside.
strong-son-2.teaser: A bodybuilder struggles to keep it together as he cares for his elderly father in this perceptive and deeply felt drama by Winnipeg’s Ian Bawa.

the-daughters-of-abraham.title: The Daughters of Abraham
the-daughters-of-abraham.synopsis:
In her feature debut, French-Moroccan director Hanaël El Yousfi reunites two estranged friends over the summer holidays, as each of them is reminded of the special bond they shared during adolescence. Away from the pressures of parents and peers, Myriam and Eva are now free to cherish young adulthood and independence.

The story expands on El Yousfi’s fascination with family, relationships, and community previously explored in the 2021 short film Mazel Brouk, which follows five young women at a bachelorette party over a weekend in France. Coming from varied cultural and religious backgrounds, the pre-wedding tradition exposes initial differences, but later unites them as they share stories of their sexual lives and troubling experiences under patriarchy.

In The Daughters of Abraham, the film’s incisive study of faith and gender in society is considerably more concentrated, focusing on Myriam’s Muslim upbringing and Eva’s Jewish heritage, where broader historical tensions inevitably influence their interpersonal dynamics. As the summer progresses, an unexpected tragedy takes place. Its effects threaten to shatter a relationship that had only just been mended, as their extended social circles react to the fallout. After strong performances in El Yousfi’s festival-touring short, César-nominated actor Mélissa Guers and Ava Baya return for a propulsive study of how external structures of gender, power, and politics affect our intimate lives despite our best attempts to connect.
the-daughters-of-abraham.teaser: A young Muslim woman raised in Marseille reunites with a young Jewish woman after a period of estrangement, reconnecting as friends over summer break. When a sudden tragedy disrupts their carefree holiday, the pair face the similarities and differences that strengthen and threaten their relationship together.

the-fortunate-isles.title: The Fortunate Isles
the-fortunate-isles.synopsis:
In Helena Girón and Samuel Delgado’s seething second feature, the brutal landscape and open skies of the Canary Islands — once home of the Guanches people, conquered by the Crown of Castile between 1402 and 1496, marking the first instance of modern European settler imperialism in Africa — are setting to a restrained epic of colonial regret and human impulse.

While the unforgiving landscape maintains ultimate power, Fátima (Luisa Ahl Laabiad), a woman enslaved to a decrepit and deteriorating Marquis on a desolate archipelago, must contend with her near-term pregnancy and the island’s few other parched and malcontent residents. As her master refuses to relinquish his paltry water supply to his desperate citizens, and his son closes in on his fief, an insurrection brews. Now, Fátima must balance her loyalty to herself, her love, and her future child against a corroded power dynamic.

Writing-directing duo Girón and Delgado (the short Neither God Nor Santa Maria, TIFF ‘15) harness the sparse landscape, weaving together its scarcity with the intensity of human tragedy. As conflicting desires emerge for Fátima, between protecting her position and protecting others from immense suffering, the tactile camera and uniquely portentous style culminate in a ruthless portrait of 16th century conquest. Ahl Laabiad’s stoic and furious performance as Fátima pulses with humanity’s insistent history of revolt, embodying those erased by retellings of colonial struggles and ecclesiastical narratives.

Fàtima’s ultimate choice in this searing, poetic tale carries the colossal weight of memory, the drama evoking Heinrich Heine’s 1820 poem “Belshazzar,” where a king’s tyranny and hubris lead to his own doom at the hands of his subjects.
the-fortunate-isles.teaser: In the 16th century, on the newly conquered Canary Islands, colonial misgivings intersect with personal desperation. Fátima, an enslaved and pregnant woman, must struggle to survive both the landscape, and the other inhabitants.

the-world-before.title: The World Before
the-world-before.synopsis:
In her second narrative feature, The World Before, Yoon Dan-bi turns from the childhood perspective of her acclaimed debut Moving On to the emotional volatility of adolescence. Set over one summer on a remote Korean island, the film follows two childhood friends who reunite as teenagers, only to discover that their relationship has been transformed by time, desire, and the knowledge that their days together are limited.

Yoon approaches first love not as a simple romantic awakening, but as an encounter capable of reshaping an entire understanding of the world. The intensity of teenage feeling emerges through awkward gestures, uncertain voices, shifting loyalties, and desires that arrive suddenly and may disappear just as quickly. Her lens sits closer to the characters than in Moving On, while the amplified sound and naturalistic performances create a raw, intimate sense of their inner lives.

The film’s distinctive rhythm finds drama within the everyday. Although the camera often remains still and attentive, events unfold with surprising speed, allowing moments of loss and change to register with quiet force. Yoon’s months spent living on the island bring authenticity to its landscapes, homes, and community, grounding the story in the textures of local life.

Winner of Rotterdam’s Bright Future Award and four prizes at Busan for Moving On, Yoon confirms herself here as one of the most compelling emerging filmmakers in contemporary Korean cinema. Tender, bittersweet, and beautifully observed, The World Before captures the moment when first love becomes inseparable from the end of one chapter and the beginning of another.
the-world-before.teaser: Yoon Dan-bi’s coming-of-age story follows two childhood best friends who reunite for a summer on a remote Korean island. This beautifully constructed slice of life captures the emotional intensity of adolescence through assured filmmaking and compelling performances.

we-are-born-good.title: We Are Born Good
we-are-born-good.synopsis:
A botched takeaway order detonates into a battle of wills in We Are Born Good, the assured feature debut of Hong Kong filmmaker Leung Chuen Yeung, developed through the Hong Kong government film-funding programme, First Feature Film Initiative.

Suet Ying Chung plays an aspiring actress, crushed by debt and disappointment. When a neighbourhood restaurant gets her order wrong and refuses to remake it at closing time, she decides to retaliate. The owner (Wai Lun Yeung), recently released from prison and struggling to rebuild his life, is equally close to his breaking point. Their escalating feud pushes both further into chaos before hostility gives way to an unexpected connection.

Inspired by a viral CCTV clip of a trivial street dispute erupting into violence, Yeung looks beyond the spectacle to ask what pressures had already brought its participants to the brink. The film’s contemporary Hong Kong is a city where money, work, family obligation, and social judgment leave people living on the edge. Its title reflects a compassionate conviction: these characters are not inherently bad, but worn down by grief, anger, and exhaustion.

An accomplished screenwriter, Yeung handles tone and narrative momentum with confidence, while veteran producer Patricia Cheng brings experience to a debut that remains highly personal and original.

The performances are a major strength. Golden Horse winner Chung brings humour, volatility, and vulnerability to her role, while Yeung makes the ex-convict’s defensiveness inseparable from his sadness. Entertaining, emotionally perceptive, and polished throughout, We Are Born Good establishes Leung Chuen Yeung as an exciting emerging filmmaker in East Asian cinema.
we-are-born-good.teaser: Golden Horse winner Suet Ying Chung and Wai Lun Yeung lead Leung Chuen Yeung’s assured debut, in which a struggling actress and an ex-con restaurant owner turn a petty dispute into an unlikely bond. Witty, moving, and accessible.

what-lies-between-us.title: What Lies Between Us
what-lies-between-us.synopsis:
The question of how far a parent will go to protect a child can lead to discomfiting answers. For proof, look no further than What Lies Between Us, director Amalie Næsby Fick’s provocative and gripping drama about a community riven both by accusations of a shocking act and by the reactions and decisions of three embroiled mothers that could change many lives going forward.

In a well-to-do Danish suburb, realtor Anne Sofie (Sidse Babett Knudsen) and shop owner Sara (Sofie Gråbøl) enjoy a close friendship that’s deeply intertwined with their respective family lives. Ulrikke (Asta Kamma August), the single mother of a newcomer to the tennis club where Anne Sofie’s teenaged son trains, is eager to get connected. But when details emerge about a potential sexual assault involving the three women’s sons, lines are swiftly drawn, with Anne Sofie proving remarkably tenacious at defending what’s hers.

One of Nordic cinema’s most formidable performers thanks to stellar work in the TV hit Borgen and films such as The Duke of Burgundy (TIFF ’14) and Limbo (TIFF ’20), Knudsen brings her customary fierceness and intelligence to a character whose maternal propensities drive her toward a moral breaking point. She’s matched at every turn by Gråbøl (TIFF ’25’s The Last Viking) and August (also at this year’s Festival in Growth of the Soil). Working from the layered yet expertly paced screenplay by Sara Jønsson and Nikolaj Arcel (The Promised Land, TIFF ’23), Næsby Fick makes a confident transition from animation and television to live-action features. With What Lies Between Us, she presents viewers with a compelling, timely story about the boundaries of love, ethics, and loyalty.

Content advisory: coarse language, bullying, mature themes, themes of sexual assault
what-lies-between-us.teaser: From Danish director Amalie Næsby Fick and a cast led by Sidse Babett Knudsen comes a compelling cautionary tale about the ethical and moral boundaries a parent may cross in order to protect a child.

wild-wild-east.title: Wild Wild East
wild-wild-east.synopsis:
Occupied Poland, winter 1943. Almost two years have passed since the Third Reich’s attack on the USSR and German forces are suffering heavy losses while the extermination of European Jews is at its height.

Enter Martin Wolff (the multifaceted Itay Tiran, Demon, TIFF ’15), a German official sent to a remote village to investigate the disappearance of a lawyer believed to be safeguarding a stockpile of gold belonging to a wealthy Jewish family. Wolff’s reputation proceeds him, and his arrival to a village of traumatized inhabitants, who include Kuliś (Piotr Trojan), his scrappy wife (Joanna Kulig, Cold War, TIFF ’18), Kaim (Robert Więckiewicz, Wałęsa: Man of Hope, TIFF ’13), and his wife (Magdalena Różczka), sends ripples through a community ripe with impoverished locals, corrupt collaborators, and gruesome — albeit paranoid — Nazi authorities.

Moreover, whispers of the hidden fortune have spread and people are getting desperate. As the gritty web of betrayal and greed is revealed, Wolff’s presence unearths more than meets the eye, revealing a landscape where the past and present refuse to be buried and where everything comes with a price. Penned by Aleksandra Takuska, Wild Wild East is full of unexpected bombshells and shocking historical truths.

Flanked by producing powerhouses Bogna Szewczyk-Skupień and Klaudia Śmieja-Rostworowska (The Testament of Ann Lee, TIFF ’25; High Life, TIFF ’18) as well as Ewa Puszczyńska (The Zone of Interest, TIFF ’23; Ida, TIFF ’16), director Jan Holoubek’s tour de force is keenly shot by Bartek Kaczmarek and enveloped by Jan Komar’s original score. A suspenseful western meets wartime noir, this genre-blending film will resonate far and wide.
wild-wild-east.teaser: Set in occupied Poland in the middle of the Second World War, Jan Holoubek’s tour-de-force is part suspenseful western, part gritty wartime noir.

zjili-a-story-of-sisterhood-and-the-burd.title: Zjili: A Story of Sisterhood and The Burdens of Excess
zjili-a-story-of-sisterhood-and-the-burd.synopsis:
What happens to the clothes you buy cheaply and then toss to make room for new ones? They end up in secondhand stores... or are shipped to African markets where women eke out a meagre living ferrying the heavy textiles around on their heads.

In Zjili: A Story of Sisterhood and the Burden of Excess — “zjili” means “heavy” in Dagbani, spoken in northern Ghana — ambitious teenager Zoya (Abdullah Rahana) leaves her village by herself and settles in Old Fadama, a precarious settlement in Accra straddling both the world’s largest secondhand clothing market and an enormous e-waste dumpsite. There, Zoya hopes to earn enough money to continue her education. She meets Teiya (Esinam Semordzi), a young mother and part-time kayayo who dreams of owning a hairdressing salon, and Charpang (Zarahawu Fuseini), a landlady haunted by painful memories. The three, drawn together by the harsh realities of urban life, powerfully represent intergenerational threads connecting women.

Stories about the tireless kayayei in Ghana are rare but co-directors Christine Boateng and Hajara Musah Chambas bring them to the screen in Zjili: A Story of Sisterhood and the Burden of Excess without sensationalism or artifice. Featuring a fantastic cast and strong visuals by American cinematographer Erin G. Wesley, the film is grounded by research and inspired by real-life stories. Dedicated to a 28-year-old mother who died under a heavy load during production, this feminist film aims to support women labourers while advocating for abolishing this dangerous and sometimes fatal work.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
zjili-a-story-of-sisterhood-and-the-burd.teaser: In their poignant debut feature, co-directors Christine Boateng and Hajara Musah Chambas depict the journey of three Ghanaian women eking out a living as kayayei or porters in the trenches of the world’s largest secondhand clothing market.

a-girl-unknown.title: A Girl Unknown
a-girl-unknown.synopsis:
Inspired by a news story and dedicated to director Zou Jing’s grandmother, whose rural upbringing, resilience, and untamed vitality are reflected in the film’s protagonist, A Girl Unknown follows a Chinese girl from age six to 18 as she moves through three different families, each giving her a new name and altered existence.

Growing up under China’s one-child policy, Wang Juan’s life changes after her father dies and her mother becomes pregnant by a new partner. She is uprooted from her rural home, sent to live with a childless couple in the city and expected to become their daughter. Beneath the apparent stability and comfort of this household, unresolved tensions gradually erode her fragile sense of belonging.

As she grows older, further ruptures force her into yet another new home and identity. Eventually, she finds work in a garment factory and begins the difficult process of defining herself on her own terms.

Structured in chapters, the film traces the emotional consequences of abandonment, displacement, and the pressure to conform. Each new name marks another family, an added burden, and a new stage in the protagonist’s search for belonging.

Zou’s assured debut pairs an expressive colour palette and meticulous attention to setting with a visual language attuned to Juan’s evolving inner world. Restrained performances by leads Cao Ruofan and Li Gengxi deepen this quiet, painful, yet ultimately hopeful coming-of-age story about identity, fortitude, and personal freedom.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
a-girl-unknown.teaser: In Zou Jing’s assured debut, Cao Ruofan and Li Gengxi (Bi Gan’s Resurrection) portray a girl passed through three different families and identities under China’s one-child policy. Visually refined, this affecting coming-of-age drama explores resilience and self-determination.

after-elena.title: After Elena
after-elena.synopsis:
When Elena dies, she leaves behind more than a grieving family. She leaves a void no one knows how to fill. Widower Roberto (Alfredo Castro, Chile’s towering figure of indie cinema) is obsessed with order and routine, and finds himself sharing his home once again with his three adult children, each carrying their own failures, secrets, and ways of coping. The siblings come to realize that their true inheritance is not material wealth — although a couple of them could certainly use some of that — but the silences, guilt, and unspoken affection that shaped their lives.

Director Shawn Garry deploys a gentle, non-judgmental take on the dynamics of a dysfunctional family on the verge of dissolution, balancing light with darkness in every aspect of the film. The narrative doesn’t wallow in heaviness or facile characterizations. Instead, it finds emotional richness in the smallest gestures and seemingly ordinary interactions, allowing each family member the space to reveal unexpected layers of vulnerability.

Amid domestic disputes, absurd situations, and unexpected moments of tenderness, the family begins to unpack the story they have told themselves for decades. With humour, melancholy, and an openness to contradiction, After Elena explores grief, family bonds, and the possibility of reinventing ourselves when the person who once held our world together is gone.
after-elena.teaser: When a family's matriarch dies, four relatives are forced to confront decades of silence, resentment, and buried affection. Led by Alfredo Castro, this sharp ensemble balances humour and melancholy in a moving portrait of grief and reconciliation.

ah-girl.title: Ah Girl
ah-girl.synopsis:
Ah Girl (Ong Xuan Jing) is a curious young girl. At the tender age of seven, she spends her days drawing, quarrelling with her sibling, catching spiders, imitating adults, and wishing her whole family could live together. Since her parents’ separation, she has lived in a small apartment with her younger sister, Ah Tian (Sydney Wong), her taciturn father (James Seah) who works the night shift, and her cantankerous grandmother (Doreen Toh). On weekends, the children see their needy, unpredictable mother (Carrie Wong) who attempts to make up for her absence with treats and gifts.

Like any child, Ah Girl desires to grow up to gain control over the decisions in her life — like keeping her hair long. She has no idea that painful and confusing times lie ahead, bringing her challenges no child should have to face.

Adulthood is rushed for this young bud, and reality prunes her prematurely. Unfortunately, the adults in her life are no gardeners — they hardly know what to do themselves. Ah Girl has only herself to depend on — but her undying, rebellious spirit will lead her to bloom regardless.

Inspired by debut filmmaker Ang’s own childhood, Ah Girl evokes a powerful sense of shared memory, making the protagonist's journey feel somehow familiar. The film’s soft cinematography and convincing mise en scène transport viewers back to 1990s Singapore, delivering the nostalgic warmth of a personal home video. By blending mundane details with dreamy sequences, Ang creates delicate, hazy moments that feel both realistic and deeply personal, creating a sense of bittersweet déjà vu.
ah-girl.teaser: Winner of the Youth Jury Award at the 55th International Film Festival Rotterdam, Ang Geck Geck Priscilla’s feature debut is a bittersweet yet heartwarming story of a young girl as she tries to figure out what it means to become an adult.

ashes.title: Ashes
ashes.synopsis:
Tackling the often painful complexities of the immigrant experience with a deft and deeply humane touch, Mexican Hollywood star Diego Luna’s fourth feature tells a mature and nuanced story that follows its heady themes to unexpected places.

In the opening sequence, young Lucila (Anna Díaz) is left to look after her little brother Diego (Sergio Bautista) as their mother Isabel (Adriana Paz, TIFF 24’s Emilia Pérez) leaves them behind in their Mexico home to look for a better future elsewhere, planning to have them join her when she can.

The film then shows Lucila as a young adult and Diego as a teen. They are now living in Madrid, having finally been sent for, years later, by their mother. Lucila is working as a nanny, while Diego struggles at school, where he acts up and lashes out at classmates. Meanwhile, Isabel is too preoccupied with a romantic relationship to properly care for her family. Lucila decides she’s had enough and moves on, this time to Barcelona, where she seems able to better carve out a space for herself. But life doesn’t go as planned, and Lucila will have to face further displacement — and her toughest trials yet — all on her own.

Díaz is superb as a vulnerable, resilient, and empathetic Lucila, carrying the narrative with a strength that resonates with the larger emotional toll immigrants all over the world face today. Luna’s directing of this adaptation of Brenda Navarro’s novel Cenizas en la boca (Eating Ashes) has more than enough tonal depth to bring the audience closer to Lucila’s seemingly endless voyage to find herself.
ashes.teaser: Diego Luna crafts a powerful and deeply humane portrait of the immigrant experience through the eyes of a young woman forced to rebuild her life in a new country, delivering a nuanced exploration of family, identity, belonging, and displacement.

babies.title: Babies
babies.synopsis:
Anchored by a pair of hugely appealing lead performances from Seth Rogen (TIFF ’25’s Good Fortune) and Oscar nominee Anna Kendrick (TIFF ’09’s Up In the Air), the second feature from writer-director Lauren Miller Rogen (Like Father) digs deep into the dilemma that comes for every couple: to parent or not to parent? Bolstered by an all-star ensemble that includes Issa Rae (TIFF ’23’s American Fiction), Dan Stevens (TIFF ’25’s Swiped), and Oscar nominees Sharon Stone (Casino) and David Strathairn (Good Night, and Good Luck), Babies is relatable, hilarious, and wise in equal measure.

After 17 years of happy coupledom, Annie (Kendrick, also at this year’s Festival in Misty Green) and Aaron (Rogen) routinely get the question: are you two going to have kids? Their answer is always a solid “maybe.” But they’re about to get an opportunity for some serious field study. Having just left her husband Luke (Stevens), their pal Eliza (Kate Berlant, TIFF ’25’s Maddie’s Secret) comes to stay while she looks for a new home — and brings her young daughter along with her. Will witnessing the joys and sorrows of parenting up close tip the scales one way or another? Will ambivalence reign until Annie and Aaron simply age out?

As her protagonists test drive someone else’s toddler, Miller Rogen rounds out her large-canvas group portrait, exploring significant life milestones such as risky business ventures, the challenges of late-in-life dating, and overcoming some serious potty-training anxiety. This is a big-hearted comedy about community, co-operation, and celebrating all the love that fits.
babies.teaser: Seth Rogen and Oscar nominee Anna Kendrick (TIFF ’09’s Up in the Air) star in Lauren Miller Rogen’s big-hearted comedy about the dilemma that eventually infiltrates every long-term relationship: to parent or not to parent?

ben-imana.title: Ben'Imana
ben-imana.synopsis:
For a long time, Rwandan cinema was primarily represented by foreign filmmakers who set up their cameras in this Central African land of a thousand hills to depict the horrific genocide of the Tutsis.

It wasn't until the 2010s that a generation of Rwandan filmmakers emerged, eager to tell their own version of history, far removed from the sensationalism surrounding the 1994 massacres. Directors like Kivu Ruhorahoza (Grey Matter), Joël Karekezi (The Mercy of the Jungle, TIFF ’18), Anisia Uzeyman (Neptune Frost, TIFF ’21), and Philbert Aimé Mbabazi Sharangabo (Minimals in a Titanic World), have all been committed to showing another aspect of their homeland their fellow citizens, and the national narrative.

For her first feature film, Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo follows in this tradition. Drawing on the accounts of women she met within the country, Dusabejambo decided to bring the gacaca courts — popular tribunals based in Rwandan traditional practice that were tasked with finding justice and promoting reconciliation after the genocide — to the screen. Is it really possible to forgive when your entire family has been wiped out or your body has been tortured? What about those who must carry the child of their abuser and raise it amid the perpetual shame of the trauma they have suffered?

With an almost entirely female cast (including the impressive Clémentine U. Nyirinkindi and Isabelle Kabano), Dusabejambo’s Caméra d'Or winner doesn't just give a voice to the silent victims. Through a powerful intergenerational narrative, it heals while empowering those born after 1994 to assert themselves.

Content advisory: themes of violence, themes of sexual violence, bullying, mature themes
ben-imana.teaser: In this powerful, feminist debut feature, which won the Caméra d’Or at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo brilliantly explores the issue of forgiveness in the wake of the Tutsi genocide in Rwanda.

congo-boy.title: Congo Boy
congo-boy.synopsis:
The second feature from Rafiki Fariala (Nous, étudiants!) draws upon the director’s own experience as a displaced Congolese finding purpose in art. Featuring a rousing performance from newcomer Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset, Congo Boy is about forging a path for yourself while never forgetting where you came from.

Robert (Fiomona Dembeasset) is still a teenager, but he’s always hustling. Civil war forced his family to flee the Democratic Republic of Congo and try to make a new life in the Central African Republic, leaving Robert to look after his four siblings while going to high school and doing whatever work he can to make ends meet to pay for food and an exam to go to medical school, following in his father’s footsteps.

As a way of finding inner peace, Robert writes poetry and seeks opportunities to perform as a rapper in the city’s small but vibrant clubs. Robert is advised by those around him to keep his heritage hidden, but for Robert, owning his roots might be the key to artistic self-actualization.

Congo Boy balances its story of youthful ambition with a bold sense of place and circumstance. We get a feel for what it’s like for Robert to placate a guard, hitch a ride, or traverse a checkpoint. Adrien Lallau’s handheld camera generates an immediacy, while César Simonot’s editing establishes the film’s singular rhythms in tandem with Robert’s rapping, which is where this inspiring film reveals its colossal heart.
congo-boy.teaser: Drawing upon director Rafiki Fariala’s own experience as a displaced Congolese finding purpose in art, this rousing character study follows a young man trying to care for his family while forging his own path as a rapper in Bangui.

eklipse.title: Eklipse
eklipse.synopsis:
Summer, 1999. The millennium is looming and “Blue (Da Ba Dee)” by the Eurodance group Eiffel 65 is topping the charts across Austria where, surrounded by pastoral beauty, two 12-year-old boys are learning about dairy farming. Between daydreaming and rabble-rousing, Tomy (Moritz Hohlrieder) and Chris (Finley Brown) are receiving lessons from Tomy’s uncle Georg (Hannes Perkmann) about how to build a dam and treat udder infections. Meanwhile, Tomy’s mother is hiding a dark secret from her son regarding the reason his father is in hospital. But gossip is hard to contain in isolated places and, when Chris is informed about Tomy’s father’s illness by a milk-truck driver, he quickly withdraws, leaving Tomy to uncover the truth about his uneasy world.

Eklipse is the feature-length debut of Manuel Wetscher, who penned the script alongside Bernhard Jarosch, and whose work as a filmmaker and photographer has explored universal themes rooted in biography and identity. While cinematographer Simone Hart’s keen lens perfectly captures what lies beyond the bucolic landscape, Wetscher and editor Anna Kirst seamlessly incorporate personal VHS footage to blend reality with fiction.

Wetscher’s marriage of poetic realism with the harsh realities of misinformation, ignorance, and bigotry is flanked by a sylvan original score by Johannes Winkler and Marco Schröder. While the highly anticipated 1999 solar eclipse comes and goes, everything that was shrouded in darkness suddenly comes to light, though the exposure may not be enough to overshadow the past and truly enlighten.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
eklipse.teaser: As the highly anticipated 1999 solar eclipse comes and goes, everything that was shrouded in darkness suddenly comes to light in Eklipse, the feature-length debut of Austrian writer-director Manuel Wetscher, whose penchant for poetic realism brings emotional turbulence to a bucolic setting.

elephants-in-the-fog.title: Elephants in the Fog
elephants-in-the-fog.synopsis:
In a Nepalese village surrounded by lush forests and wild elephants, Pirati (Puspa Thing Lama) is the matriarch of a Kinnar community — a guru-led society populated by third-gender individuals with their own rites and rituals. New members, or daughters, are initiated into their chosen families through a ceremony in which they take a vow of chastity and a commitment of care to each other. These rules, along with her obligations as a mother, complicate things for Pirati, who has fallen in love with a local man (Aashant Sharma) and wishes to run away to Delhi.

Newcomer Aliz Ghimire is memorable as Pirati’s daughter Apsara, an exuberant young woman with a penchant for blonde wigs and partying. When she disappears into the thick of the woods as an act of rebellion, Aspara’s absence is felt by all, which especially sends a surge of protective instinct into Pirati. With tension between tradition and modernity, the film offers kaleidoscopic possibilities of what femininity can look like, and the different constellations of family that can be arranged.

Anchored by sensitive performances from non-actors and exquisitely rendered images of the verdant setting, this fierce but tender debut feature by director-writer Abinash Bikram Shah promises a stirring emotional journey. In the characters’ pursuit of safety and liberation, Elephants in the Fog asks what we owe to our kin, and what it takes to flourish as our fullest, most authentic selves.
elephants-in-the-fog.teaser: A village matriarch (Puspa Thing Lama) must choose between her heart’s desires and her duty to her community when a young woman disappears into the forest in this delicate, riveting thriller.

evil-genius.title: Evil Genius
evil-genius.synopsis:
Chilling, fascinating, and darkly hilarious, Courteney Cox’s second feature as director boldly dramatizes the bizarre web of stories behind the infamous “pizza bomber” incident. Featuring lived-in lead performances from David Harbour (Stranger Things) and Oscar winner Patricia Arquette (Boyhood), Evil Genius is an astonishing true-crime story brimming with bloodshed, betrayals, and a hopeless case of amour fou.

Erie, Pennsylvania, 2003. From a phone booth outside a waffle joint, Bill Rothstein (Harbour) calls the police to report the corpse of a murdered man stashed in a freezer in the garage of Bill’s former paramour, Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong (Arquette). But who is this murdered man? And exactly how did his body wind up in that freezer?

To answer these questions — and raise many more — we backtrack several months to the day Marjorie threatened the entire staff of her local bank, which led Marjorie to plan a murder, which led Marjorie and Bill to devise a bank heist that would involve several of the duo’s seediest, drug-addled associates, require a pizza delivery man to pretend to be a bomb-carrying hostage — and prompt even more murders.

Reminiscent of the Coen Brothers at their most cunningly funny, Evil Genius thrives on a strong sense of place and a killer cast of demented conspirators embodied by Michael Chernus, Garret Dillahunt, Danielle Macdonald, and Thomas Michael Allen. For all the stranger-than-fiction, psychopathic twists, the story’s greatest mystery might be the invincible affection of the wildly disturbed kind-of couple at the peak of this pyramid of ruin.
evil-genius.teaser: Featuring David Harbour (Stranger Things) and Oscar winner Patricia Arquette (Boyhood), Courteney Cox’s second feature as director boldly dramatizes the chilling, darkly hilarious web of stories behind 2003’s infamous “pizza bomber” incident.

four-seasons-in-java.title: Four Seasons in Java
four-seasons-in-java.synopsis:
TIFF is a long-time fan of Kamila Andini, ever since we fell in love with The Seen and Unseen (2018) and the TIFF Platform Award winner Yuni (2021). Her latest feature is the most ambitious yet, as she challenges herself to something new to demonstrate her maturing artistic vision. Undoubtedly excelling in what she does best — telling a strong female-centred narrative with breathtaking visuals — Andini blends in the element of fantasy into Four Seasons in Java, charging the film with deep metaphors that speak loudly.

Pertiwi (Putri Marino) returns to her remote hometown after 20 years to rebuild her life. The introduction of electricity seemed hopeful for the village at the time of her departure, but to her surprise, it hasn’t done much for the place. In fact, the village is darker than ever. Her best friend married her ex-boyfriend; her parents are hostile about her return; and a motherly figure she often found comfort in was ousted. The worst of it all is that the men responsible for sending her to prison are now the most powerful. When a deaf-mute girl is found mirroring her past, Pertiwi struggles to stop the cycle of violence and mobilises an army of the broken and marginalised to shine light on the monster that has long been festering.

Using nature and technology as metaphors for truth and power, Four Seasons in Java is a complex look into the realities of the victims of sexual violence. Putri Marino embodies the relentless Pertiwi, a name that translates to Mother Earth in Indonesian.

Content advisory: sexual violence, self-harm, coarse language, drug use, mature themes, strobing effects
four-seasons-in-java.teaser: Kamila Andini, the brilliant mind behind TIFF ’21 Platform Award winner Yuni, returns with another polished and picturesque film with a strong women's narrative, starring Indonesia’s biggest talents Putri Marino, Christine Hakim, and Arya Saloka.

furies.title: Furies
furies.synopsis:
“In 2019, Lebanon’s economy collapsed after rampant political corruption. Overnight, banks stopped giving millions of people access to their own money. No one realized that this crisis would last for years, with ordinary people unable to retrieve their life savings.”

In just a few lines, Rami Kodeih immediately plunges us into the heart of his characters’ dilemma, set three years after those pivotal events.

In a stifling, sticky Beirut, two sisters (Maria Nakouzi and Rym Mroue, demonstrating great chemistry) devise a meticulously planned, yet dangerous, nighttime caper to recover their money and fund a life-saving procedure. Teaming up with two men with shady pasts (Issam Bou Khaled and Hasan Akil), the sisters go all out in a thrilling race against the clock.

In Furies, time is money. So, if the characters are running out of money, they are also running out of time and the fast-paced editing conveys all the tension the characters are experiencing. Beyond the personal stakes for our protagonists, the situations in which they find themselves reveal political issues that are far deeper than they initially appeared to be.

Produced by the Brazilian Rodrigo Teixeira (Call Me By Your Name, TIFF ’17; The Lighthouse, TIFF ’19), drawing on the conventions of heist films, Furies offers the exhilarating pleasure of depicting the strength of ordinary people who decide to take on a corrupt system. That’s why Kodeih’s debut thriller has all the makings of a great movie.
furies.teaser: Set in a bankrupt and sweaty Beirut, Rami Kodeih’s impressive thriller follows two sisters in need of money for an important surgery.

future-tense.title: Future Tense
future-tense.synopsis:
Cape Town, South Africa. In a near future on the brink of climate collapse, Lwando (Lawrence Maleka) and his girlfriend Tara (Kristen Raath) are among the privileged few who win the opportunity to travel back to 1647 and a pre-colonial past to experience nature in its wildest form. Lwando is an underground activist who dreams of changing the course of history. Tara wants to save her relationship with him. Together, the couple must choose whether to risk life as they know it for a potentially better world.

At a time when the climate crisis has become a priority for some and an excuse for others to conquer space, Jenna Cato Bass (TIFF ’19’s Flatland and TIFF ’21’s Good Madam) returns to the Festival with an extremely insightful and inspiring science fiction film. Exploring not only humanity’s ability to shape the future but also its potential to destroy itself, the South African director invites us on a thrilling journey through time, enhanced by masterful cinematography (Jared Lawson-Paisley) and editing (Jacques de Villiers).

Both the past and the future are filled with threats, visible and invisible. It takes courage to face them — particularly as a mixed-race couple in South Africa’s violent and complex past. By pitting the intricacies of a romantic relationship against the imperatives of environmental activism, Bass simultaneously explores current events and universal human truths.
future-tense.teaser: With Future Tense, Jenna Cato Bass deals with climate change, human guilt, and South Africa’s identity in this bold time-lapse story based in the near future.

girl-group.title: Girl Group
girl-group.synopsis:
Rebel Wilson takes the lead — writing, directing, and starring — in this story of Tassie Young, a pop singer who leaves her hit band to attempt a solo career, until some ill-advised choices tank her ambitions. After a DUI, she finds herself paying for the consequences of her actions. Booked to do community service, she’s assigned to be the mentor for a handful of young girls who aspire to be in the spotlight themselves.

At first, there’s apprehension from all sides as the group struggles to find their voices and to establish a connection with their reluctant mentor. But as Tassie lets her guard down and gets to know each girl's story, the group starts to gel and even the jaded pop-star burnout begins to see new glimmers of light in her life. Tassie just might be the mentor she never had. Wilson assembles a hilarious cast of comedians and entertainers including Jennifer Coolidge, Randall Park, Nicole Scherzinger, Judi Love, and Sally Hawkins. True to the genre, the energized girl group is full of fresh faces, talent, and personality. With a fantastic soundtrack that includes classic earworms and original songs, this is at once an ode to some of our favourite pop acts and vibrant proof that the hits just keep on coming.

Content advisory: self-harm, sexual content, crude content, bullying, coarse language
girl-group.teaser: Rebel Wilson writes, directs, and stars in this story of a pop star who, following a downward spiral, finds a new sense of purpose by assembling a bunch of young up-and-comers to form a group of their own.

god-bless-you-mr-kopu.title: God Bless You, Mr Kopu
god-bless-you-mr-kopu.synopsis:
"Unhappy? Need a change?" It's a question, a sales pitch, and perhaps a warning. When charismatic American salesman Marco (Simon Rex, Red Rocket) arrives in New Zealand touting a revolutionary new cleaning product, he's looking for ambitious recruits to build an army of door-to-door salespeople. Struggling to make ends meet, Mafu Kopu (TIFF 2021 Rising Star Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi, Predator: Badlands) sees an offer too good to refuse. Drawn in by Marco's effortless charm and uncanny powers of persuasion, he quickly becomes his star protégé. As the money starts to roll in, Mafu feels a growing distance from his Tongan family, his community, and the cultural values that have long defined him.

Written and directed by Alex Liu, God Bless You, Mr Kopu deftly blends sharp social satire with the swagger of late-1970s hustler and action cinema, building from an offbeat character dramedy into a propulsive thriller where loyalties fracture, motives prove more complicated than they first appear, and every decision carries consequences. Built around by a magnetic lead performance from Schuster-Koloamatangi and an irresistibly slippery turn from Rex, the film never loses sight of the emotional stakes beneath its escalating momentum.

Finding both humour and heartbreak in the seductive promises of modern capitalism, Liu explores how the pursuit of wealth and status can quietly erode social bonds, belonging, and even our sense of self. God Bless You, Mr Kopu — his confident feature debut — is at once an entertaining dark comedy, an empathetic moral thriller, and a deeply personal exploration of cultural identity that asks what we're willing to sacrifice when opportunity comes knocking.
god-bless-you-mr-kopu.teaser: A charismatic salesman promises wealth, success, and a fresh start — but at what cost? Alex Liu's wildly entertaining debut blends dark comedy, social satire, and a propulsive thriller into a sharp exploration of ambition and identity.

ha-chan-shake-your-booty.title: Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!
ha-chan-shake-your-booty.synopsis:
Featuring a beautifully detailed lead performance from Oscar nominee Rinko Kikuchi (TIFF ’06’s Babel), the latest from director Josef Kubota Wladyka (Catch the Fair One) is at once graceful and quirky, fleet-footed, and profound. Following a Tokyo ballroom dance enthusiast through spells of bliss and sorrow, Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! surely ranks among the most inventive and playful stories of grief on film.

Haru (Kikuchi) always has one foot in fantasy. When she and her husband Luis (Alejandro Edda) take to the dance floor, they ascend high above their fellow hoofers. When Luis is suddenly taken from Haru, her passion for ballroom dancing — her passion for life — is gutted in tandem.

Depression sets in, her dog goes to live with her sister, and she is visited regularly by a colossal crow, an emblem of the man with whom she once shared her life.
