It is only when destiny presents Haru with a new Spanish dance instructor (Alberto Guerra) that a sense of purpose returns in the form of romantic pursuit, fuelled by vibrant new daydreams — including the realm of Dirty Dancing. But can Haru make room in her heart for another poised partner?

Written by Kubota Wladyka and Nicholas Huynh, Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! is a stylized melange of melodrama and fantasia in which the pain of life’s transitions is eased by the spirit of art, imagination and the joy of movement.
ha-chan-shake-your-booty.teaser: Oscar nominee Rinko Kikuchi (TIFF ’06’s Babel) stars in this fantasy-fuelled fable from director Josef Kubota Wladyka (Catch the Fair One), which follows a Tokyo ballroom enthusiast as she dreams and dances her way through spells of bliss and sorrow.

iron-boy.title: Iron Boy
iron-boy.synopsis:
For young Christophe, life on a rural French farm comes with a lot of hard work, not a lot of passion, and precarious health. Dizzy spells sabotage his day-to-day activities. In need of balance, he gets fitted with an iron back brace which helps with his posture but draws derision from outsiders. Coming of age is not an easy road for anyone, let alone someone feeling a literal and figurative weight on his back.

Pushing through that, Christophe discovers new passions including playing the church organ and connecting with those around him. Putting his pain into newfound forms of expression permits Christophe to transcend his limitations.

Former Pixar animator Louis Clichy creates a beautiful and whimsical hand-painted story of a boy — voiced in the film by his own son, Gary Clichy and drawn from the director’s childhood — trying to find his way in a difficult and sometimes unforgiving world.

Winner of the Special Jury Prize at Cannes last spring, Iron Boy tells a unique and beautiful story. For anyone who has felt alone or out of place in their surroundings, Christophe’s tale reminds us that we can all use some form of support, regardless of where it comes from.
iron-boy.teaser: Winner of the Special Jury Prize at Cannes last spring, Pixar animator Louis Clichy’s gorgeous hand-painted animation tells the story of a boy in need of a back brace who seeks the courage to stand alone.

ken-russells-the-devils.title: Ken Russell's The Devils
ken-russells-the-devils.synopsis:
Ken Russell’s 1971 The Devils remains one of cinema’s most transgressive and incendiary provocations, a feverish account of the Loudun possessions witchcraft trial in 17th-century France. Oliver Reed stars as Urbain Grandier, a wildly charismatic libertine priest who defies Cardinal Richelieu’s consolidation of power. Vanessa Redgrave’s Sister Jeanne is a sexually repressed, hunchbacked Abbess obsessed with Grandier with an intensity that ignites accusations of demonic possession among her convent’s nuns. Already a target for reprisals due to his political resistance, Grandier’s promiscuity eventually lands him on the wrong side of a powerful family.

Adapting from Aldous Huxley’s The Devils of Loudun, Russell vividly stages the mass hysteria, torture, and exorcism as history, horror, and political allegory. As Russell’s most political film, it condemns the collusion of church and state for the purposes of wielding unchecked and self-serving powers. Influential artist Derek Jarman contributed a stark, white production design which sharply contrasts with the baroque excesses and saturated colours of the film now rendered more vibrant in this 4K restoration.

Ken Russell's The Devils was infamously rated X, banned, censored, recut in many territories for decades, and is still controversial for its depictions of religious hysteria — which includes several writhing nuns defiling a crucifix — and its body horror. This director’s cut restores Russell’s original intent. Alternately hailed as a masterpiece and derided as pornography, its anti-authoritarian outrage and critique of institutional hypocrisy feel more urgent than ever.

Assembled from the original camera negative, this new 4K restoration presents Ken Russell’s definitive vision of The Devils by referencing the edit he privately constructed in 2004. The film’s sound has been remastered from original English Composite 35mm Mag Film, transferred at 96kHz, plus other original film elements in selected spots as needed. The Picture and Sound restoration was performed by Warner Bros. Post Production Creative Services, Water Tower Color, and Warner Bros. Sound.

Content advisory: crude content, sexual content, coarse language, violence, mature themes

kissed.title: Kissed
kissed.synopsis:
Initially a controversial outlier, Lynne Stopkewich’s singular debut Kissed (TIFF ’96) is a subversive, tender drama about sexual awakening that shares the same ethereal atmosphere as erotic Canadian classics David Cronenberg’s Crash (1996) and Atom Egoyan’s Exotica (1994).

In a breakout role that won her a Genie Award, Molly Parker plays Sandra, a young woman who becomes enraptured by the sensory experience of death. As a child, Sandra performs rituals in the woods, giving dead animals a sacred burial and examining their lifeless bodies with a trace-like focus. This lifelong fascination leads Sandra to study as an embalmer at a mortuary school, where her feelings about death develop into necrophilia. She describes the act as “crossing over,” straddling the realm between the living and the dead as she reaches a newfound sexual satisfaction with the cadavers. A fellow student, Matt (Peter Outerbridge), becomes obsessed with Sandra and her sexual preferences, projecting his own selfish desires onto her while desperately attempting to seduce her so he too can be treated like one of her deceased lovers.

On its original VHS release trailer, Lynne Stopkewich’s film is described as being at the “bizarre intersection of desire, sex, and death.” While the subject matter appears taboo at first blush, Kissed subverts expectations, shaping Sandra's sexuality through her struggles with intimacy. She longs for a kind of safety and satisfaction that no living person can give her. Sandra yearns to lose herself completely without the fear of being hurt. The film strikes a profound balance between reality and fantasy with Sandra fumbling towards ecstasy, as the Sarah McLachlan song featured in the film suggests.

TIFF is honoured to bring Kissed back to the Festival in a new 4K restoration from Canadian International Pictures 30 years after its World Premiere.

Kissed was restored in 4K by Canadian International Pictures from the original 16mm A/B camera negatives and master mix magnetic soundtrack.
kissed.teaser:
World Premiere of 4K restoration!

Initially a controversial outlier, Lynne Stopkewich’s singular debut Kissed (TIFF ’96) is a subversive, tender drama about sexual awakening that shares the same ethereal atmosphere as erotic Canadian classics David Cronenberg’s Crash (1996) and Atom Egoyan’s Exotica (1994).

lautre.title: L'AUTRE
lautre.synopsis:
Anyone who has spent too long in a hospital bed will connect with the experience of the increasingly agitated protagonist in Alexandre Franchi’s third feature, a darkly comedic thriller about a mind and body in peril.

An actor most recently seen by Festival audiences in Monia Chokri’s The Nature of Love (TIFF ’23), Pierre-Yves Cardinal stars as Stan, an ad man and aspiring fantasy author who’s recovering in a hospital in Quebec from a surgery to remove a cancerous section of bone in his leg. Addled by pain medication and largely immobilized due to his struggle to adapt to his metal knee prosthesis, Stan spends his waking hours weathering the many intrusive visits from doctors, nurses, and concerned loved ones like his girlfriend Bénédicte (Karine Gonthier-Hyndman, Falcon Lake, TIFF ’22) and her sardonic sister Fleur (Nahéma Ricci, Antigone, TIFF ’19).

This patient’s grasp on reality is already shaky when he gets an unwelcome roommate: Darius (Bilel Chegrani, La Gravité, TIFF ’22), a young man in a coma following a shooting. As tensions between the two build, Stan is drawn into an increasingly volatile situation where danger may be closer than he realizes.

Inspired in large part by his own experience with cancer, Franchi has crafted a film experience that’s uniquely visceral, sometimes harrowing, and continually surprising. And while much of the action is confined to Stan’s hospital room, the film maintains the same bristling energy and inventive flair that distinguished The Wild Hunt, which won the director the award for Best Canadian First Feature at TIFF in 2009.
lautre.teaser: Wild delusions and genuine dangers threaten a patient recovering from cancer surgery in this visceral and darkly comedic thriller by Quebec’s Alexandre Franchi.

la-gradiva.title: La Gradiva
la-gradiva.synopsis:
This intimate coming-of-age film follows a group of French high school seniors on a trip to Pompeii, transporting viewers into an arena of eternal ruin and decay to watch them transition into an uncertain future. The messy, hormonally-charged teenagers explore desires and fears, ambitions and hesitations, romantic entanglements and rivalries — big feelings all rendered with weight and poetry in the skillful hands of director Marine Atlan.

As their journey progresses, the dynamics of the ensemble shift, with pressure building between the students as they spend time in close proximity and confront the hidden economic realities that structure their social lives. Characters are bathed in southern Italy’s hazy sunlight as they navigate interpersonal tensions and hold political arguments about class, balancing visual poetry with an intellectual rigour that acknowledges the rich inner lives of teenagers. The film takes its title from Gradiva by Wilhelm Jensen, a novel that became the basis for a Freud essay on psychoanalysis in 1907 and continues to inspire works on fantasy and the unconscious today.

A sensitivity arises from the natural performances and a documentary-like approach to shooting, balancing perspectives between individuals and the group with ease. Known for her work as a cinematographer in Thunder (TIFF ’22) and Jessica Forever (TIFF ’18), Atlan marks her feature debut with a potent story that captures the fleeting nature of adolescence and summer with sensuality and vitality.
la-gradiva.teaser: A pack of rowdy French teenagers embark on a school field trip to Pompeii, where desire, passion, angst, and class tensions in the present unfold against the ruins of the ancient past.

light-pillar.title: Light Pillar
light-pillar.synopsis:
In the seemingly endless winter of a future that feels both distant and near, a near-bankrupt Chinese film studio lies wrapped in a white, snowy grip — a ghostly vestige of the decline of traditional cinema as a form of entertainment. Once a bustling production facility, the compound — featuring replicas of the world’s most famous monuments, from the Forbidden City to the Great Sphinx — now stands eerily empty, suspended between memory and abandonment.

Lao Zha (Da Peng), a lonely caretaker and one of the studio’s last remaining employees, tends to the decrepit facility alongside his only companions: a cat “actor,” who seems to have wandered in from a Miyazaki reverie, and a solitary little robot vacuum, gliding through the empty studio like a relic of domestic automation.

When the studio owner, unable to pay Lao Zha’s salary, gives him a virtual-reality headset instead, the weary worker retreats into a seductive digital world, where ordinary pleasures glow with revelation and romance takes the form of a beautiful player who draws him into the dream of interstellar travel.

Xu Zao’s remarkable debut feature is a melancholic, visually audacious meditation on alienation, technology, and the future of cinema. Collapsing the boundaries between animation and live action, reality and illusion, Light Pillar turns the familiar logic of cinematic escape inside out: Lao Zha’s “real” world is rendered in delicate hand-drawn animation, while the virtual realm appears in live action, more vivid and apparently more tangible than life itself. The result is formally daring and emotionally precise. A quietly immersive, visually subversive experience.
light-pillar.teaser: A lonely caretaker, a dying film studio, and a seductive virtual world collide in Xu Zao’s formally daring animated debut feature: a melancholic, visionary parable about cinema, technology, alienation, and the fragile promise of renewal.

long-long-night.title: Long Long Night
long-long-night.synopsis:
This deeply moving debut from Kyu Bock Youm is a radiant animation chronicling the peripatetic lives of a rhino and a penguin. Together, this unlikely duo encounter adventure, tragedy, and wonder as they traverse a vast, ever-changing wilderness brimming with natural beauty and human-generated danger.

Raised by elephants for reasons never revealed, Norden is a soulful, peace-loving creature — and, as he will eventually learn, he is the last white boulder rhino on Earth. When he comes of age, he leaves the elephant orphanage of his childhood and wanders the world at will, running with zebras through swaying grass and beholding the infinite evening stars.

One day, Norden finds others that resemble him. He falls in love and fathers a child, but his familial idyll is short-lived. Soon he’s trying to escape from a zoo, and later finds himself escorting a penguin with an abandoned egg to some mythical place called “the ocean.” Stalked by jackals and desperately trying to avoid human poachers, these lovable pals forge an alliance that can weather any misadventure.

Every detail in Long Long Night is vividly, livingly rendered, from the wrinkles in Norden’s leathery flesh to luminous fireflies and leaping frogs, each accentuating a world full of awe-inspiring colour and fascinating strangeness. Alternating between mirth and profound loss, Norden’s long journey is above all distinguished by his open heart and enduring capacity for friendship.
long-long-night.teaser: This deeply moving debut from Kyu Bock Youm is a radiantly detailed animation chronicling the peripatetic lives of a rhino and a penguin as they traverse a vast, ever-changing wilderness brimming with natural beauty and human-generated danger.

love-is-the-monster.title: Love is the monster
love-is-the-monster.synopsis:
Eerily reminiscent of our dark contemporary times, this bold tropical dystopian story features Silver Bear winner Paulina García (Gloria, TIFF ’13) as a grandmother who’s aware that she may not live much longer and trying to spend as much time as possible with her beloved six-year-old granddaughter. A series of unexpected events, however, leads her daughter to cut off all contact. After painstakingly earning back her trust, tragedy strikes again: while under the grandmother's care, the child is kidnapped for ransom, throwing everyone into a spiral of desperation.

Marking a striking departure from the warm and gentle humour of his previous Festival selections, All About the Feathers (TIFF ’13) and Helmet Heads (TIFF ’18), director Neto Villalobos Brenes creates a tense, deeply unsettling vision of a society fractured by fear and inequality, an atemporal world of have and have-nots where nannies are armed to the teeth to protect the children of the wealthy from unspecified threats lurking beyond their walls.

Mixing elements of genre storytelling, the narrative centers Latin America's enormous inequality to foreboding effect, focusing on an older woman who refuses to comply while being part of an unsustainable social order built on fear, privilege, and exclusion. Gradually losing any control of her circumstances while clinging to love to retain some hope, the grandmother enters muddy moral waters to answer the eternal question: how far are you willing to go to protect the ones you love?
love-is-the-monster.teaser: In a chilling dystopian thriller shaped by fear and inequality, Neto Villalobos Brenes follows a grandmother, powerfully portrayed by Paulina García, whose granddaughter's kidnapping forces her into impossible moral choices.

muyi.title: Muyi
muyi.synopsis:
Young teenager Muyi lives in a village on a mountaintop in China reserved exclusively for women. Raised by her grandmother, she’s had to adhere to the strict rules within her community, but has a youthful curiosity for what might exist beyond.

When a group of travelling theatre performers arrive, Muyi becomes entranced with them and the story they perform, The Handsome General. It’s a tale of a mystical warrior whose devastatingly good looks require him to wear a mask to frighten off anyone who should gaze upon him. The performance causes a calamity among the village women, and very quickly certain ancient secrets start to reveal themselves. The world opens up to Muyi in ways she never expected. Her adventure beyond home has her encountering peculiar characters, including a vegetarian tiger and a magical guide.

Filmmaker Julien Chheng, alongside his co-screenwriter Sujuan Xu, has crafted a gorgeous animated film showcasing a young woman coming of age, trying to find her space, and looking for a sense of belonging. As time passes, she finds that writing your own destiny is the most important adventure of all. Muyi is a charming, imaginative, and visually stunning experience, one that tells us that some legends and myths can carry more weight once you start to unravel the entire picture.
muyi.teaser: A teenager undertakes a fantastic journey in order to save her mountaintop village where men are forbidden, in Julien Chheng’s charming and magical animated feature.

onwards-and-sideways.title: Onwards and Sideways
onwards-and-sideways.synopsis:
With heartache, laughter, and hard-won connection, the latest from Oscar-nominated director John Madden (Shakespeare in Love, TIFF ’05’s Proof) stars Oscar nominee Laura Linney (TIFF ’08’s The Savages) and Rhys Ifans (TIFF ’23’s Mother Couch) as strangers whose lives become gradually entwined when both are diagnosed with Parkinson disease at the same clinic, on the same day.

Tony (Ifans) is a schoolteacher. Emma (Linney) is a composer and piano teacher. Both lead busy lives in their charming East Anglia village — and both find their status quo shattered upon learning they have Parkinson disease. They meet, minutes after hearing the news, in the health clinic lounge, and immediately start to compare symptoms and strategies: Emma suffers a tremor — she dubs herself “Emma with the tremma” — while Tony does not. Emma resolves to raise awareness while Tony prefers to keep his condition on the down low, so as not to endanger his employment. But as time passes — those “five good years” their neurologist prognosed — their lives increasingly intersect, most especially at the Parkinson ballet class, where they find community — and each other.

Written by Paul Mayhew-Archer (The Vicar of Dibley), Onwards and Sideways takes a sober look at what it’s like to navigate life with a degenerative disease, yet never loses its sense of wonder — nor its sense of humour. Linney and Ifans embrace their characters’ irreverence and desire to live life fully, while also embodying the formidable physiological challenges that come with Parkinson disease. This is a story about the myriad ways the body can surprise and frustrate. It’s also about the undeniability of love.
onwards-and-sideways.teaser: The latest from Oscar-nominated director John Madden (Shakespeare in Love) stars Oscar nominee Laura Linney (TIFF ’08’s The Savages) and Rhys Ifans (TIFF ’23’s Mother Couch) as strangers whose lives become entwined when both are diagnosed with Parkinson disease.

our-loves.title: Our Loves
our-loves.synopsis:
The latest from veteran writer-director Avi Nesher (TIFF ’16’s Past Life) is a dramatic network narrative about the ways that love intensifies in the face of mayhem. With a cast that features many of Israel's biggest stars, such as Lena Fraifeld (TIFF ’22’s Valeria is Getting Married), Hadas Yaron (TIFF ’14’s Félix & Meira), and Hisham Suleiman (Munich), Our Loves expresses the fortitude of the human spirit.

A religiously observant young woman (Daniel Gimpel) is suddenly rejected by her fiancé in a voice message. A retired policeman (Shalom Michaelshvili) in the throes of a bitter divorce demands that his teenage son testify against his mother. A hard-nosed community relations officer (Magi Azarzar) in a same-sex relationship seeks to keep her sexuality and lover (Yaron) hidden from her aging mother. Sometimes a good lie is better than a bad truth, she explains.

These and other characters are preoccupied with their personal dramas and grievances. But once catastrophe strikes, they merge to become a community struggling for survival, forced to connect and search for a chance at redemption.

With grace and empathy, Nesher pivots between each of Our Loves’ narrative threads, weaving them into a rich tapestry that exposes the roots of trauma and the necessity of hope. Centring the film on the intimate details of ordinary human lives, Our Loves is moving and profound.
our-loves.teaser: The latest from Avi Nesher (TIFF '16's Past Life) is a gracefully woven drama about the ways that love intensifies and second chances are possible in the face of adversity and mayhem.

pretenders.title: Pretenders
pretenders.synopsis:
Tough, stylish, and effortlessly cool, Chrissie Hynde is the real thing. Surveying her five decades of work with the Pretenders, you’d think she came out of the gate a rock star. The truth is more complicated — and more fascinating. Helmed by documentarian Joss Crowley (the Shania Twain biography Not Just a Girl), Pretenders chronicles the emergence, prominence, and evolution of one of music’s most singular icons.

Born into a middle-class postwar family in Akron, Ohio, Hynde was a rebellious youth with a taste for the unconventional. Her love of rock ’n’ roll arrived in tandem with a predilection for drugs and biker gangs, the latter of which would put her in harm’s way and a move to London. There she worked odd jobs, wrote criticism, befriended musicians, and stayed on the cusp of realizing her potential for years before finally assembling the Pretenders’ original lineup. The band found success almost instantly, but it would not be long before tragedy struck, leading Hynde to adapt her approach to life and art.

Aside from the interviews with Hynde that provide the film with its structure — and the stories behind hits like “Brass in Pocket” and “Back on the Chain Gang” — Crowley’s in-depth profile boasts a spectacular collage of archival material, featuring Paul McCartney, Elvis Costello, Viv Albertine, Nick Lowe, and Johnny Marr, plus thrilling performance footage. With her mixture of fearlessness and craftsmanship, attitude and vulnerability, Hynde has redefined rock longevity. Pretenders is a fitting testament to her ongoing legacy.
pretenders.teaser: Tough, stylish, and effortlessly cool, the Pretenders founder Chrissie Hynde is the real thing. Grounded in extensive interviews with Hynde and archival materials, Pretenders chronicles the evolution of one of rock’s most singular icons.

soumsoum-the-night-of-the-stars.title: Soumsoum, The Night of the Stars
soumsoum-the-night-of-the-stars.synopsis:
Twenty years after his masterpiece Dry Season (TIFF ’06), Mahamat-Saleh Haroun has changed course. After men's revenge, set in an urban setting, comes women's wrath, set in a rural setting. By choosing a legendary sandstone massif located in northeastern Chad, the Ennedi plateau, Haroun aims to depict both the loneliness of characters cut off from their communities and the power of human connections that have bridged the past and the present for millennia.

Kellou (Maïmouna Miawama), a young adult living alone with her father (Ériq Ebouaney, Lumumba, TIFF ’00), has haunting visions. She can see the past but also the future — a gift that no one looks upon favorably and that must not be revealed. In her village, Kellou lives, runs, thrives, and above all, loves. But Kellou is mocked as a “girl of blood,” the daughter of a woman who died in childbirth.

Struggling with this ostracism, Kellou meets Aya (Achouackh Abakar Souleymane, Lingui, TIFF ’21 ), a single woman who has been herself rejected by the community that blames her for all its ills. As they grew closer, Aya teaches Kellou how to shape her view of the world.

Taking a realistic approach to the fantasy genre (including a reference to the Nigerian-British author Ben Okri), Haroun drew inspiration from the fortune-tellers of his childhood, as well as from the place the dead held in everyday life. By choosing to shoot his film not far from where the remains of Toumaï, the first hominid, were discovered, Haroun invites us to engage in philosophical reflection on the world of the living and the dead.
soumsoum-the-night-of-the-stars.teaser: Five years after Lingui, the Sacred Bonds, Chadian director Mahamat-Saleh Haroun returns to TIFF with his latest feature, winner of the FIPRESCI Award at the 2026 Berlinale.

the-difficult-bride.title: The Difficult Bride
the-difficult-bride.synopsis:
One of the most arresting voices in contemporary female-centred cinema, Bangladeshi filmmaker Rubaiyat Hossain (TIFF ’19’s Made in Bangladesh) possesses a unique gift for navigating the liminal spaces between the sacred and the sensual, the mythical and the mundane. Her latest examines the pressures applied to brides in a milieu where weddings demand a feminine ideal so rarified as to be asphyxiating.

“Happy?” a bridal consultant asks Zaineen as the pair gaze into a mirror at the bride-to-be’s immaculately made-up face, sculpted hair, and bejeweled body. The answer is complicated. In the weeks leading up to her wedding to the handsome, wealthy, “perfect” Aarman, Zaineen is overwhelmed by anxieties about her weight, her blemishes, and her insomnia.

All perfectly normal feelings, she’s told. But what about the dreams and visions that increasingly haunt her, of catfish, snakes, and bloodied bodies? What about the mysterious scratches she discovers on her belly, or the feeling of something moving under her skin? Zaineen is a modern woman, but it seems like some unseen, perhaps ancient force is trying to send her a message.

The Difficult Bride is awash in striking images — at one point a snail traverses the sole of a red spike heel — but there’s a way in which the film’s true potency lies in the unseen, in its heroine’s indomitable psyche. This is a story about the power of female volition in the face of rigid cultural and familial expectations — and about what happens when that power is suddenly unleashed.
the-difficult-bride.teaser: Following the strange visions afflicting a woman on the cusp of marriage, the latest from Rubaiyat Hossain (TIFF ’19’s Made in Bangladesh) examines the pressures applied to brides in a milieu where weddings demand an asphyxiating feminine ideal.

the-dreamed-adventure.title: The Dreamed Adventure
the-dreamed-adventure.synopsis:
In a mountainous Bulgarian border region, amidst a turf war between gangsters involved in smuggling, we meet Said (Syuleyman Letifov), a man living on the fringes of society, crossing into Turkey with a cargo of diesel. There, he encounters a former colleague, Veska (Yana Radeva), an archaeologist who grew up not far from the dusty site. Veska has a past with both Said and local kingpin, Ilya (Stoicho Kostadinov), whose underground business is facing competition from a newcomer called Raven. After turning down Raven’s offer to help with a lucrative and expanding people-trafficking network, Said (and his car) are nowhere to be found, and Veska, whose past includes associating with uncouth networks, takes it upon herself to sell the contraband materials that Said was bootlegging. At the same time, she intends to confront Ilya, whose illegal dealings threaten to involve a teenage girl working on her site. These plot points, dreamed, or, as real as it gets, are blips in something bigger and more nebulous taking place inside this masterful slow-burn, which unearths the past and along with it, memory, local lore, regional history, as well as unspoken and ever-shifting rules of engagement that a passerby could miss with the blink of an eye.

Garnering the Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival, Valeska Grisebach’s gritty knockout is shot by Bernhard Keller (who previously collaborated with the auteur on Western (TIFF ‘17). In the words of Pedro Calderón de la Barca (circa 1635): What is life? A frenzy. What is life? An illusion, a shadow, a fiction, and the greatest good is small; for all of life is a dream and dreams themselves are but dreams.
the-dreamed-adventure.teaser: Winner of the Jury Prize in the competition section of the Cannes Film Festival, The Dreamed Adventure is German auteur Valeska Grisebach's highly anticipated and exceptional follow up to Western (TIFF ’17).

the-life-and-deaths-of-wilson-shedd.title: The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd
the-life-and-deaths-of-wilson-shedd.synopsis:
Starring Oscar nominee Amanda Seyfried (The Testament of Ann Lee, TIFF ’25) and Scoot McNairy (Nightbitch, TIFF ’24), the latest from Tim Blake Nelson is a psychologically rich prison story about crime, punishment, and love.

Featuring sizzling performances from Oscar nominee Amanda Seyfried (who entranced TIFF ’25 audiences in The Testament of Ann Lee) and Scoot McNairy (TIFF ’24’s Nightbitch), the latest from indie icon Tim Blake Nelson (TIFF ’09’s Leaves of Grass) is a psychologically rich tale exploring themes of crime and punishment, desperation and retribution — and the strange ways lonely hearts sometimes connect.

Karen (Seyfried) is a teacher who finds work at a maximum security prison. It’s there that she encounters Wilson (McNairy), an inmate whose arresting charisma and unexpected tenderness pierce the emotional armour Karen has cultivated over the course of her abusive marriage. The charge between the two is undeniable, leading Karen to risk everything for the possibility of Wilson’s freedom.

Set in Nelson’s home state of Oklahoma, The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd poses tough questions regarding American justice and the moral purpose of incarceration. The film is also the finest example yet of the writer-director-actor’s singular ability to follow troubled characters as they tumble headlong into unfathomable dilemmas. In Seyfried’s brilliant depiction, Karen brims with emotional complexity, while McNairy immerses himself in a demanding role, one that keeps us wondering how much we can ever really surmise about someone else’s inner life — and how we survey the limits of our own humanity.
the-life-and-deaths-of-wilson-shedd.teaser: Starring Oscar nominee Amanda Seyfried (The Testament of Ann Lee, TIFF ’25) and Scoot McNairy (Nightbitch, TIFF ’24), the latest from Tim Blake Nelson is a psychologically rich prison story about crime, punishment, and love.

the-only-living-pickpocket-in-new-york.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
the-only-living-pickpocket-in-new-york.synopsis:
Anchored by John Turturro’s charismatic performance, this low-key crime drama from Noah Segan (Blood Relatives) harkens back to the character-driven films of 1970s New Hollywood.

Anchored by an all-too-rare lead performance from John Turturro, the latest from writer-director Noah Segan (Blood Relatives) combines low-key crime drama with a meditation on changing times. Buoyed by a stellar supporting cast that features Turturro’s fellow independent film legends Steve Buscemi and Giancarlo Esposito — not to mention Canada’s own Tatiana Maslany (TIFF ’18’s Destroyer) — The Only Living Pickpocket in New York harkens back to the character-driven films of 1970s New Hollywood, while showcasing the titular metropolis in all its alluring complexity.

A craftsman pickpocket from the old school, Harry (Turturro) adheres to a routine, operates alone, and doesn’t own a smartphone. He works mainly on public transport, sells his spoils to his pawnbroker pal Ben (Buscemi, also at this year’s Festival in Wild Horse Nine), and goes home to his Bronx apartment every night to look after his ailing spouse. But hubris gets the best of Harry: he winds up stealing from Dylan (Will Price, TIFF ’25’s Eleanor the Great), the insufferable scion of a connected crime family, and must traverse the city in an attempt to crawl out of a potentially deadly bind before the day is through.

Segan adroitly revamps a familiar story with attention to detail, affection for every last character, and a critical view of modern life. At the film’s heart is Turturro, who never shies away from exposing Harry’s questionable ethics, yet cannot help but render him a natural charmer.
the-only-living-pickpocket-in-new-york.teaser: Anchored by John Turturro’s charismatic performance, this low-key crime drama from Noah Segan (Blood Relatives) harkens back to the character-driven films of 1970s New Hollywood.

the-violinist.title: The Violinist
the-violinist.synopsis:
A journalist’s curiosity over the story behind a virtuoso’s violin unearths the melodic tale of Fei and Kai, two children drawn close at the cusp of WWII through music while surviving the turbulent historical changes happening in Singapore.

Fei is a young girl from an affluent family whose deepest concern is her upcoming violin recital. Kai enters her life as the adopted child of Ying Jie, Fei’s family servant. When Kai’s perfect pitch and musical talent are discovered, Fei and Kai develop a strong bond — as musicians, friends, and later, lovers. But the Japanese occupation separates them. The only thing that keeps Fei going is the unfinished sonata Kai promised they would play together upon his return. Torn apart by external circumstances, the violin that first brought them close keeps them bonded over the span of eight decades.

The Violinist is a treat for the ears. Its recurring original theme music stands out even among the great classics, lingering far beyond the credits. It’s no surprise the film was awarded best original soundtrack at the Annecy Animation Film Festival, as well as the Cristal, the highest honour, for best feature film.

Music and film — the ultimate storytelling tools — work in harmony in The Violinist, delivering an emotional ride, traversing loss, remembrance, resilience, and healing. This rare animation from Singapore is also a rare exploration of the nation’s wartime past.
the-violinist.teaser: Winner of this year’s Annecy Cristal award, this intimate animation about two violinists in Singapore circa WWII highlights the healing power of music while pulling heartstrings.

the-bovine-with-the-curved-horns.title: The bovine with the curved horns
the-bovine-with-the-curved-horns.synopsis:
The historic abandonment of entire regions and populations by the Colombian establishment has led to different armed actors taking over the functions of the state and subjugating civilians in rural areas. In the case of the northern areas surrounding the Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta’s vast swamps, far-right, narco-trafficking-associated, and extremely cruel paramilitary groups dominated during the 1990s and to this day. This is the setting for The bovine with the curved horns, but the film is a mix of Caribbean fantasy and magical realism, telling its story through the eyes of a child, and letting imagination take them to a safer place.

It’s been days since Amado’s father went out to the swamp with the other fishermen. At night, the power has been going out, and someone is taking advantage of the darkness to put on a mask made from a bull’s skull to watch over the empty town. Uncertainty grows as rumours of the presence of armed groups are becoming harder to ignore. Amado is sent to find a lantern in one of the further stilt-houses, but first he’ll have to face the titular bovine, a sort of demon that has terrorized the village for generations.

Working with a cast of non-professional actors, director Omar E. Ospina Giraldo weaves oral traditions and a penchant for mixing reality and myth with the cadence of rhythms of daily life, letting the narrative unfold poetically. The cinematography by Rafael Gonzales elevates the whole story with an incredibly nuanced black-and-white treatment that elicits how indelible pain inhabits the same places as unending beauty.
the-bovine-with-the-curved-horns.teaser: Blending Caribbean fantasy, magical realism, and Colombia’s painful history, The bovine with the curved horns follows a boy searching for his missing father through a landscape where myth and violence coexist. A haunting, poetic debut of remarkable beauty and emotional power.

toy-gun-bandit.title: Toy Gun Bandit
toy-gun-bandit.synopsis:
Smooth criminals have always been highly alluring for movie audiences. Yet this wildly energetic and entertaining second feature by Quebec’s Rémi St-Michel proves that a very different and far less suave variety of crook can be equally compelling.

At the centre of Toy Gun Bandit’s escalating mayhem is Félix (Félix Munger), an amiable but impulsive 15-year-old living in the suburbs of Quebec City. Though playing videogames and skateboarding with buddies are the teenager’s highest priorities, Félix’s life takes an unexpected direction after a prank unintentionally turns into a bona fide robbery.

Félix tumbles further into trouble when his exploits attract allies such as Dave (David Beaudoin), an aspiring gangster many years his senior, and Sara (Sara Montpetit), a young drug addict on a similarly worrisome downward trajectory. This motley crew’s considerable success as bank robbers in spite of their ineptitude brings them to the attention of heavier characters in the city’s seamy underbelly, thereby increasing the peril for the film’s hapless young hero.

That Félix remains such an engaging and even sympathetic figure is a testament to the warmth, humour, and authenticity that St-Michel and his cast bring to Toy Gun Bandit. Providing the film with much of its restless, reckless vitality, first-time actor Munger gets terrific support from more seasoned talents like Montpetit, seen here in a much different role than in past successes like Charlotte Le Bon’s Falcon Lake (TIFF ’22) and Ariane Louis-Seize’s Humanist Vampire Seeking Consenting Suicidal Person (TIFF ’23). St-Michel’s unconventional crime comedy feels just as fresh and surprising.
toy-gun-bandit.teaser: A prank gone wrong launches a Quebec teen into a life of crime in Rémi St-Michel’s energetic and unpredictable second feature.

up-against-it.title: Up Against It
up-against-it.synopsis:
Post-marital acrimony and parental devotion make strange bedfellows in Trudie Styler’s wicked comedy, starring Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas (TIFF ’19’s Pain and Glory) and Eva Birthistle (TIFF ’05’s Imagine Me & You) as co-parenting divorcees faced with an indecent proposal.

Post-marital acrimony and parental devotion make strange bedfellows in this wickedly clever comedy from director Trudie Styler (Posso entrare? An ode to Naples). Centred around the perfect pairing of Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas (TIFF ’19’s Pain and Glory) and Eva Birthistle (TIFF ’05’s Imagine Me & You), Up Against It slyly considers whether a long-dormant sexual companionship can be revived for the sake of a child’s well-being.

Álvaro (Banderas) and Saffron (Birthistle) are very divorced. Their marriage was a disaster from which the only good thing to emerge was their beloved daughter Rose (Eden Hamilton). Their mutual abhorrence is such that they can barely endure the minimal communication required to share custody, so they’re thrown for a serious loop when it’s discovered that, not only does Rose have a rare form of leukemia, but that, given the nature of Rose’s genetic disorder, their best bet at keeping the child healthy and alive is to for Álvaro and Saffron to produce a second child who could provide a transfusion. The ex-spouses balk at the idea — and their new partners don’t fancy it either — but they may have no choice but to bury the hatchet (in bed).

Written by Chloe King (B. Monkey) and Camille Griffin (TIFF ‘21’s Silent Night), Up Against It is an inventive spin on the screwball comedy. Co-starring Oscar nominee Richard E. Grant (TIFF ’18’s Can You Ever Forgive Me?) and Oscar winner Forest Whitaker (TIFF ’06’s The Last King of Scotland), the film is also a winsome showcase for Styler’s ferociously talented ensemble.
up-against-it.teaser: Post-marital acrimony and parental devotion make strange bedfellows in Trudie Styler’s wicked comedy, starring Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas (TIFF ’19’s Pain and Glory) and Eva Birthistle (TIFF ’05’s Imagine Me & You) as co-parenting divorcees faced with an indecent proposal.

we-are-all-strangers.title: We Are All Strangers
we-are-all-strangers.synopsis:
From the award-winning filmmaker behind Ilo Ilo (TIFF ’13) and Wet Season (TIFF ’19) comes the last instalment of his Growing Up trilogy. Aligned with its predecessors in its overarching themes, Anthony Chen’s final chapter follows the emotional journey and growing pains of a constructed family as they grapple with class divides in a shifting world.

We Are All Strangers follows the parallel romances of a father and a son. Boon Kiat (Andi Lim), a hardworking cook at a kopitiam (a traditional Southeast Asian coffee shop), is drawn to Bee Hwa (Yeo Yann Yann), a “beer auntie.” Meanwhile, Boon Kiat’s good-for-nothing son, Junyang (Koh Jia Ler), is madly in love with Lydia (Regene Lim), a model student. Although Lydia puts in her best efforts to please her strict mother, she soon delivers the ultimate disappointment: an unplanned pregnancy.

The films in the trilogy are standalone stories never intended as a set, but they connect more deeply than imagined. One obvious link is the two leads, appearing in every instalment, shot over the span of 13 years. Over that time, Chen’s characters and their actors have matured, and so have the settings. From the 1990s backdrop of Ilo Ilo to the 2010s of Wet Season, and 2026 in We Are All Strangers, his work is a chronological record of Singaporean history.

The themes threading the films together recur, but they never bore thanks to Chen’s unique touch in adding timely perspectives. The trilogy has come to a close, but this won’t be the end of Chen’s cinema, which keeps on Growing Up.
we-are-all-strangers.teaser: Anthony Chen, a Festival favourite and the helmer behind Ilo Ilo, reunites with muses Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler in an emotionally charged drama about a constructed family to close his “Growing Up” trilogy.

where-the-river-begins.title: Where the River Begins
where-the-river-begins.synopsis:
Working with an extraordinary cast of non-professional actors, Juan Andrés Arango returns to the Festival with a vividly rendered story of migration, memory, and resilience that may be the Colombian Canadian director’s strongest work to date.

Arango’s third feature stars Girleza Duave Cerezo as Yajaira, a young Indigenous woman living in Bogotá after being displaced from her Emberá village in the Chocó rainforest due to paramilitary violence. By day, she sells handiworks on the street while caring for her daughter María (Ana Michell Nama Dumaza); by night, she dreams of the world she was forced to leave behind. In the wake of another tragedy, Yajaira sets out on an arduous and sometimes dangerous voyage home alongside María and Jhon (Juan David Junca Linares), a teenage gang member with a terrible weight on his conscience.

Arrango earned international renown for La Playa DC (2012) and X500 (TIFF ’16), two other gritty dramas featuring remarkable young casts. While his latest shares those films’ urgency and richly textured naturalism, it also introduces elements that are more poetic and more poignant.

Equally affecting is the way in which Yajaira’s story becomes a means to convey wider hopes of finding ways forward — and homeward — after decades of war and displacement. With its powerful flow of images and emotions, Where The River Begins becomes an uncommonly moving experience in every sense.
where-the-river-begins.teaser: In Juan Andrés Arango’s bracing and poetic third feature, an Emberá woman displaced by violence undertakes a dangerous journey to find a better life for herself and her daughter.

ancestors.title: Ancestors
ancestors.synopsis:
David Turpin’s (writer of The Lodgers, TIFF ’17) debut feature is a mesmerizing journey through a dreamlike 1980s London. Evoking the tactile beauty of old photographs, Turpin — who also wrote the screenplay — conjures a city at a time that forever altered the lives of gay men.

An Irishman abroad at a time when homosexuality was still illegal in his homeland, Beau (Éanna Hardwicke) spends his days working in a neighbourhood café and his nights with his loyal confidante, Shell (Jessica Reynolds). When the enigmatic Tiny (Jack Wolfe) enters Beau’s life, an unlikely bond forms — until Tiny suddenly disappears. Beau embarks on a search that reveals not simply what has been lost, but the unseen threads of love, friendship, and care that bind one generation to the next. Along the way, visions of the enigmatic Gloria (Christina Hendricks) draw him ever deeper into a world where memory and longing become impossible to separate, while the lived experience of the unforgettable Maurice (gay screen icon Rupert Everett, My Policeman, TIFF ’22) embodies the resilience of a generation.

Turpin has crafted a rare film. Heartbreaking without ever surrendering to despair, Ancestors is less a chronicle of the AIDS crisis than a contemplation of the haunting legacy it left behind. He lovingly recreates a distinctly gay world, from late-night cruising to the rituals of chosen family to the playful cadences of Polari (a secret slang used to communicate discreetly). It is a deeply felt tribute from a younger gay generation to those who were there, honouring not only those lost, but those who loved, cared for, and carried each other forward.
ancestors.teaser: A haunting journey set in 1980s London, David Turpin’s mesmerizing debut transforms one young man’s search for a missing friend into an unforgettable story of love, loss, and gay legacy.

magazine.title: Magazine
magazine.synopsis:
Set in the microcosm of New York’s literary scene circa 2011, where everyone is maneuvering to either seize a foothold or maintain one, writer-director Alexandra Pechman’s strikingly confident feature debut chronicles the sentimental education of a young aspiring poet who rapidly becomes tangled in a web of eros, cultural gatekeeping, and office intrigue.

Newly transplanted from Arizona, Nora (Lily McInerny, TIFF ’24’s Bonjour Tristesse) is excited to begin an internship at the tastemaking literary journal, Platen. Her duties include reading slush-pile submissions, making coffee, and tending to the needs of high-profile guests during Platen’s many exclusive fêtes. While snobbery and name-dropping dominate, Nora’s feeling of alienation is tempered by her crush on associate editor Thomas (Joshuah Melnick) who, though only slightly older, seems to know everything about piloting the scene. Nora gradually comes to comprehend the advice of Platen publisher Mickey (Carol’s Jake Lacy): the most important thing for interns to know is when to leave the party.

The film’s 15-year-old time-stamp is pre-#MeToo but far from a mere cautionary tale. Magazine immerses us in the complexity of its milieu’s politics — where outright predation coexists with shades of complicity among the staff — but also the promise of genuinely meaningful friendships between the interns that bloom within this minefield of subterfuge. Ultimately, like all great artists, Nora is able to mine her experiences for lessons in the art of writing, business, and life.
magazine.teaser: Set in New York’s cliquish literary scene, writer-director Alexandra Pechman’s feature debut chronicles the sentimental education of an aspiring poet (Lily McInerny, TIFF ’24’s Bonjour Tristesse) who becomes tangled in a web of eros, cultural gatekeeping, and office intrigue.

masc.title: Masc
masc.synopsis:
We all perform, contorting ourselves to fit into a given moment or situation. For Robin (a raw and unguarded Joshua Griffin), the negotiation between who he is and who he thinks he needs to be never stops, no matter the setting.

In his striking, deeply original debut feature, co-written with Griffin, director Bertil Nilsson draws on his own experiences as a neurodivergent gay man navigating the contradictory demands of masculinity. And he has crafted something genuinely rare: a film built not around crisis or coming out, but around the subtler, ongoing work of simply figuring out how to exist as oneself. In this evocative portrait, people — both queer and straight — will recognize the gap between how we see ourselves, how we imagine others see us, and the elaborate, often unconscious adjustments we make between the two.

Structured in five chapters and shot over a year, Masc tracks Robin’s shifting appearance and environments with real ingenuity, with London’s many facets bringing different versions of Robin to the surface. The title nods to masking, the act of hiding an aspect of ourselves to feel accepted. But the film does the opposite. It gently and fearlessly exposes the parts of Robin that are sometimes uncomfortable, unfinished, or simply never given room to exist. In the end, Nilsson offers an unexpected finale as a way of embracing emotional truths that words alone cannot express.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
masc.teaser: This debut feature from London-based artist Bertil Nilsson is a tender, unflinching portrait of self-performance, identity, and the quiet but persistent work of learning to exist as oneself in an often prescriptive world.

purgatory.title: Purgatory
purgatory.synopsis:
First-time feature director Lindsay Lanzillotta has assembled a stellar cast, including J.K. Simmons (Saturday Night, TIFF ’24), Abby Elliott (The Bear), John Reynolds (Search Party), Jack Innanen (Big Mistakes) and Mary Walsh (This Hour Has 22 Minutes), who expertly navigate the drama and comedy in the 1980s-set Purgatory.

Ruby McGurrin, in her first feature film role, stars as Beatrice, a scrappy 13-year-old who’s left questioning family structures, the Catholic church, and basically everything else, after her mother chooses to take some time away from her family to find herself.

Bea is determined to reunite her parents, Parent Trap-style, while also dealing with bullies, adolescence, and a sanctimonious “good” family at her local congregation. Guided by her closest confidante, her church’s priest (Simmons), she makes bold, and sometimes inadvisable, choices as she navigates this tricky time in a young girl’s life.

The film also gives depth to the characterization of the parents. Elliott, starring as Bea’s mother Marianne, is both charming and melancholy, as she’s torn between her duties to her family and to herself, while Reynolds plays Joe, her husband, who is trying his best to keep up with Marianne and their two daughters. Purgatory is a charming, gentle, and funny film that ably joins the long list of coming-of-age dramas, like Lady Bird and Eighth Grade.
purgatory.teaser: This coming-of-age dramedy, set in the 1980s, follows Beatrice as she tries to reunite her recently separated parents, and stars J.K. Simmons, Abby Elliott, John Reynolds, and Jack Innanen.

salvation.title: Salvation
salvation.synopsis:
Writer-director Tom Nicoll’s assured debut feature understands something many films about youthful masculinity miss: that misplaced ambition is less about arrogance than hunger for purpose. This is what ultimately fuels Danny (Liam Harkins) — an overly confident man in his late twenties — to pursue a career as a life coach, inspired by a Svengali-like figure who promises riches and influence. But the road to wealth proves more treacherous than expected, particularly in Scotland’s post-industrial Inverclyde region. Deeply in debt and increasingly desperate, Danny finds himself enticed into reckless schemes to keep the lights on and the illusion intact.

Into this precarious situation comes Scott (a marvellous Stephen McMillan), Danny’s first client who’s perhaps even more adrift than his coach and struggling beneath an overbearing, unkind father. Nicoll has a sharp eye for the language of male self-improvement culture and online influencers who promise the world but only feed delusion; he never lets the film curdle into caricature at his characters’ expense.

Harkins’ skilfully played Danny invites us to cringe at his grandiosity and self-deception while never losing sight of his sincerity, loneliness, or very real need to matter to someone, including himself. That balance gives Salvation its unnerving depth. Nicoll lays bare the impacts of extended adolescence with clarity rather than condescension, building a vivid world that announces a fresh voice in British cinema.
salvation.teaser: A hunger for purpose and a flair for delusion in a small Scottish town: Tom Nicoll’s debut is a sharp, empathetic portrait of young men adrift.

voices.title: Voices
voices.synopsis:
In an unassuming Detroit motel room a stone’s throw from Motown Records, circa 1967, Jordan (Francis Edemobi), a starry-eyed bellhop with a song in his heart, shoots his shot after overhearing that an up-and-coming musical act is checking in ahead of their local debut. Enthusiastically waiting on them in the hopes that they will throw him a break, he is instead met with condescension and derision. But when an accident cuts the duo's career suddenly short, Jordan devises a brash plan to assume their identity and seize their gig.

Set almost entirely within the claustrophobic confines of a motel suite, director Deantè Gray’s remarkable and resourceful feature debut insightfully reflects the anxieties and frustrations of every artist who has the passion, but lacks the means. Further interrogating the pursuit of fame’s corrupting influence, Sam Buckner III and Charlie T. Savage’s nuanced and noir-ish script is profoundly enlivened by a riveting breakout performance from Edemobi, and supported by the terrific Ezekiel Ajeigbe and Raél Ba who portray reluctant co-conspirators to Jordan’s desperate con. Ajeigebe and Ba especially shine in the film’s infectious musical reveries composed by Buckner with Marcus Shaky and Kev Keys. These numbers endearingly crystalize the character’s emotions as any good musical should, and they are also certifiable bangers that effectively inhabit the soulful sound of the era.

A bonafide marvel of indie ingenuity, Voices was shot on a shoestring, but its ambition meets its grasp more often than most made at its scale. And in Gray, Buckner, Savage and their players, there is an auspicious band of talent to behold.
voices.teaser: A starry-eyed bellhop (Francis Edemobi) enlists his friends to help him exploit an unsavoury opportunity that could secure them fame and fortune in Deantè Gray’s soulful, suspenseful 1960s-set musical chamber thriller.

back-in-black.title: Back in Black
back-in-black.synopsis:
Christopher Walken’s performance as a memorably foul-mouthed mortician is just one reason Back In Black is one of the funniest films you may see this year. The inimitable screen icon stars in director Ron Murphy’s deliciously macabre black comedy as Clyde Mortimer, the patriarch in charge of a funeral home in a sleepy small town whose health-conscious inhabitants just aren’t dying at the rate his business requires.

Weighed down by the sight of Clyde and his beloved wife Autumn (Jane Curtin) having to struggle so much in their golden years, their taciturn granddaughter Sam (Ella Ballentine, Black Conflux, TIFF ‘19) happens upon a potential means of reversing the clan’s decline. Soon enough, people all around town are falling prey to “accidents” that help provide the Mortimer Family Funeral Home with a bounty of new clients.

A sabre-toothed satire about the zero-sum thinking and ethical flexibilities that prevail in even the most seemingly idyllic corners of polite society, Back In Black brandishes a loopy and unpredictable sense of humour thanks to the contributions of a terrific cast. Demonstrating the comedy chops he developed as a longtime director of shows such as Trailer Park Boys and Jann, Murphy ensures that his performers’ boldest moments and the wildest turns in the script he co-wrote with Nick Torokvei land with the requisite bravura. Just as delightful are Walken’s streams of invective and expressions of glee as an undertaker who can’t believe his change in luck.
back-in-black.teaser: Christopher Walken leads a terrific cast in director Ron Murphy’s hilarious satire about a failing family funeral home that experiences a reversal of fortune thanks to their town’s suspicious spike in fatality rates.

how-we-stand.title: How We Stand
how-we-stand.synopsis:
Based on writer-director Marie Clements’ (Bones of Crows, TIFF ’22) own play Tombs of the Vanishing Indian, How We Stand is a riveting drama of sisters whose lives are shaped by government policies meant to eradicate Indigenous people.

In 1950s Oklahoma, a single mother (Cara Jade Myers, Killers of the Flower Moon) and her three young daughters take a risk on the Native American Relocation Program, and journey to Los Angeles. But instead of the promised career and stability, they find the opposite. A traumatic event takes place in the Los Angeles’ river’s concrete channel, which then becomes a crucial place for the sisters in its aftermath.

Divided into different foster homes, we meet them again 20 years later, as young women. Jessie (Amber Midthunder, Rez Ball, TIFF ’24) is a doctor, about to start a new job at a clinic alongside her husband, while her sister Miranda (Alyssa Wapanatâhk, Bones of Crows, TIFF ’22) is an activist trying her hand at acting. Lastly, Janey (Isabel DeRoy-Olson, Fancy Dance) is in distress, fresh from a trauma she can’t express. Their paths are very different, but all are tinged by historical injustices.

Inspired by true events, Clements infuses How We Stand with magic realism, a dose of humour — in particular with a send-up of Hollywood westerns —and compelling characters to craft a timely story about forced separation and finding connection.

Content advisory: sexual violence, racist language, coarse language, mature themes, drug use, scenes of surgery, violence, sexual content
how-we-stand.teaser: How We Stand combines magical realism, a story of sisters separated by tragedy, and a cast of rising Indigenous talent. Starring Amber Midthunder, Alyssa Wapanatâhk, Isabel DeRoy-Olson, and Cara Jade Myers.

lemonade.title: Lemonade
lemonade.synopsis:
After years in Ireland’s foster care system, Danny is required by law to leave the home that has been his world. On the day he turns 18, he finds himself alone in a tiny Dublin studio apartment, working an entry-level factory job, and navigating the bewildering freedoms and responsibilities of adulthood. As he struggles to find his footing — and a way back to the younger brother he was forced to leave behind — the reappearance of his former social worker Josh (Barry Keoghan, TIFF ’24’s Bring Them Down and Bird) offers both an unexpected lifeline and a painful reminder that trust, once broken, is never easily rebuilt.

Drawing on a distinguished documentary career, including time spent alongside young people living on society’s margins, writer-director Kim Bartley brings humanity and compassion to her first narrative feature. Yet Lemonade never settles for the conventions of grim social realism.

Instead, Bartley observes Danny tenderly, discovering warmth, humour, romance, and gentle beauty in everyday moments while refusing to define him by the circumstances that have shaped his life. Lewis Brophy is a revelation as Danny, carrying the film with extraordinary authenticity, honesty, and emotional intelligence as he adroitly traverses the fragile threshold between adolescence and adult life. Co-star and executive producer Keoghan is a grounding force as the social worker who knows all too well the challenges Danny faces.

Lemonade is ultimately less about the failures of a system than the resilience and dignity of a young man determined to build a life on his own terms.
lemonade.teaser: Lewis Brophy delivers a breakout performance in Kim Bartley’s compassionate debut drama about Irish teen, forced to leave foster care on his 18th birthday, who must find his way in a world that suddenly expects him to be a man.

neverman.title: Neverman
neverman.synopsis:
Lucia (Justin Vivian Bond) has spent her life fighting for gay and trans rights, often to the detriment of her own personal relationships. As she gets older, all she wants is to find a facility that can help her with her worsening Alzheimer’s and that shares her fundamental values. But when she enters the nursing home — one that claimed to be trans-friendly — she quickly notices that the treatment she’s receiving, particularly from one very involved nurse, is a far cry from the supportive safety that was promised.

The cold, austere, and threatening institution is a sharp contrast to Lucia’s colourful, gorgeous dresses and the vibrant life that she’s lived — experiences we see in flashback and that she’s increasingly struggling to hold on to. With the help of some newly formed friendships she makes in the home, she must navigate this difficult environment as best she can, even as her memory begins, sadly, to let her down.

This second feature film from award-winning Cuban-Canadian filmmaker Rodrigo Barriuso (A Translator) features strong supporting turns by Eva Everett Irving — who plays the younger Lucia in flashbacks with vivacious energy — as well as Marie-Josée Croze (The Barbarian Invasions, TIFF ’03), Elias Koteas (Crash, TIFF ’94), Jess Salgueiro (TIFF 2018 Rising Star), and Zaiba Baig (Sort Of). But it is Bond’s captivating performance — it’s no wonder that they have long been a muse for Jonathan Anderson, the creative director at Christian Dior — that is the heart of the film and its enduring presence.
neverman.teaser: Broadway and cabaret icon Justin Vivian Bond stars as a transgender gay rights activist with worsening Alzheimer disease suffering from the treatment in her nursing home, in Rodrigo Barriuso’s poignant second feature.

smudge-the-blades.title: Smudge the Blades
smudge-the-blades.synopsis:
A spiritual relative to The Bad News Bears and The Mighty Ducks, Smudge the Blades sets the story this time in Northern Alberta, with the unlikely coach begrudgingly helping a rag-tag Indigenous hockey team.

This second feature film from director, and actor, writer Cody Lightning is grittier and more dramatic than his debut, Hey, Viktor, but with more heart — and a cast from Rez Ball, Reservation Dogs, The Office, and Rutherford Falls.

The Treaty 6 Blades are a struggling U-18 team of teen boys — and one girl, Jaycee Pipestem (Paulina Alexis) — led by their coach (Ed Helms), in their last year of eligibility. When their team is kicked out of the league, the local arena’s Zamboni driver (Lightning) offers to coach. Technically, his intentions aren’t pure, as he has his sights set on wooing hockey mom Chanelle Okimâw (Jana Schmieding), but despite his shortcomings, the underdog team begins to finally come together.

The sports-team movie blueprint covers new territory here. These Indigenous kids have distinct personalities — like the traditional one, who smudges his hockey equipment — and their challenges and triumphs feel unique to reserve life. At the same time, this dramedy has high-energy hockey play — many of the actors are hockey players first — raw storylines, and laughs that should earn it a spot alongside its forebearers.

Content Advisory: racist language, coarse language, mature themes, sexual content, violence
smudge-the-blades.teaser: A fresh take on the underdog sports film, centring on an Indigenous hockey team in Northern Alberta, from actor and director Cody Lightning (Hey, Viktor!, TIFF ’23) and starring Ed Helms, Jana Schmieding, and Paulina Alexis.

sunburn.title: Sunburn
sunburn.synopsis:
A hang-out movie set in St. James Town, a high-rise community in Toronto, Sunburn follows a group of young people trying to stay cool during the summer’s hottest day. The temperature triggers a power outage, which sends them out of their buildings and into the street. On sidewalks, on rooftops, in parks, and beyond, three pairs of kids chat about crushes or play games, each on their own adventure until their paths ultimately intersect. Despite the shadows from the apartment buildings, and the pockets of greenery, you can feel the heat radiating from the screen — it’s sweaty, vibrant, and saturated with colour.

Sunburn is a loose, funny, coming-of-age film that shares the same spirit of Dazed and Confused, if it were set in present-day downtown Toronto, with a cast made up of Filipino, Jamaican, Guyanese, and Black actors. Standouts are Joshua Obra and Dashawn Blackwood, who play Shay and Vince, respectively, the friends who tease each other ruthlessly, like only real friends can.

Throughout the hazy day, connections are made between the pairs, lessons are passed along on everything from the small things, like whistling, to the big ones, like falling in love. The film is directed and written by Serville Poblete, a local talent to watch, whose In the Morning Sun recently won the SXSW Documentary Short Award.

TIFF Next Wave: Celebrating the highs and lows (and everything in between) of young voices in today’s fast-moving world. This film has been selected for the next generation of film lovers by the TIFF Next Wave Committee.
sunburn.teaser: Over one hot summer day in Toronto, a group of young people try to survive the heatwave and a blackout by making jokes, roaming the city, and forming tangible connections that feel like they can disappear at any moment.

tangles.title: Tangles
tangles.synopsis:
Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir Tangles: A Story about Alzheimer’s, My Mother and Me comes to life in hand-drawn 2D animation, in director Leah Nelson’s deeply moving feature debut.

Set in San Francisco in the ’90s, Tangles follows the story of Sarah, a young woman whose life is just beginning to tip into the stuff her dreams are made of — new opportunities to illustrate, a new romance with a bad-ass motorcycle-riding girlfriend named Donimo — when the pull of responsibility calls for her. Sarah’s lively mother Midge is battling Alzheimer’s disease, and the rest of the family is struggling to come to terms with the diagnosis.

The animation is perfectly paired with an incredible cast. Sarah is voiced by Broad City’s Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus (Enough Said, TIFF ’13) is unforgettable as Midge, Bryan Cranston (The Upside, TIFF ’17) voices Midge’s husband Rob, Beanie Feldstein plays Sarah’s sister Hannah, and Samira Wiley is Donimo.

Levity — the film’s top-notch supporting voice cast also includes comedians Seth Rogen, Bowen Yang, Sarah Silverman, Wanda Sykes, and Pamela Adlon — balances the heavy material, as Sarah tries to make sense of what’s happening with her mom’s failing mental acuity and the sudden, daunting role reversal of caring for a parent.

Tangles deals with memories, family, and, most importantly, love, rendered in black and white animation, with bursts of colour. A film about memories, this one will stay with you.
tangles.teaser: A young woman deals with her vibrant mother’s Alzheimer diagnosis in this deeply moving animation adapted from a graphic memoir, with a voice cast including Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Seth Rogen, and Bowen Yang.

the-betrayers.title: The Betrayers
the-betrayers.synopsis:
In this gripping and elegant adaptation of his own second novel, Toronto-based filmmaker and writer David Bezmozgis vividly captures a charismatic man whose overlapping personal and professional crises foreshadow the much greater ones soon to engulf the world around him.

Like the director’s 2014 literary prize-winner, The Betrayers is principally set in the sunny streets, beaches, and nightclubs of Yalta, though the events now take place just a few months before Russia’s conflict with Ukraine escalated into the large-scale war that began in February of 2022. A former Soviet dissident who’s now a prominent Israeli politician, Baruch (Michael Aronov) has come to the resort city after making the brash decision to leave his wife and escape political troubles in Jerusalem. Accompanied by Leora (Kaelen Ohm), the younger staffer who’s become his mistress, Baruch adopts a freer kind of life in Yalta, a place of great significance in his childhood but one whose lustre has faded in the years since Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea. These lovers’ idyllic retreat from their obligations and responsibilities proves to be short-lived when they encounter a man from Baruch’s past in the Soviet Union, one whose own decisions had life-changing repercussions.

By perching his characters on this historical precipice, Bezmozgis adds urgency and resonance to a deft exploration of themes of love and loyalty. Together with his exemplary cast — which also includes the great Simon McBurney as Baruch’s former friend — Bezmozgis compels viewers to consider where they may situate themselves within the gulfs that so often open up between high ideals and the compromises that may be necessary for survival.

Content advisory: coarse language, drug use, sexual content (innuendo, language), violence
the-betrayers.teaser: In adapting his own literary prize-winner, Toronto’s David Bezmozgis delivers a deft political thriller about the limits of love and loyalty.

the-surgeon.title: The Surgeon
the-surgeon.synopsis:
As fun as it is thrilling, The Surgeon stars Michelle Yeoh as a gifted doctor who steps down after an accomplished career, only to return to the operating room at gunpoint. In her newfound retirement, she is abducted by a criminal gang (led by Martin Freeman) that forces her to work on a member with a life-threatening medical condition. Thanks to her extensive knowledge of human anatomy and decades of experience with a scalpel, she fights back, equally capable of healing and wounding with her gifts of precision and dexterity. Appearing in two Official Selections at this year’s Festival (the other being Bai Xue’s It’s My Time) after winning the Oscar for Everything Everywhere All at Once, Yeoh proves that she’s here to stay.

After his 2025 romantic comedy A Nice Indian Boy, director Roshan Sethi draws from his unique background as a physician to deliver a pulse-pounding ride that pays homage to genre films, from kidnapping thriller to surgical drama to home invasion. Elevating the action sequences is a killer soundtrack featuring delightful needle drops — including Thin Lizzy, our protagonist’s music of choice in the operating room. With equal attention to constructing breathless fight scenes and fleshing out character histories, this “scalp ‘em up” signals the return of the classic 2000s action blockbuster.

Content advisory: extreme violence, scenes of surgery, accident trauma, coarse language, crude content, mature themes

The screening on September 15 will be the 2026 Sloan Science on Film Showcase Official Selection, featuring a special post-screening Q&A with director Roshan Sethi and a scientific expert.
the-surgeon.teaser: Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh (Everything Everywhere All at Once) is back in action as a kidnapped surgeon forced to perform one last operation in this fun, pulse-pounding thriller.

trash-mountain.title: Trash Mountain
trash-mountain.synopsis:
A dead hoarder’s houseful of holdings yields hope for a young man’s self-reckoning in this funny, wise film from director Kris Rey (It Was Great, But I Was Ready to Come Home). Featuring winsome performances from Caleb Hearon (The Devil Wears Prada 2), Zooey Deschanel (500 Days of Summer), and Oscar nominee Jackie Weaver (TIFF ’12’s Silver Linings Playbook), Trash Mountain is a homecoming story for anyone who dreads coming home.

After fleeing his rural Missouri roots years ago, Gavin (Hearon) found his community in Chicago, where he emcees a drag show. When his sister Abbi (Deschanel) calls to inform him of their reclusive father’s death, Gavin heads back to help sort through the old man’s mountainous personal effects and return to civilization ASAP. But death proves complicated: turns out they can’t process the paperwork without Dad’s social security card, which could be anywhere in his heaps of seemingly random possessions.

Meanwhile, Grandma Helen (Weaver) is loudly performing the grief neither Gavin nor Abbi have the energy for, and the local cutie (Jaboukie Young-White) Gavin hooks up with just won’t stop being cute. The longer Gavin stays in Missouri, the greater the danger that he might make peace with his home, his family, and himself.

Written by Hearon and Ruby Caster (Bleeding Love), Trash Mountain overflows with irreverence and tenderness. Growing up gay in a conservative region, Gavin’s wicked wit has always been his go-to survival technique, but he’s now confronted with a situation in which everyone is disarmingly supportive. This is a moving comedy about the difficulty of offering forgiveness and accepting love.
trash-mountain.teaser: After the death of their hoarder father in rural Missouri, two siblings (Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel) reunite to sort through the baggage — both literal and emotional — in Kris Rey’s poignant and funny exploration of love and grief.

alice.title: Alice
alice.synopsis:
La Belle Époque: a time of prosperity and tantalizing innovation. As Paris flourishes with cultural and scientific advancements, some traditions remain frustratingly unchanged. The expectations placed on women, for example, are maddeningly decorous for Alice (Bérénice Bejo, The Artist, TIFF ’11), who dreams of a life beyond the domestic. When she secures a position working in the office of Léon Gaumont (Thibaut Evrard, TIFF ’17’s Submergence), the aperture of her life widens irrevocably.

Gaumont is a craftsman, tirelessly tinkering with his designs for a camera that can capture moving images. While his mechanical genius ensures the capabilities of his equipment, the question of what to show quickly becomes a point of inspiration for Alice. Her innate understanding of narrative as the driving force behind cinema’s connection to an audience catches Gaumont’s attention, as well as that of rival Charles Pathé (Yannick Choirat, Rust and Bone, TIFF ‘12) and his associate Mitchell (François Arnaud, TIFF ’09’s J'ai tué ma mère). Also intrigued by Alice’s creativity and ambition is Herbert Blaché (Oscar Lesage, The Substance, TIFF ’24), who Alice comes to admire as they share their passion for this exhilarating new art form.

While even the most casual cinephile likely knows the names of Gaumont and Pathé, history has — as it so often does — obscured the essential contributions of a pioneering woman at the centre of an emerging industry. Alice not only brings the triumphs of the titular character to the screen, but this sweeping series captures the thrilling blend of technology and creativity that captivated early audiences of cinema — and continues to do so today.
alice.teaser: Amidst the advent of modern cinema, trailblazing artist Alice Guy becomes the first female film director in this lush historical series starring Academy Award–nominee Bérénice Bejo (The Artist).

blindspot-berlin.title: Blindspot Berlin
blindspot-berlin.synopsis:
Roughly one week before Christmas in 2016, a truck was driven into the popular holiday market at Breitscheidplatz — a major public square, crowded with revellers and holiday shoppers. A dozen people were killed, and many more injured, in what became the deadliest terror attack in Germany in decades. The attacker was a 24-year-old man, not only known to police but who had been under surveillance for nearly 18 months before the attack. In the days and weeks after the tragedy, the shock of the devastation gave way to one major question — how could this have happened?

Based on these real events, Blindspot Berlin imagines the months leading up to the attack. Detective Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, All Quiet on the Western Front, TIFF ’22) has been monitoring worrying activity through his networks of informants and surveillance, assisted by the translation efforts of newly-recruited, Iraqi-born police officer Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla, Elaha). Laudin forms a special unit to investigate further, looking to convince his higher ups the threat is real. He recruits a well-connected informant, Murat Cem (Tamer Tıraşoğlu), who is well connected but inscrutable. When Murat Cem embeds within a particular group of men, his reports become more alarming each day — especially concerning one young man who seems ready to do absolutely anything he’s asked.

A compelling procedural thriller, with the looming spectre of an unfathomable outcome, Blindspot Berlin is unflinching. Concerned with questions of state power, surveillance, radicalization, political accountability, and personal cost, this series asks what it is that we fail to see, and why.
blindspot-berlin.teaser: This gripping thriller depicts the investigation — and its shortfalls — in the months before the December 2016 attack at the Christmas market at Breitscheidplatz, Berlin.

oxygen-masks-will-not-drop-automatically.title: Oxygen Masks Will (Not) Drop Automatically
oxygen-masks-will-not-drop-automatically.synopsis:
Young flight attendant Nando (Johnny Massaro, The Son of a Thousand Men) leads a glamorous, carefree life, revelling both in Brazil’s neon-lit 1980s club scene and a passionate affair with a closeted football star. Everything changes, though, when Nando begins experiencing strange and frightening symptoms, and is diagnosed with HIV.

At first, Nando tries to ignore the looming danger of his disease, which carries great stigma. But when a beloved performer and friend is struck down in her prime, she makes a dying request to her adopted son Raul (Ícaro Silva): tell people what happened to me, and speak its name. Raul and Nando are galvanized. Nando soon realizes that, with the help of his colleague and best friend Lea (Bruna Linzmeyer), he can access AZT — a new, life-saving drug — during his frequent trips to the US, smuggling it back into Brazil where it is hard to access, thus helping the wider community, possibly saving lives.

At a time when joy and dread were intertwined, Oxygen Masks Will (Not) Drop Automatically poignantly surveys a queer cohort forced to save itself. The vibrancy of these characters and those they represent — so very young to be grappling with a devastating epidemic, and unaided by the institutions that should protect them — is a testament to their strength, tenacity, and rapturous determination to live.
oxygen-masks-will-not-drop-automatically.teaser: The first-ever series from renowned Brazilian filmmaker Marcelo Gomes tells the true story of a group of young flight attendants who smuggle treatment drugs from America into the hands of patients with AIDS in 1980s Brazil.

yaga.title: YAGA
yaga.synopsis:
Carson (Clark Backo, The Changeling) is a local detective, at once weary and protective of the small coastal town she serves and its inhabitants.
