After the disappearance of commercial fishery heir and local party boy Henry Park (Hudson Williams, Heated Rivalry), Carson begrudgingly partners up with Rapp (Noah Reid, Cardinals, TIFF ’17), a private investigator hired by the Park family. Rapp arrives on the scene with a bemused swagger and a personal connection to the case that immediately raises Carson’s hackles. When their initial lines of questioning lead them to an enigmatic and seductive university professor (Carrie-Anne Moss, The Matrix franchise), it becomes clear that it’s going to require all hands on deck to uncover the truth hidden underneath these shrouds of secrecy.

Adapted from the hit stage play of the same name by writer and showrunner Kat Sandler, YAGA is infused with a preternatural air: the feeling that no one is giving a straight answer, everyone has something they’d rather keep hidden, and something uncanny and monstrous might just be lurking in the shadows. With a strong ensemble cast of Canadians, and a powerfully subversive story, YAGA blends elements of horror and whodunnit, conjuring an ancient magic to examine our modern myths — why they persist, and who benefits from their continued survival.
yaga.teaser: Starring Canadians Hudson Williams, Noah Reid, and Carrie-Anne Moss, this adaptation of Kat Sandler’s award-winning play unfurls the truth behind a mysterious disappearance in a small coastal town.

american-hostage.title: American Hostage
american-hostage.synopsis:
In Indianapolis in 1977, local radio reporter Fred Heckman (Jon Hamm, Mad Men) enjoys widespread trust from his listening public and respect from his colleagues. He’s even caught the interest of some New York media bigwigs; their job offer is weighing on his mind, spurring him to repeatedly discuss the pros and cons with his wife (Mireille Enos, TIFF ’18’s The Lie). But Heckman’s personal quandaries are suddenly sidelined when the station hears word of a developing story unfolding downtown.

Tony Kiritsis (Giovanni Ribisi, TIFF ’18’s A Million Little Pieces) is a desperate man with a desperate plan: he’s decided that his only available course of action, after being denied an extension on his mortgage payment plan, is to take his broker hostage. Kiritsis begins a stand-off with local police, and one of his earliest demands is a phone call with the most reliable newsman in town: Fred Heckman. The station’s staff and regulators are faced with a series of impossible and novel decisions — can the station ethically air a live interview with a kidnapper? What does the reporter’s duty to the public require him to divulge? Will they be fined into oblivion for airing Kiritsis’ inventive stream of curse words?

Set long before live coverage was available at our fingertips, American Hostage captures the murky boundaries between participant and observer. Adapted from the hit podcast of the same name, and based on real events, this series examines a sensational, national news story that rests on the relationship between a local man and the reporter he trusts to always deliver the truth.
american-hostage.teaser: Jon Hamm stars in this adaptation of the hit podcast, which tells the true story of an Indianapolis radio reporter thrust into a high-stakes situation when a local man takes a bank employee hostage and demands to be interviewed live on air.

below.title: Below
below.synopsis:
In the small coastal village where Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett, Bunraku, TIFF ’10) lives, there’s a long tradition of intimate connection to the sea. Commercial fishery and, more recently, harvesting ice from icebergs that have drifted into the bay, are the backbone of the local economy. It’s a family way of life that Calvin hopes to sustain and pass down to at least one of his children — the wayward Wade (Charlie Heaton, Stranger Things), the adventurous Mary (Ruby Stokes, Where is Anne Frank, TIFF ’21), or the entrepreneurial Jay (Rohan Campbell, The Monkey), home for a visit from his money-making venture in Alberta.

The family reunion happens as the local townspeople are due to vote on a government initiative for relocation, offering cash for resettlement and creating tension between those who see opportunity, and those who can’t imagine leaving their home. But the debate is put on the back burner when strange events start happening near the harbour: harvested ice starts to exude a strange odour, and a couple of tourists seem to have gone missing. As Calvin seeks the help of local marine biologist Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) in trying to understand what’s happening in the waters, his history on the island becomes something he can no longer ignore.

Created by Canadian screenwriter Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy), Below strikes a rich balance between the warmth of a close-knit family, steeped in tradition and the genuine love of a place, with the chilly depths of marine monstrousness. As the times change around them, the locals know one thing always remains true: the sea holds many mysteries, and is very, very deep.
below.teaser: Something monstrous lurks off the coast in this suspenseful, Newfoundland-set limited series, starring Josh Hartnett (Trap) and Mackenzie Davis (Station Eleven).

crystal-lake.title: Crystal Lake
crystal-lake.synopsis:
Camp Crystal Lake: to the uninitiated, the name sounds pastoral, serene, perhaps even a little nostalgic. To those who know the name Jason Voorhees, it’s ground zero for what will become the many horrors of Friday the 13th. The tragic drowning of young Jason (Callum Vinson), and its impact on his loving mother Pamela (Linda Cardellini, Green Book, TIFF ’18; DTF St. Louis), spark a spiral of violence that will come to have a very high body count.

Pam is a devoted single mom: she works hard at her job in the camp’s kitchen, glad to be able to stay close to Jason but wary of the other kids’ cruelties. When negligent counsellors leave the kids unsupervised in the lake, tragedy strikes: Jason disappears in the water, surely having drowned. As time goes by and the town moves on, Pam struggles to cope; she’s encouraged to rejoin the community by one of her few friends, local chief of police Levon Brooks (William Catlett, A Thousand and One). But when shadowy figures from Pam’s past come knocking at her door, her paranoia doesn’t seem so far-fetched. Pushed to the brink of grief, how far will Pam go to protect herself and avenge her son?

Created by Brad Caleb Kane (It: Welcome to Derry) and produced by A24, Crystal Lake takes us back to the beginning. Featuring an electrifying lead performance by Cardellini, the series delivers a moving portrait of a mother consumed with grief, intriguing new details from the Voorhees family’s past, and a bloody good time.
crystal-lake.teaser: Set long before the events of Friday the 13th, Linda Cardellini stars as Pamela Voorhees in this captivating, A24-produced origin series.

slow-horses.title: Slow Horses
slow-horses.synopsis:
Since making its debut in 2022, Slow Horses’ singular take on the spy thriller genre has made it one of television’s most critically acclaimed, widely popular, and utterly captivating series. As a new season begins, River Cartwright (Jack Lowden, Dunkirk, TIFF ’17; Benediction, TIFF ’21) had hoped to escape the purgatory of Slough House, after the glimmering hope of a promotion seemed just in his grasp. But the endless machinations of newly-ascended First Desk Diana Tavener (Kristin Scott Thomas, Darkest Hour, TIFF ’17) land Cartwright back on MI5’s island of misfit toys, under the reluctant governance of Jackson Lamb.

After the chaos of last season’s entanglement with Libyan operatives, accidental assassinations, and Roddy’s (Christopher Chung) love life, the Horses could use a breather. But as River deals with personal matters, spurring the return of ruthless mercenary — and River’s father — Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving, The Royal Hotel, TIFF ’23), another maelstrom of revenge and retaliation for old wounds begins to form.

Characteristically clever, and unsentimental with a clear-eyed affection for the riff raff of espionage and high intrigue, Slow Horses maintains a propulsive energy and dark humour into its sixth season. The robust ensemble cast, featuring Jonathan Pryce, Saskia Reeves, Aimee-Ffion Edwards, Joanna Scanlan, Olivia Cooke (also at this year’s Festival in A Talent for Murder), and Samuel West, render this espionage thriller a quick-witted and always entertaining ride through the less-than-glamorous world of spycraft.
slow-horses.teaser: The sixth season of this smash hit series finds the motley crew of disgraced MI5 agents in Slough House, working under the cantankerous Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman, TIFF ’17’s Darkest Hour), thrown once again into the fray.

the-diary-of-a-chambermaid.title: The Diary of a Chambermaid
the-diary-of-a-chambermaid.synopsis:
Set in present-day Paris, Radu Jude’s The Diary of a Chambermaid is a variation on Octave Mirbeau’s Decadent-era novel. The anarchist writer’s text gained prominence during the infamous Dreyfus affair, a momentous scandal that exposed deeply seeded, systemic prejudices and reshaped European politics. First published in serialized form from 1891 to 1892, the original was reworked before appearing in the Dreyfusard journal La Revue blanche in 1900 and has since been revived in several significant adaptations (including by Jean Renoir and Luis Buñuel). While no foreknowledge of Mirbeau’s turn-of-the–19th century work (or its high-stakes landscape) is required to sink into Jude’s version, the source material provides fascinating historical parallels for this slapstick skewering of modern-day slavery.

In Jude’s version, Gianina (Ana Dumitrașcu, Dracula), a Romanian migrant (whose own life is paralleled with the original novel’s heroine Célestine) is a live-in housekeeper for an upper-class, pseudo-intellectual couple. In the evenings, she prepares for an amateur production of The Diary of a Chambermaid at the behest of her hoity-toity employers. On her own time, she FaceTimes with her crestfallen tween daughter who lives with her grandma while her mother supports the family from abroad. Everything is going according to Gianina’s plan, until one day, it isn’t.

Offering his most provocative work yet, the latest from art-house cinema sweetheart Jude (Do Not Expect Too Much from the End of the World, TIFF ’23) is a surprisingly tender socioeconomic satire in which the protagonist — presenting herself as an apolitical, obedient, and unobtrusive member of the servant class — highlights how the cycle of exploitation remains unbroken over a hundred years later.
the-diary-of-a-chambermaid.teaser: Offering his most provocative work yet, the latest from Romanian provocateur Radu Jude is a surprisingly tender socioeconomic satire.

once-upon-a-time-in-harlem.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
once-upon-a-time-in-harlem.synopsis:
One afternoon in August 1972, at the behest of legendary, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves, a coterie of luminaries from the Harlem Renaissance gathered — with cameras rolling — for an intimate party in Duke Ellington’s townhouse. Fifty years later, completed by Greaves’ son David, Once Upon a Time in Harlem has emerged as a rapturous living archive of one of the most important artistic movements of the 20th century and, posthumously, one of the most important works in the Greaves filmography.

A towering constellation of artists, poets, painters, musicians, scholars, and other notables appear throughout — among them Aaron Douglas, Arna Bontemps, Richard Bruce Nugent, James Van Der Zee, and Countee Cullen’s widow, Ida Mae Cullen. Free from any institutionalized gaze and structure, they congregate around a large punch bowl to drink, reminisce, banter, and passionately debate their legacy. The conversations we’re privy to flow naturally and candidly, marked variously by humour, fervour, reflexive insight, and not a bit of melancholy, as they take stock of their achievements in their older age.

Greaves’ multiple 16mm cameras are at the heart of the action, capturing and partaking in the collegial repartee, while the deft, contemporary editing balances the original ’70s textures with an exhilarating, contemporary immediacy, tracing the urgency of these artists and their ideas from the 1920s through to the 1970s and to our present moment.

Functioning as well as a dynamic inquiry into the ways culture is actively inherited and sustained across disciplines, and creates communities of protest and survival, Once Upon a Time in Harlem is a monumental reclamation of cinematic and cultural memory.
once-upon-a-time-in-harlem.teaser: Conceived in 1972 by legendary filmmaker William Greaves and completed 50 years later by his son David, Once Upon a Time in Harlem is an essential work of living archive, documenting a lively gathering of luminaries from the Harlem Renaissance during a cocktail party at Duke Ellington’s home.

growth-of-the-soil.title: Growth of the Soil
growth-of-the-soil.synopsis:
Now enjoying a wave of international prominence and success thanks to filmmakers such as Joachim Trier and Dag Johan Haugerud, Norwegian cinema continues to go from strength to strength with this remarkable achievement by one of the country’s most venerable talents. A director best known for his collaborations with actor Stellan Skarsgård, Hans Petter Moland demonstrates formidable command of his art with this powerful and richly textured adaptation of Growth of the Soil, the 1917 novel that won its author Knut Hamsun the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Sharing the original’s fervently realistic style and reverence for the natural world, Moland’s latest feature opens as the captivating story of one man’s battle with a dauntingly rugged environment. Herbert Nordrum — familiar to Festival audiences for his role in Trier’s The Worst Person in the World (TIFF 2021) — stars as Isak, a solitary man who stubbornly struggles to start a farm in a remote patch of land in northern Norway in the early 20th century. He finds an ally — and eventually a wife — in Inger (Asta Kamma August, also at the Festival in What Lies Between Us), a woman with her own reasons for being on the edge of their society. They build a life together piece by piece. But the inexorable march of modernity brings changes and challenges of many kinds.

Marshalling a heroic effort of their own, Moland and his superb cast ensure that Hamsun’s story of how this couple’s hard-won home cannot protect them from history’s wider forces — or from more human sorts of frailties and failings — comes to the screen with all the grace and gravity it deserves.
growth-of-the-soil.teaser: Nobel Prize-winner Knut Hamsun’s novel about a farmer’s struggles in early 20th-century Norway gets a powerful and richly textured adaptation by director Hans Petter Moland and his superb cast.

making-waves-with-hudson-williams.title: Making Waves With... Hudson Williams
making-waves-with-hudson-williams.synopsis: As part of TIFF Next Wave, our year-round initiative empowering young people through the art of cinema, join us for an intimate conversation with Hudson Williams, one of the stars of the Festival Primetime series YAGA from Kat Sandler. Born and raised in British Columbia, Williams spent his youth balancing the arts and sports — training in theatre, music, and dance while simultaneously playing competitive basketball and practicing mixed martial arts. After graduating from Vancouver's Langara College Film Arts program in 2020, he continued to dive deep into his craft with professional theatre classes. Williams began navigating the Canadian film and television industry while at the same time being a disruptor by writing, directing, producing, and starring in independent short films with a close-knit circle of creative collaborators. His massive breakthrough came when he was cast as Shane Hollander in Jacob Tierney’s award-winning series Heated Rivalry, adapted from the bestselling novels by Rachel Reid. Since its debut in fall 2025, the series has become a global phenomenon, catapulting Williams to international stardom. Williams joins us to discuss his roles in the Crave Original series YAGA and Heated Rivalry, as well as the upcoming independent feature Apparatus. The conversation will explore his cinematic and cultural inspirations and reflect on the early short films, community, and collaborations that helped shape his unique artistic voice.
making-waves-with-hudson-williams.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

pelechian-project.title: Pelechian Project
pelechian-project.synopsis:
One of the year’s greatest cinematic gifts, this programme brings together five newly restored films by the pioneering Armenian filmmaker Artavazd Pelechian, each a harrowing ode to humanity, and its natural cycles of existence.

The new restorations of Artavazd Pelechian’s films are unquestionably among the year’s greatest cinematic gifts. Born in Soviet Armenia in 1938, the reclusive, trailblazing filmmaker and theorist has created some of the most indelible images of all time, teeming with startling vibrancy and passages of pure exhilaration and pathos. His visionary practice employs his signature concept of distance montage to create rhythmic echoes between images, extending thematic motifs like electrified brackets.

Mixing archival images with documentary footage, Pelechian’s films are wordless, though visually and musically maximalist. This programme comprises five of his major works, each a harrowing ode to humanity, and its natural cycles of existence. They include the city symphony Land of the People (1966); The Beginning (1967), which employs a novel staccato effect to conjure the rush of the October Revolution; We (1969), a masterpiece portrait of Armenian resistance that transforms “we” from the localized to the universal; and his best-known work, The Seasons (1975), which includes the oft-referenced scenes of Armenian shepherds embracing their herds as they sluice down snowy hills. We conclude with The End (1992), a gentle hymn to travel and faces filmed during a train ride from Moscow to Yerevan.

Greatly admired by the likes of Sergei Parajanov and Jean-Luc Godard — and a major influence on contemporary filmmakers Pietro Marcello and Oliver Laxe, among others — Pelechian remains one of today’s towering cinematic figures, and yet still deserving of wider recognition.

The restoration of Artavazd Pelechian’s films was launched by Coproduction Office in partnership with Cineteca di Bologna under the director’s supervision. The best available elements were selected by the director and scanned in 4K at the Public Television Company of Armenia. Restoration and color grading were carried out by L’Immagine Ritrovata laboratory.
pelechian-project.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

in-conversation-with-lee-min-ho.title: In Conversation With... Lee Min-ho
in-conversation-with-lee-min-ho.synopsis: Paging all devoted Minoz (미노즈): Join us at TIFF ’26 for an exclusive event celebrating the extraordinary career of global Hallyu icon Lee Min-ho. Here in Toronto for the World Premiere of his new film, The Assassin(s), co-starring Yoo Hai-jin (Exhuma) and Park Hae-il (Decision to Leave, TIFF ’22), and directed by Hur Jin-ho (A Normal Family, TIFF ’23). For nearly two decades, Lee Min-ho has been one of the defining figures of Korean popular culture, introducing generations of global audiences to the world of K-content. His iconic portrayals of Gu Jun-pyo in Boys Over Flowers (2009) and Kim Tan in The Heirs (2013) helped shape the global K-drama phenomenon, while City Hunter (2011) and the historical fantasy Faith (2012) showcased his remarkable versatility, moving effortlessly between stylish action and period drama. He made a successful transition to the big screen with his first leading film role in Gangnam Blues (2015), before further cementing his global popularity as “the king of fantasy romance” through The Legend of the Blue Sea (2016) and The King: Eternal Monarch (2020), captivating audiences worldwide. Pushing the boundaries of his craft, Lee joined the acclaimed Apple TV+ series Pachinko (2022–present), earning an Independent Spirit Award alongside the ensemble cast and widespread critical recognition. Named the most popular Korean actor in the Overseas Hallyu Survey for 13 consecutive years and recipient of 13 SBS Drama Awards, the undisputed “Hallyu King” regularly sells out arenas across Asia. Now, Lee joins us to discuss his defining career journey and his highly anticipated new film, The Assassin(s).
in-conversation-with-lee-min-ho.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

in-conversation-with-rachel-morrison.title: In Conversation With... Rachel Morrison
in-conversation-with-rachel-morrison.synopsis: Following the acclaimed premiere of her feature directorial debut, The Fire Inside, at TIFF ’24, Academy Award–nominated cinematographer and filmmaker Rachel Morrison returns to the Festival for the World Premiere of her highly anticipated sophomore feature, Love of Your Life — a romantic drama from Amazon MGM Studios starring Margaret Qualley, Aaron Pierre, Patrick Schwarzenegger, Gabriel Basso, and Catherine Keener, and produced by Ryan Gosling and Jessie Henderson. Grounded in photography and backed by formidable technical craft, Morrison has spent two decades moving seamlessly across film, television, fiction, and documentary, establishing herself as a premier visual storyteller. After gaining recognition for her haunting, arresting cinematography on indie highlights like Ryan Coogler’s Fruitvale Station and Dee Rees’ Mudbound (TIFF ’17) — where she made history as the first woman nominated for an Oscar in cinematography — she re-teamed with Coogler to shape the visual identity of Black Panther. Morrison further honed her directorial voice on hit series like The Morning Show and The Mandalorian before bringing the story of boxing legend Claressa Shields to the screen in The Fire Inside, a film celebrated for transcending sports tropes by foregrounding the human weight of victory. Morrison joins us to discuss her remarkable journey from NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts to shooting and directing award-winning indies and major studio blockbusters.
in-conversation-with-rachel-morrison.teaser: TIFF is a charitable cultural organization with a mission to transform the way people see the world, through film.

at-night.title: At Night
at-night.synopsis:
After nearly two decades of exceptional shorts, including I Hope I’m Loud When I’m Dead (TIFF ’18) and Someplace in Your Mouth (TIFF ’24), British filmmaker and artist Beatrice Gibson arrives with her much-anticipated and deeply affecting debut feature, At Night.

Shot in Paris with the city’s gleaming streets, metro lines, neighbourhood bars, and shuttering corner shops creating a richly textured setting, Gibson weaves an intersecting portrait of six women from varying backgrounds and professions seeking connection over the course of an ambulatory, neon-lit night.

Central to the configuration is B (director Gibson, performing with brave vulnerability), a filmmaker in the midst of losing her grasp on her current project, and wanting to reconnect with her now-distant friend Didi (Diocouda Diaoune), a single mother defiantly resisting society’s systemic attempts to confine her. Other women include a former sex worker reflecting on the complexities of her past and a poet who confronts the unspoken grief caused by infertility. Together, these nocturnal denizens give voice to a rare and liberating dialogue, exploring womanhood, motherhood, sexual desire, isolation, class privilege, race, societal malaise, and the delicate nature of family and care.

Exquisitely shot on 16mm by Ben Rivers (Mare’s Nest, TIFF ’25), At Night boldly transcends traditional narrative, opting instead for a form of poetic, collaborative autofiction guided in spirit by cult literary figures like June Jordan, Kathy Acker, Bernadette Mayer, and, especially, Alice Notley. Melding an atmosphere of urban anxiety with moments of tenderness and self-reflection, At Night is equally mesmerizing and melancholic as it shifts between narrative, documentary, and dream.
at-night.teaser: Mesmerizing and melancholic, the much-anticipated debut feature by British filmmaker and artist Beatrice Gibson is a work of choral autofiction that shifts from narrative to documentary to dream over a single night in Paris, reflecting on the nature of womanhood, privilege, and solidarity.

double-freedom.title: Double Freedom
double-freedom.synopsis:
Twenty-five years have elapsed since Argentine auteur Lisandro Alonso’s debut film La libertad emerged as an instant landmark of international cinema. His day-in-the-life portrait of a young man’s humble, solitary, yet seemingly fulfilled life in La Pampa proved to be an invigorating rejection of traditional narrative.

Now, with Double Freedom (La libertad doble), Alonso rejoins the stoic, noticeably older Misael (non-professional Misael Saavedra), still living the same life of cutting and supplying wood, and sheltering in a makeshift abode, surrounded by tall trees shimmering in the blazing sun. Less follow-up or sequel than a sly and clever echo — one need not have seen the first one to experience the wonders here — the film begins where La libertad looped in on itself, with a shirtless Misael enjoying wild game over an open flame. Shot on 35mm in both instances by Cobi Migliora (this time in widescreen), there is a pervasive uncanniness that attends Double Freedom, tethered not only to the large gap in time but also to cinematic memory.

We learn that Misael has a long-institutionalized sister Misaela (Catalina Saavedra, no relation) who will soon be released due to governmental austerity measures forcing the closure of her caretaking clinic, meaning she will require housing and around-the-clock supervision. As each sibling is forced to grapple with their new circumstances, the film’s quietly moving depiction of care invites a meditation on freedom (who has it? how can it be obtained or maintained?) and our complicated contemporary moment, all portrayed with incomparable clarity, grace, and luminous beauty.
double-freedom.teaser: Less follow-up or sequel to his breakout debut than a sly and clever echo, Lisandro Alonso’s graceful and extraordinarily beautiful Double Freedom returns us to the daily life of Misael, a solitary labourer in Argentina’s rural La Pampa.

everything-else-is-noise.title: Everything Else is Noise
everything-else-is-noise.synopsis:
At once a capstone to and departure from his recent string of exceptional work — including Fauna (TIFF ’20), Lázaro de noche (TIFF ’24), and Copper (TIFF ’25) — prolific Mexican-Canadian auteur Nicolás Pereda delivers his sharpest and most amusing film yet with Everything Else is Noise, a sly, self-reflexive comedy of manners and mishaps interrogating the polyvalent nature of noise, both literal and metaphorical, by way of its presumed antithesis: music.

Working again with his preternaturally talented troupe of actors, the filmmaker employs a chamber piece structure (pun intended?), grounded in a trio of women classical composers and musicians. For her interview with a local Mexico City television channel, Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas) has asked to use the cozy, plant-filled apartment of her friend Teresa (Teresita Sánchez) as backdrop.

However, upon the arrival of journalist Lázaro (Lázaro G. Rodríguez) and cameraman Paco (Francisco Barreiro), the production is quickly derailed by the banality of the crew's questions and an escalating series of everyday annoyances, including a cacophony of gridlocked traffic and an interminable barking dog that pervades the otherwise tranquil space. Teresa’s aimless daughter Luisa (Luisa Pardo) is also lurking about, complicating the interlocutors’ lines of enquiry with as much relish as exasperation.

Shot with Pereda’s typically light, practically Lubitschian touch, and an inspiring economy of form, Everything Else is Noise incisively skewers gender biases in the creative fields while exploring the blurred line between reality and performance, as well as the refusal to conform to expectations — be it as a mother, a daughter, or an artist.
everything-else-is-noise.teaser: Prolific Mexican-Canadian auteur Nicolás Pereda has delivered his sharpest and most amusing film yet with Everything Else is Noise, a sly, self-reflexive comedy of manners and mishaps involving a trio of women classical composers and musicians.

life-of-jorge-luis-borges.title: Life of Jorge Luis Borges
life-of-jorge-luis-borges.synopsis:
Few writers of the twentieth century hold a more vaunted position than Jorge Luis Borges, the Argentine literary icon capable of inventing entire worlds within the span of mere pages. His was both a life and a body of work full of forking paths, contractions, paradoxes, mistruths, and generative lacunae, and which couldn’t be better suited for a filmmaker as obsessed with stories as his countryman Mariano Llinás ( La Flor, TIFF ’18).

Self-described as “an attempt to narrate Borges' biography through objects and places,” the starting point of the film is a sizeable collection of material overseen by one Ernesto Montequin, who joins Llinás on his quest as a sidekick and sparring partner.

With the erudition and insight of a literary scholar and the gumption of an amateur detective, the filmmaker travels to New York, Texas, Geneva, Reykjavik, and the rural border of Uruguay and Brazil, working through both biographical episodes as well as major texts like “El Aleph,” “Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius,” and “Death and the Compass.” The film simultaneously broadens to consider Borges’ expanded artistic demimonde — which included writers like Adolfo Bioy Casares and Silvina Ocampo, as well as filmmaker Hugo Santiago — while mapping the writer’s life within Argentina’s political history and in doing so, admirably rises above hagiography to confront Borges’ racism and dalliances with the far right.

Itself deeply Borgesian — full of adventure, curiosity, creativity, and mystery — Life of Jorge Luis Borges is one of the year’s great documentaries that — appropriately — blurs the line between the real and the invented.
life-of-jorge-luis-borges.teaser: With the erudition and insight of a literary scholar and the gumption of an amateur detective, Argentinian auteur (and raconteur) Mariano Llinás (La Flor, TIFF ’18) explores the life and fiction of the legendary writer Jorge Luis Borges through objects and places.

london.title: London
london.synopsis:
A unique and deeply moving entry into the canon of experimental road movies, Sebastian Brameshuber’s award-winning London is a portrait of the elegant and elusive Bobby (Bobby Sommer, Museum Hours TIFF ’12). Grey-haired and at times world-weary, but always affable, he supplements the fuel costs for his trips between Vienna and Salzburg on the iconic West Autobahn by offering rides to strangers through an app.

London transforms this seemingly ordinary succession of commutes into a profound meditation on connection, movement, and the traces people leave on one another, not unlike the marks of history impressed into landscapes. Drawing inspiration in part from James Benning and Bette Gordon’s 1975 avant-garde classic The United States of America, Brameshuber foregrounds the humans whose lives we pass through as much as the places themselves.

Here the liminal zone of the car variously evolves into a confessional, a waiting room, or a refuge, where strangers — played mostly by non-professionals — meet in circumstances that are at once anonymous and intimate. They include an unsettled soldier; a woman preparing for a wedding that her parents reject; and an academic (played by filmmaker Ted Fendt) researching the highway’s Nazi past. With each new passenger, the vehicle becomes a shifting social landscape of existential colloquy, revealing lives shaped by loneliness, hope, grief, desire for freedom, and the uncertainties of the present.

Deceptively simple, richly layered, and produced with an impressive formal prowess — it was meticulously shot in-studio using vintage rear-projection techniques — London is a rare work whose structural artifice reveals the mysteries of the real.
london.teaser: An experimental yet tender road movie about an enigmatic man’s shared commutes across Austria’s scenic West Autobahn — shot in-studio with vintage rear-projection techniques — Sebastian Brameshuber’s award-winning London is a rare work of technical prowess that never belies its emotional core.

my-wife-cries.title: My Wife Cries
my-wife-cries.synopsis:
In several of her finest films, German auteur Angela Schanelec (I Was at Home, But…TIFF ’19; Music, TIFF ’23) traces the lingering effects of shock on the human spirit. It’s a phenomenon she further explores, with tremendous pathos, in My Wife Cries, an understated elegy to the pains of romantic misalignment. Pairing a precise, minimal approach to compositions and style with expressive, logorrheic monologues, Schanelec here trades modern melodrama for emotional distance and anguish in her examination of a marriage in crisis.

Thomas (Vladimir Vulević) receives a midday summons to pick up his wife Carla (Agathe Bonitzer) from the hospital. He finds her weeping outside; she has survived a car crash in which the driver has died. As Carla attempts an aggrieved confession disguised as a plea for affection, Thomas recedes, and the pain of disloyalty shortly manifests itself physically. As the couple strives to make themselves understood — to each other and others — the confines of their love and grief become as straightforward as they do existential.

Shot on wonderfully textured 35mm by talented cinematographer Marius Panduru (who also shot Radu Jude’s Festival Official Selection The Diary of a Chambermaid), My Wife Cries is austere and solemn in tone, yet filled with surprising bursts of life, as the mix of painterly still life compositions and hypnotic tracking shots are punctuated by delightful, eccentric intrusions, such as a rehearsing orchestra in the middle of a park or a choreographed dance scene. As in all of Schanelec’s films, any study of life’s intricacies and disappointments leaves room for unexpected moments of pleasure and beauty.
my-wife-cries.teaser: With My Wife Cries — a startling, minimalist study in romantic misalignment — German auteur and Festival favourite Angela Schanelec employs her singular style to portray the crushing anguish and vertiginous confusion brought forth by marital crisis.

nobodys-violence.title: Nobody's Violence
nobodys-violence.synopsis:
In the over 20 years since the French Canadian director first earned international acclaim for his 2005 feature debut Drifting States, Denis Côté has rarely declined the opportunity to take viewers in a direction they didn’t expect. Yet the filmmaker’s latest is so bold and daring in its shifts in tone and tactic, that Nobody’s Violence may be Côté’s most surprising feature to date.

It also boasts an exceptionally striking lead performance by Larissa Corriveau, the actor whose previous collaborations with the director include Mademoiselle Kenopsia (TIFF ‘23). Corriveau stars as Mira, an enigmatic and largely silent young woman who works for an equally mysterious organization that facilitates requests for euthanasia. Seemingly stone-hearted as she travels from client to client in the film’s eerie dystopian society, Mira nevertheless comes to question her mission after encounters with two unconventional men: Pierric (Xavier Bergeron), a free spirit she meets at a wintry outdoor rave party, and Ludo (Philippe Rebbot), her charismatic and hedonistic boss.

Like these two live wires who come into Mira’s path, Nobody’s Violence exudes a restless, relentless vitality, a quality that only intensifies as the film shape-shifts from sci-fi parable to conspiracy thriller to Buñuelian comedy. Indeed, several scenes — including one set to a vintage banger by Quebec prog-rockers Morse Code — have the electrical charge of a Bacchanalian ritual. It’s therefore hard to imagine a more forceful means of reaffirming Côté’s reputation as one of Canadian cinema’s most reliably exciting talents.

Content: mature themes, violence, coarse language, drug use, sexually suggestive scenes
nobodys-violence.teaser: Larissa Corriveau delivers a striking performance as an enigmatic death-dealer in this bold, bracing, and Buñuelian feature by Denis Côté.

redefined-short-film-showcase.title: REDEFINED | Short Film Showcase
redefined-short-film-showcase.synopsis: Created by the NFB and TIFF, REDEFINED brings together five Canadian and Indigenous filmmakers from across the country to celebrate the differences that unite us and to explore culture, belonging, identity, and sovereign(ties) through personal storytelling. Produced over the course of a year and supported by the NFB’s state-of-the-art tools and mentorship resources, the films offer a powerful portrait of a generation reimagining what Canada is — and what it could become.

the-black-box-is-orange.title: The Black Box is Orange
the-black-box-is-orange.synopsis:
The debut feature by Toronto artist and filmmaker Yuula Benivolski, The Black Box is Orange is a multimodal, autobiographical essay film that deploys both personal memory and incomplete archives to reflect on an upbringing in a militarized border town.

The central locus of the film is the former Palestinian village of al-Bassa, near the Lebanese border, which after the 1948 Nakba became the Israeli town of Shlomi, and where Benivolski spent her childhood and teenage years. Now, from the perspective of adulthood, she unpacks an adolescence spent under the spell of settler ideology by probing the nagging points at which state-mandated and population-supported occlusion meets the frayed fringes of memory.

The film’s ambitious structure consists of 10 dynamic and stylistically distinct chapters. These range from first-person, guided investigations into lingering traces of pre-Israeli infrastructure, to formal plays with contrapuntal sound and image, to hand-processed experiments that wordlessly invoke the colossal weight held in the image of the landscape. While certain chapters are deeply researched and nearly scholarly in nature, the majority are raw, personal, and bravely confessional. One constant, however, is an astute balance between a sense of politics and poetics, with the latter elevated through the use of textured 16mm and an exceptionally refined sound design.

A film not just several years in development, but one could say a lifetime, The Black Box is Orange reckons with grand questions of place, belonging, responsibility, memory, and narratives — situating them in an urgent present as much as the past — with both moral clarity and artistic sophistication.
the-black-box-is-orange.teaser: The debut feature by Toronto artist and filmmaker Yuula Benivolski, The Black Box is Orange is a multimodal, autobiographical essay film that deploys both personal memory and incomplete archives to reflect on a childhood in a militarized border town.

the-remotes.title: The Remotes
the-remotes.synopsis:
In 2019, TIFF welcomed noted Filipino auteur John Torres to Wavelengths with his short We Still Have to Close Our Eyes, an experimental hybrid which employed documentary footage captured behind the scenes on the sets of Filipino feature films (including one belonging to Lav Diaz) to craft an eerie, speculative story about app-controlled human avatars.

Now Torres returns with The Remotes, a stylish, ambitious, and mournful narrative expansion of the short’s initial concept. Employing the armature of a greater budget and professional actors, the film interrogates insidious mechanisms of control, including state surveillance and tech platforms, as well as wraithlike expressions of generational anguish.

The premise revolves around a voice-guided system designed to “retrain” reckless drivers, but which may be more sinister than it seems. When the grieving Detective Mijares arrives to investigate a number of unusual road incidents, he becomes entangled with the enigmatic sisters Eva and Gill Cantero, each navigating their own losses and sorrows. Together, the three find themselves caught up in a mystery in which nothing — even one’s sense of self — feels at all secure.

Largely taking place after dark and replete with sinuous, hypnotic night drives, the film captures the spectral neon regions just beyond Manila in the claws of light. Spacious and elliptical in its exploration of post-colonial grief and increasing automation, The Remotes borrows liberally from the conventions of sci-fi, noir, the police procedural, and the gloss of commercial Filipino cinema, while subverting and reimagining each through Torres’ signature poetic sensibility and vision.
the-remotes.teaser: This ambitious, beguiling narrative debut from acclaimed Filipino filmmaker and experimentalist John Torres follows a grieving detective who finds himself increasingly ensnared while investigating a case involving a sinister navigation app causing physical and psychological debris.

wavelengths-1-house-and-home.title: Wavelengths 1: House and Home
wavelengths-1-house-and-home.synopsis:
Across these six films the nature of an abode is examined through its connections with privilege, family, memory, objects, and state control. Reflecting on shelters both fixed and temporary, these films explore the limits of refuge and the connection between people and place.

A coda to his 2024 Festival selection Being John Smith and a rumination-in-miniature, Two Pids is English avant-garde legend John Smith’s reflection on the fleeting roles we play and the temporary places we occupy. In the elegant, dreamlike After Image, local filmmaker Rita Ferrando similarly considers her family’s history of migration by way of archival fragments and a conversation across time with her artist grandfather.

Family is also the core of Moon Palace by Chinese filmmaker Jiaqi Yu. Both grounded and cosmic, the film conjures a (non-)space that connects his loved ones across different realms. Yu’s open, porous space is contrasted with Danaya Chulphuthiphong’s examination of enclosure, with her poetic, tactile Microcosmic Orbit: Encased presenting containers of both plants and people, asking how such barriers might not only protect but stifle.

The titular index in The Address Book, by Montreal-based Turkish artist Mustafa Uzuner, belonged to the American iconoclast artist and recluse Joseph Cornell, and as we progress through its pages it not only figuratively maps out a constellation of artists — among them Yayoi Kusama and Carolee Schneemann — but also their geographical location in mid-century Manhattan.

The programme closes with Natalia Marín’s quietly yet resolutely incensed Chronicle of Tiredness, tracing the connections between capitalism, precarious housing, gendered discrimination, and intergenerational poverty in an urgent defence of the chronically exploited.

wavelengths-2-this-suffocating-now.title: Wavelengths 2: This Suffocating Now
wavelengths-2-this-suffocating-now.synopsis:
Bookended by films that examine the possibilities and limits of artistic refusal, this programme speaks to the political potential of creative work, creative scenes, and companionship.

In Maryam Tafakory’s Ghazal-e Sorkh, the artist returns to the Festival with a layered, lucid essay film that connects national, international, and personal histories, incorporating narrative fragments, documentaries, and industrial cinema to recount the 1976 boycott of the Shiraz Art Festival.

In TM, a newly rediscovered 8mm gem by legendary Fluxus artist and composer Takehisa Kosugi, the skies and trees in a Tokyo park are filmed through playful, lyrical in-camera effects. Effectively unseen since 1974, this new restoration by Collaborative Cataloging Japan reveals Kosugi as an unsung polymath who regrettably never pursued the form further.

Kosugi’s sunlit, sylvan experiment is balanced by Zheng Lu Xinyuan’s nocturnal Fire Flies, in which the filmmaker is led on a flashlight-illuminated stroll through the mountains — with the green, digital images of a night vision camera capturing flora, fauna, and distant stars.

Balancing paranoia with an affirming sense of social and artistic solidarity, Simon Liu’s eerie, enveloping Splits in Two takes influence from Cantonese Ghost Stories as it parses both the physical and figurative landscape of contemporary Hong Kong, a city whose underground art scene persists as a larger cultural identity risks dissipation.

The programme ends with This Suffocating Now, a vital, visceral short, in which artist Vika Kirchenbauer exploits tensions — between sound and silence, between moving and still images — to level a direct accusation against the hypocrisies of life in contemporary Germany.

wavelengths-3-time-and-tide.title: Wavelengths 3: Time and Tide
wavelengths-3-time-and-tide.synopsis:
Bridging eras, epochs, and the cosmos, this programme brings together new works by three major artists and a tribute to a recently departed legend, each reflecting on the fluid nature of time and its passing.

Shot on 65mm film using a self-constructed camera and projected on a 70mm print, Forever…Forever by Austrian experimentalist Johann Lurf captures a year of days, nights, passing clouds, and flowing water. Dedicated at once to the artist’s late father and newborn son, the film rises above formalism to offer a deeply felt reflection on time as fleeting and eternal. Perspective and permanence also inform Ben Russell’s playful La Prospettiva (1653), filmed in the Colonnade at the Palazzo Spada in Rome, capturing the central composition of the Baroque illusionism masterpiece but also modest moments of the labour dedicated to its upkeep.

Next, we pay homage to the recently departed Armenian-Italian artist Yervant Gianikian, whose work with Angela Ricci Lucchi offered an invaluable contribution to world cinema writ large, and to the history of Wavelengths in particular. In their 2001 piece, Electric Fragments No. 1 - Rom (Men), 8mm footage documenting a Roma family’s migration across Italy trades a cold ethnographic regard for one of pathos.

The programme concludes with James Richards’ Fevers. Taking as his starting point — less by way of invocation than summoning — the text from Marguerite Duras’ Les Mains négatives and Tony Conrad’s The Flicker, Richards weaves together stirring fragments composed over the last four years, including repurposed material from friends and collaborators — like Wavelengths alum Steve Reinke — to produce a haunting reflection on the present-day.

wavelengths-anoushahpour-aljafari.title: Wavelengths: Anoushahpour/Aljafari
wavelengths-anoushahpour-aljafari.synopsis:
Bringing together new work by Parastoo Anoushahpour (The Time that Separates Us, TIFF ’22) and Kamal Aljafari (With Hasan in Gaza, TIFF ’25), this programme’s two films reflect on the meeting point between imagination and memory — both personal and collective — as experienced from the perspective of children and the aged.

Shot in multiple Kurdish-majority villages on the border of Iran and Turkmenistan, and edited over the past decade, the starting point of Anoushahpour’s Peacocks Come with the Clouds is a series of elegant wedding embroideries. Anoushahpour invokes these precious objects by way of workshops with local children, whose (re)interpretations of their images expand and evolve with a sense of wonder. Meanwhile, the filmmaker similarly expands the frame, folding in moments of life around these villages — including farm fields and slaughterhouses — offering a portrait of a place where history and narratives appear at once fixed and malleable.

The film is paired with Palestinian filmmaker Aljafari’s Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo. In 2000, Adachi, one of Japan’s great maverick artists, was deported back to his homeland after 27 years of exile — including three inside a Lebanese prison — having initially travelled to the country in support of the Palestinian liberation struggle. Upon his repatriation his passport was swiftly confiscated and, in the decades since, all efforts to obtain a new one have been summarily refused. As the title suggests, Aljafari’s understated documentary observes the octogenarian’s final attempt to attain this vital document. Unhurried and attuned to the minute details of the long-running photo studio — particularly its charming matron — the film offers an invaluable audience with a truly singular figure.
